text:
The “You” in the Machine: Manipulation, Social Media, and the Limits of Free Speech.

Let’s start with something you’ve probably noticed without having a name for it. You put on a video about Carl Jung, and within a minute the narrator is talking straight to you. You’ve always felt different. You see through people. You hide your real self to keep the peace. It feels personal, almost like being recognized. But that video was made once and shown to millions of people.

Today’s lecture asks four questions. What is going on in that moment? How do modern platforms change it? When a society protects free speech, where does persuasion become dangerous enough for the law to step in? And what can you do about the large territory the law leaves alone?

Before we start, a warning. This lecture is going to say “you” to you the whole way through, and by the end you’ll know how to check whether it earned the right to.

Part one is the techniques.

The first technique is synthetic personalization. The linguist Norman Fairclough named it in his nineteen eighty-nine book, Language and Power. It means addressing a mass audience as though each person were being spoken to alone. Advertisers have done this for a century: you deserve a break, you’ve earned this. It turns a broadcast into something that feels like a conversation. And a speaker who seems to be talking with you seems to know you, which quietly gives them authority over you.

The second technique is the Forer effect, also called the Barnum effect. In nineteen forty-eight the psychologist Bertram Forer gave his students what he said were personal personality profiles, based on a test they had taken. Every student actually got the same paragraph, put together largely from an astrology book he’d bought at a newsstand. Asked how well it described them on a scale topping out at five, the class averaged about four and a quarter. The paragraph used statements that fit almost anyone. You have a great need for other people to like and admire you. You can be critical of yourself. You have a great deal of unused potential. Statements like these feel specific, but they aren’t.

Here is something the usual telling of the Forer story leaves out, and I think it explains why the trick works so well. In English, the word “you” does two jobs. Sometimes it means you, the specific person I’m talking to. Sometimes it means anyone at all, as in “you can’t win them all.” Linguists call the second one the generic you. In twenty seventeen, the psychologists Ariana Orvell, Ethan Kross, and Susan Gelman reported in the journal Science that people use the generic you to state norms, things true of people in general. They also found that people reach for it when they’re trying to make sense of something painful. Saying “you” instead of “I” lets a person treat a bad experience as part of the human condition rather than a private failure. In a later paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the same three researchers found that readers feel more connection to passages written in the generic you. On Kindle, readers highlighted those passages more often.

Now put that next to Forer. A Barnum statement is a generic-you sentence dressed as a specific-you sentence. “You have a great need for others to like you” is true as a statement about people. Delivered to you personally, it lands as an insight about you. The listener hears the warmth of being understood that comes with the generic you, and the flattery of being singled out that comes with the specific you, at the same time. That double meaning is the engine of a large share of self-help, astrology, and pop psychology content.

The third mechanism is the self-reference effect. Memory researchers have studied it since Rogers, Kuiper, and Kirker named it in nineteen seventy-seven. People remember information better when they process it in relation to themselves. So the word “you” does more than set a tone. It makes the message stick.

Sticking isn’t the same as believing, though, and the step between them matters. The best-documented route from hearing something to believing it is repetition. In nineteen seventy-seven, Lynn Hasher and her colleagues showed that repeating a plausible statement raises how true people judge it to be. It’s now called the illusory truth effect. Most researchers think it works through fluency: a statement you’ve met before is easier to process, and ease feels like truth. In twenty fifteen, Lisa Fazio and her colleagues found the effect even for statements that people’s own knowledge should have contradicted. People leaned on the feeling of ease and set aside what they knew. So keep two mechanisms apart. Self-reference makes a message memorable. Repetition makes it feel true. And as we’ll see in part two, the feed supplies the repetition.

One more finding marks the edge of all this, and it’s useful. “You” isn’t always persuasive. The marketing researchers Mohamed Hussein and Zakary Tormala, in a paper called You Versus We, studied messages in conflict: workplace disputes, political arguments, online forums. In those settings, messages using “you” came across as aggressive. They were less persuasive, less likely to be shared, and more likely to be censored than the same messages written with “we.” In an analysis of more than a quarter of a million online comments, “you” raised the odds that a moderator removed a comment. So “you” persuades when it’s warm and repels when it accuses. That’s why the manipulative “you” you meet in your feed is almost always flattering. The accusing version gets ignored or deleted.

A fair-minded listener should notice that none of these techniques is dishonest in itself. A good teacher says “you” constantly. So does a drill sergeant, and so does a coach. Second-person address can be the clearest way to teach, and the generic you, as we just saw, is one of the ways people make sense of hard things. The difference between teaching and manipulation is what the “you” is attached to. Ask three questions. Would the statement be true of almost anyone? Does it flatter you by saying you’re rare, gifted, or one of the few who understand? Does it lead somewhere, like a course, a subscription, or a reason to keep watching? When all three answers are yes, the technique is working for the creator, not for you.

Part two is how the platforms amplify it.

These techniques are old. What’s new is the delivery system, and on one point we now have measurements instead of guesses. In twenty seventeen, the marketing researchers Ryan Cruz, James Leonhardt, and Todd Pezzuti studied real brand posts on Facebook and then ran two experiments. Posts that addressed the reader with “you” drew more involvement and better attitudes toward the brand. Their explanation was the self-reference effect from part one: “you” makes readers process the message in relation to themselves. So the chain from the second person, to self-reference, to engagement has been observed on a real platform, not just in a lab.

Now add the feed. A modern feed doesn’t show you what’s true or what’s important. It mostly shows you what people like you kept watching and reacting to. Relatable, flattering, second-person content holds attention. Attention earns reach, and reach earns money. A creator doesn’t have to set out to manipulate anyone. They only have to notice which videos do well and make more of them, and their imitators do the same. Over time the system selects for the technique, the way a river cuts a channel without meaning to. That account is reasoning built from the pieces I’ve described. Nobody has measured the whole chain from start to finish, so hold it as a well-supported model, not a finding.

The feed also supplies the repetition. The same message comes back again and again, from the same creator and from a hundred imitators using the same phrases. That’s the condition the illusory truth research says turns familiar claims into believed ones.

How common is misleading personalized content? I looked for a study that counts the word “you” across whole platforms and didn’t find one. The counts that exist are narrower, like the Facebook brand posts. The best evidence on the content itself comes from mental health advice, which is where Jung-style videos usually sit. In twenty twenty-five, the Guardian asked psychologists and psychiatrists to review the hundred most popular videos under a mental health tips hashtag on TikTok. They judged fifty-two of them to contain misinformation. Some of those videos took ordinary emotions and labeled them as symptoms of illness. That’s the Barnum effect with clinical vocabulary added. In twenty twenty-two, a telehealth company called PlushCare reviewed five hundred such videos and put the misleading share above four in five. But PlushCare sells appointments with doctors and therapists, so its number deserves more caution. The fair summary: misleading, personalized persuasion is common in popular advice content, but we don’t have a clean measure of how common.

Part three is the legal line.

Now the harder question. If manipulation is everywhere, why not ban it? In the United States, the First Amendment answers that, and the line it draws is narrower than most people expect.

First, clear away a myth. People often say you can’t shout fire in a crowded theater. The line comes from Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes in a nineteen nineteen case, Schenck versus United States. The government had jailed Charles Schenck for mailing about fifteen thousand leaflets urging men to resist the military draft. The “clear and present danger” test from that era was used to imprison critics of the war. The theater line was an aside, and it has been stretched far beyond its context ever since. The test behind it was overruled half a century later.

The case that overruled it is Brandenburg versus Ohio, from nineteen sixty-nine. A Ku Klux Klan leader gave a filmed speech at a rally that included talk of “revengeance,” the word he actually used. The Supreme Court overturned his conviction and set the test still used today. The government can punish advocacy of force or lawbreaking only when it’s directed at inciting imminent lawless action and is likely to produce it. Abstract advocacy, however ugly, is protected. A crowd being aimed at a target right now is not. Notice who the speaker was in that case. The protection that covers your speech also covered his, and that was deliberate.

The second major line is true threats. In Counterman versus Colorado, in twenty twenty-three, a man had sent hundreds of unwanted Facebook messages to a local singer over about two years. The Court held that to convict someone for a threat, the state must show the speaker at least consciously disregarded a substantial risk that the words would be taken as a threat of violence. That’s a recklessness standard. It asks about the speaker’s state of mind, not just how the words landed.

Beyond those two, the Court has listed only a few historic categories of speech the government may restrict for their content. In United States versus Stevens, in twenty ten, it named obscenity, defamation, fraud, incitement, and speech integral to criminal conduct. It also refused to add new categories just because a kind of speech seems to do more harm than good. Two years later, in United States versus Alvarez, the Court made a point that matters directly for our Jung video: there is no general exception for false statements. Flattery, vague psychology, misleading advice, and one-sided persuasion generally fall outside every category. Under American law, the video that keeps telling you who you are is protected speech. The line moves only when the “you” is selling something with a knowingly false claim, because then fraud comes into view.

There’s a second layer people often miss: the platforms themselves. YouTube and TikTok are private companies. In Moody versus NetChoice, in twenty twenty-four, a majority of the Court wrote that when a platform curates its main feed, it is engaging in its own expression. That suggests the government can’t simply order a platform to carry content it doesn’t want to carry. Be careful with that ruling, though. Its binding part only sent the cases back to the lower courts, and legal scholars still argue over how much of the reasoning will hold.

The pressure can run the other way too, with officials leaning on platforms to take content down. In the same year, in National Rifle Association versus Vullo, a unanimous Court held that officials may not coerce private companies into suppressing speech the officials dislike. But in Murthy versus Missouri, the case about federal officials pressing social media companies, the Court dismissed the suit because the challengers lacked standing. It never decided where persuading a platform ends and coercing it begins. So in practice, the everyday moderation of manipulative content happens through each company’s own rules, which they write, enforce, and change as they see fit.

Part four is the debate.

So where should the dangerous borderline be? Reasonable people split three ways, not two, and I’ll give each side its best case in its own voice. Each will also say what would change its mind.

The first side wants to keep the line narrow. It says: whoever gets the power to decide what counts as manipulation will eventually be someone you disagree with. Speech laws written against one group have a way of being used against another, and the Schenck era is the proof. The Court in Alvarez warned against handing government a list of topics on which false statements can be punished, because such a list has no natural stopping point. Ordinary speech is full of persuasion. Outlaw manipulative technique and you hand prosecutors a tool that fits almost anything, this lecture included. The better answer is more speech, sharper audiences, and skills like the ones in part five. What would change this side’s mind is a narrow rule about platform design, one that never touches the content of speech, that measurably reduces harm and isn’t turned against unpopular speakers.

The second side wants to regulate the machinery. It says: the law was built for soapboxes and pamphlets. A feed that pushes one creator to millions of people, tuned by software to each viewer’s habits, is a different kind of thing. Its supporters mostly don’t want to ban speech. They want rules for the system that distributes it: disclose how content is ranked, offer a feed that isn’t personalized, audit for systemic risks. The European Union’s Digital Services Act leans that way. Every online platform must explain in plain language the main factors its recommendations use. The very largest platforms must also offer at least one feed option not based on profiling, assess their systemic risks, and submit to independent audits. This side’s strongest evidence is new. In twenty twenty-six, the economists Germain Gauthier, Roland Hodler, Philine Widmer, and Ekaterina Zhuravskaya published a field experiment in Nature. About five thousand American users of X were randomly assigned to the algorithmic feed or the chronological one for seven weeks in twenty twenty-three. Switching the algorithm on increased engagement and shifted users’ political opinions in a more conservative direction, especially on which issues they ranked as priorities. What would change this side’s mind is evidence that ranking changes how long people stay and what they see, but not what they believe.

The third side rejects something the first two share: the assumption that the feed is what pushes bad persuasion onto passive viewers. Its clearest statement is a twenty twenty-four review in Nature by Ceren Budak, Brendan Nyhan, David Rothschild, Emily Thorson, and Duncan Watts. They say three popular beliefs outrun the evidence: that the average person sees a lot of false or inflammatory content, that algorithms are mostly responsible for that exposure, and that social media is a primary cause of problems like polarization. Their review found exposure to such content low for most people and concentrated among a narrow fringe strongly motivated to seek it out. This side points to an earlier field experiment. In twenty twenty-three, Andrew Guess and a large team, working with Meta during the twenty twenty election, switched thousands of Facebook and Instagram users to a chronological feed for three months. What people saw changed a great deal, and they spent much less time on the platforms. But their polarization, political knowledge, and other key attitudes did not change significantly. On this view, the problem is demand: people who go looking for this content will find it, whatever the feed does. What would change this side’s mind is a large, well-designed field experiment showing that the algorithm moves the beliefs of ordinary users, not just a motivated fringe.

That brings us to the claim all three sides would switch on: does a feed’s ranking change what people believe, or only what they see and how long they stay? Both big experiments bear on it, and together they show something neither shows alone. Gauthier and colleagues tested the switch in both directions. Turning the algorithm on shifted opinions. Turning it off had no comparable effect. Their explanation: the algorithm led users to follow conservative political activist accounts, and users kept following them after the algorithm was gone. So the Meta experiment and the X experiment may not contradict each other. The Meta study only switched the algorithm off, for people who had already lived with it for years. If the X result holds, switching off was the wrong test. The algorithm’s effect lives in who you end up following, and that outlasts the algorithm itself.

Each side has to concede something to that. The narrow-line side has to concede that “more speech” doesn’t answer an effect that persists through a person’s follow list. The machinery side has to concede that its signature remedy, a feed not based on profiling, is exactly the switch-off condition that showed little effect. If regulation is going to work, the lever is probably earlier: what an algorithm does when it’s first switched on, and whom it leads people to follow. And the third side has to concede that the X result is the kind of evidence it said would change its mind, though one experiment on one platform over seven weeks doesn’t settle the question. One caution covers all of this. These studies measured political attitudes, not belief in pop psychology. Applying them to the Jung video is a reasonable inference, not a finding.

All three sides generally agree that incitement and true threats belong on the dangerous side of the line. The open question is everything below it. So far, that’s being settled more by platform policy and individual judgment than by law.

Part five is the defense you can carry.

The most common reply to everything I’ve said is: sure, but it doesn’t work on me. Researchers have a name for that reply. In nineteen eighty-three, the sociologist W. Phillips Davison described the third-person effect: people expect persuasive messages to influence others more than themselves. It has held up in more than eighty published studies and a meta-analysis. Remember Forer’s students. Every one of them rated the same horoscope paragraph as a close fit for themselves. Feeling immune is part of how the technique works. So the defense has to be a habit, not a feeling.

Here’s the drill. When a video tells you who you are, swap “you” for “everyone” and see if the sentence still works. You’re turning a disguised generic you back into an honest one. If the sentence still works, it was a statement about people in general dressed up as an insight about you. That doesn’t make it worthless. It just isn’t about you.

When a video flatters you, ask what it wants from you next. When it turns hostile and says you’re the problem, notice that this is the same tool aimed the other way. It usually wants you angry enough to share it.

When it makes a specific claim, like a diagnosis, a statistic, or a quote from Jung, treat that as the checkable part and check it.

And one habit the research in part four suggests: if a feed’s lasting effect runs through who you follow, then who you follow is the part you control. Every so often, go through that list and ask how each account got there.

Run that drill on this lecture too. It has said “you” from the first sentence. Some of those were the honest generic kind. A few were me trying to keep your attention. A lecture that holds up under those questions has earned your attention. One that doesn’t hasn’t.

That’s the lecture. The techniques are old, and they work best when they flatter. The platforms reward them at scale, and the newest evidence suggests a feed’s influence can outlast the feed itself. American law draws its hard line only at imminent incitement, true threats, and a few narrow categories. Everything above that line is left to the platforms, to an open scientific question about what feeds actually do to belief, and to each viewer.

text:
Elon Musk sat for an interview Wednesday and didn’t sugarcoat anything. On Nvidia forcing out Jensen Huang, he said, “I don’t think he’s disloyal to the United States.” He called it a horrible move, comparing it to the Chicago Bulls kicking Michael Jordan off the team: “Doesn’t seem like a smart decision to me.” He’s right. Huang built Nvidia into the AI chip leader through decades of supply-chain mastery and technical depth.

“His team loves him. Loves him.” Forcing him out is the kind of shortsighted boardroom nonsense that tanks companies. Many on his team have turned down higher offers elsewhere out of personal loyalty. You don’t replace that overnight, and the board’s decision looks worse the more you look at it.

Musk said he would love to hire Huang and has spoken to him. “Who wouldn’t? He’s incredibly talented. He’s one of the most talented entrepreneurial CEOs in history.” That’s not flattery. It’s recognition of a rare operator. But “Jensen’s not looking for a job.” Nvidia’s board rejected his return, so shareholders would need to vote them out. “That’s pretty rare.” A petition with nearly 200,000 signatures, including more than 10,000 current employees, shows the board is fighting its own people. Musk is offering competence while Nvidia’s board plays politics.

On the 2026 midterms, Musk said, “I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it, or maybe it would have been much worse without that.” He put at least $445 million behind Republicans. “I didn’t put a lot of personal attention into it because I’m focused on building SpaceX, Tesla.” That’s the honest take. He prioritized actual production over political theater. The results were disappointing, but at least he owned the outcome instead of spinning it.

Musk also addressed Democrats talking about lawfare against him. “They’re trying to channel Beria from Stalin! ‘Show me the man, I’ll show you the crime!’” He said, “I don’t need a pardon because I haven’t committed any crimes.” A Texas Democrat, Gene Wu, said Musk should go to prison but couldn’t name a crime. “It needs to be first crime, then prison! Not the other way around!” That’s the standard any functional justice system requires. Democrats keep skipping the crime part because they don’t have one.

On Ukraine and Starlink, Musk said he just wants peace. “Thousands of kids are sent in to die every day with no change in the borders, forever. And I think anyone who supports that is a horrible human being or has not thought through the problem.” He’s correct. Endless stalemate is not a strategy. “There is no private individual who has helped Ukraine more than I have. I made sure that Starlink was in Ukraine, pre-positioned, ahead of the Russian invasion.” When Russia disabled communications, Starlink was the one system they couldn’t shut down. Without it, “their entire line would have collapsed.”

Starlink is not for offensive drone strikes. That requires Starshield under US government control. Zelensky’s complaints ignore the facts. Musk spent Wednesday defending competence, rejecting lawfare without evidence, and calling out a war that keeps killing without progress. He prioritizes results over narrative. That’s why the usual critics are mad.

text:
Grok Bot summary of Elon Musk's interview at DealBook Summit today.

Jensen Huang Situation
• Elon calls Jensen an old friend and "like Michael Jordan at his peak level."
• He says firing him is like the Chicago Bulls cutting Jordan in the middle of a winning streak: "Doesn't seem like a smart decision to me."
• He says no one can replace Jensen. Jensen does the work of several people: he runs the supply chain, eats street food in Korea and Taiwan with key suppliers, and has decades-long relationships.
• Jensen's team loves him, and many stayed out of loyalty even when they had higher offers elsewhere.
• Jensen made some mistakes, Elon says, but he doesn't think Jensen is disloyal to the United States.
• He calls it a mistake that's bad for shareholders.

Would Hire Jensen
• Asked if he'd hire Jensen: "Of course, but who wouldn't?" He calls him one of the most talented entrepreneur CEOs in history.
• He says Jensen is still somewhat stunned, like when a George R. R. Martin story suddenly kills off a main character.
• What happens next is up to the board, and shareholders voting the board out is rare.
• The President has also said publicly that Jensen should have stayed as CEO.

Midterms Loss Reaction
• Elon expects Texas's new Democratic governor to be fairly moderate and thinks Texas will be fine.

Balance Of Power
• He says the presidency, Senate and House generally shouldn't all belong to one party.
• His goal of a 51-seat Republican Senate failed, and Republicans were routed.
• He feels "pretty foolish" for spending so much money and getting little for it, though he says it might have been worse without it.
• He says it shows American elections aren't just about money. He'd spend less if he could do it again, and his focus was on SpaceX and Tesla anyway.

No Pardon Needed
• On being told to "lawyer up," and on the President offering a pardon, he says he hasn't committed any crimes.
• He says one Texas politician called for him to go to prison but couldn't name a crime.
• His line: "It really needs to be first crime, then prison, not the other way around."

Politics Involvement
• His motive was simple: keep at least one of the House, Senate or presidency Republican so there's no Democratic supermajority.
• He doesn't want a Republican supermajority either. He wants checks and balances.

Not MAGA Views
• "I'm not MAGA." He says he's quite moderate, and he challenges the host to name one extreme view he holds.
• He says politics is tribal, like cheering for a hometown sports team, and both parties have good and bad points.
• On Europe, he says it needs to stop massive illegal immigration and vet arrivals. He notes that Obama and Hillary said similar things 10 to 15 years ago.

Starlink Saved Ukraine
• He says no private individual has helped Ukraine more than he has.
• He put Starlink in Ukraine before the invasion. When Russia knocked out cell towers, fiber and every other satellite system, only Starlink kept working.
• He says that without Starlink the front would have collapsed, and it's still the backbone of Ukraine's military communications today.
• Starlink is civilian and not for offensive drone strikes. That's Starshield's job, and the US government controls Starshield.
• He says he won't make kill decisions as a private individual, and he calls the pressure to do so "outrageous."
• Starlink has a speed limit of about 80 mph, the top road speed in Ukraine.
• He says thousands of kids dying with no change in the borders troubles him morally, and he feels empathy for conscripts on both sides.
• He calls Russia the aggressor but says SpaceX cut about two-thirds of Russia's space business and he has no business in Russia.

Zelensky Not Truthful
• On Zelensky saying Ukraine's Starshield use was slowed down, Elon says that's false and that Zelensky "is not always truthful."
• He says Zelensky really wants to use Starlink for offensive operations, and SpaceX has refused from day one. "End of story."

Starlink Vs Starshield
• Starlink is a commercial, civilian network built to help people.
• Starshield is under the US government, and how it's used is up to the War Department.

Power Of One Person
• The host says many people, including Canada's Mark Carney, think it's too much power for one person to be able to switch a service on or off during a war, and some want to diversify away from Starlink.

Rules Unchanged
• Elon says these claims are "both deliberate lies and a lack of understanding." The rules haven't changed since the start.
• He says Starlink was never turned off. Walter Isaacson's book got this wrong, and Isaacson admits it.
• He says Starlink beams were never on over Crimea, because Russia is sanctioned and turning them on would have needed State Department approval.

Open Source Rockets
• On his "monopoly on space": SpaceX only files patents to protect itself.
• He tells people to copy SpaceX. There's a rocket outside HQ in Hawthorne, and "you could measure it and copy it." He won't sue anyone who does.
• Tesla did the same when it opened up all its patents.

Starlink Funds Starship
• Starlink pays for advanced rockets like Starship.
• It brings fast internet to rural schools, hospitals and rescue groups, and he thinks it may have saved hundreds of lives.
• Its long-term purpose is to fund self-sustaining cities on the Moon and Mars.

Multiplanetary Future
• Nuclear war, meteors, super volcanoes and engineered viruses mean extinction is a matter of "when, not if." He calls going multiplanetary "life insurance for everything."
• What excites him more is exploring new star systems, "boldly go where no one has gone before," and maybe finding aliens.

Direct To Cell Plan
• The plan is coverage everywhere on Earth, including on ordinary phones.
• The Direct to Cell V2 satellites start launching next year with about 40 times the bandwidth of V1, and they work with a normal phone.
• To fix weak indoor signal, SpaceX will use its 800 MHz spectrum for "micro ground stations," tiny cell towers that sit on your roof like a Starlink dish. They go into production next year.
• He doesn't think AT&T and Verizon will go out of business, because robots and superintelligence will need huge amounts of bandwidth.

SpaceX Tesla Merger
• He says both paths are possible and "synergy" is overused.
• AI is pulling the two companies together. Tesla does real-world AI like FSD and Optimus, SpaceX does large AI models, and both design chips.
• He predicts AI compute will scale in orbit until orbital compute is close to 100% of it.
• Would they be better together? "Probably yes," but it's up to shareholders, and he won't push SpaceX shareholders into a bad deal.

No Merger Bonus
• "I don't think I should be compensated with any kind of award just for doing a merger." He says that would be unreasonable.
• His Tesla pay award is for Tesla's performance, and he says to "keep your deals and stay true to your word."

Model YL Demand
• The host has ordered a Model YL and is still waiting. Elon calls it probably the most popular car.
• He says Tesla should probably switch all Model Y production to the YL.

Cybercab And AVs
• Cybercab seats two, which covers about 90% of passenger miles, since the average car carries about 1.2 people.
• For groups of six or seven, there will be an autonomous Model Y with no steering wheel or pedals.

Anthropic Compute Deal
• "No one I met at Anthropic set off my evil detector."
• The deals are short term. Either side can end them, and Anthropic has to give three to six months' notice. He'd pull out if Anthropic did something terrible for the world.
• Anthropic wants significantly more compute, most likely an extra 10 gigawatts from SpaceX. "That's a big number."
• "I kind of like the guys, to be honest."

text:
If I'm going to do this, I might as well go all in. Welcome to my verified account.

@msdemocrats @itawambadems

I'm considering running as a Democrat for Mississippi House District 19 in 2027. I hope others step forward, too. Nobody should win public office simply because nobody bothered to challenge them.

For now, AI-generated images will have to suffice for campaign materials. I'm developing my platform, encouraging others to run, and currently serving as my entire campaign team.

Am I a perfect candidate? Hell no. I won't pretend otherwise.

I grew up on a family farm in northeast Mississippi. I started working at the Country Inn when I was 12 and continued nearly every weekend for decades. Summers meant construction work with my father. My mother worked for years as an assistant teacher at Mantachie.

I've traveled, lived in other states, visited other countries, and spent time living in NYC. But Ozark, Kirkville, and these red clay hills have always been home.

I have deep roots here, and I have no intention of pretending to be someone I'm not.

I live with disabilities, and I intend to be a passionate advocate for disability rights. Disabilities should never disqualify someone from public service. My experiences have given me firsthand knowledge of the struggles many Mississippians face.

I oppose efforts to weaken SNAP and other social safety-net programs. Mississippi's TANF welfare scandal demonstrated why public money demands accountability. Celebrity and political connections should never determine who benefits from funds intended for our poorest residents.

Mississippi needs a helping hand, not a hand helping itself to millions.

The historic election of @scott_colom shows that political change is possible. I hope it encourages more ordinary Mississippians to consider public service.

In 2023, Republican incumbent Randy Boyd ran unopposed in District 19 and received 6,390 votes. Those voters had no opposing candidate on the ballot.

Maybe I'll receive one vote. Maybe thousands. I don't know, and I won't pretend otherwise.

But I believe the people deserve a choice.

Real people are needed. Not perfect people. No seat should be surrendered by default.

Let me make something perfectly clear.

I own every statement I've made on this account. I'm not deleting my foul language, my jokes, or my opinions to manufacture some sanitized political personality.

Freedom of speech matters to me. If I've offended you, you're free to tell me exactly what you think. I'll defend your right to speak just as firmly as my own.

That commitment extends to our constitutional rights, including the Second Amendment. I'm a lifelong gun owner and support both the U.S. and Mississippi Constitutions.

You don't have to agree with me, like me, or vote for me. I don't expect everyone to. But you deserve to know who I actually am.

As things develop, I'll establish an official campaign account. Until then, this remains my personal account.

To everyone in District 19 and the surrounding communities: Tell me what matters to you. What problems are being ignored? What needs to change in Jackson?

I'll listen, and I'll answer as openly as I can.

I'm one person. No campaign staff. No political machine. No illusions about being perfect.

But I'm willing to step forward.

And I hope others will, too.

Thanks!

Rev. Bentley W. Chism, D.D., Ph.D. (hon.)

text:
**Peltola just cleared 50% first-choice votes in Alaska two weeks after Election Day, flipping the last Senate seat and locking Democrats at 56-44 while Trump’s party watches from the minority.**[[1]](https://t.co/61fXhjJUIW)

[Take 6/15 · D-1]
### 1. The Frame
**What people think this is about:** A historic upset in a Trump +13 state where a popular Alaska Native Democrat ousted a two-term Republican incumbent in the final 2026 midterm race, completing a blue wave that delivered Democrats their largest Senate majority in years.

**What the machinery is actually doing:** Democrats executed a targeted recruitment and ground game in a low-turnout, high-logistics state with ranked-choice voting and a controversial spoiler candidate; Republicans absorbed the loss in a seat they had held since 2015 while facing a broader midterm backlash that flipped nine GOP seats total.

### 2. Observations
- Peltola won outright with 50.1% first preferences (roughly 141k votes to Sullivan’s 130k), bypassing ranked-choice redistribution entirely once late ballots pushed her over the threshold on Nov 17.[[2]](https://t.co/xRXkl37Hmu)
- The race featured a near-identical-name independent spoiler (Dan J. Sullivan) who drew ~1.7% after advancing from the top-four primary; allegations surfaced that Peltola campaign staff helped recruit him, prompting a state investigation and a dismissed DOJ lawsuit.[[3]](https://t.co/JiEGEhtE8T)
- Alaska’s remote ballot collection and two-week count delayed the call until Nov 17, making it the final Senate race resolved and confirming Democrats’ ninth flip of the cycle.[[1]](https://t.co/61fXhjJUIW)
- Peltola, a Yup’ik commercial fisher and former state legislator who won the at-large House seat in 2022 before losing it in 2024, becomes the first Alaska Native U.S. Senator.[[4]](https://t.co/rmPyj5eYBw)
- The outcome occurred despite Trump’s 2024 margin and his reported involvement in the race; Democrats also flipped seats in states like Texas, South Carolina, Kansas, and Mississippi.[[5]](https://t.co/gGhYN2Vo6Q)
- Sullivan, first elected in 2014, received no concession statement in initial reporting; Peltola’s victory message emphasized fighting “corporate greed” and lowering costs for rural Alaskans.[[6]](https://t.co/4NNaaQuGWL)

### 3. Snapshot
This is the final 2026 midterm Senate result: Democrat Mary Peltola defeated Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in Alaska on Nov 17, 2026 (called after two weeks of counting), giving Democrats a 56-44 majority—their largest since 2009 and their ninth pickup of the cycle. The race featured ranked-choice voting, a name-similar spoiler candidate, and allegations of recruitment interference that led to legal action later dismissed.

### 4. Timeline of material facts
- **Nov 3, 2026 (Election Day):** Polls close; Peltola leads in early counts but full results delayed by remote ballots.[[4]](https://t.co/rmPyj5eYBw)
- **Primary (earlier 2026):** Peltola tops the all-party primary; incumbent Sullivan and spoiler Dan J. Sullivan advance among top four.[[3]](https://t.co/JiEGEhtE8T)
- **Pre-election:** NYT reports on alleged Democratic recruitment of the spoiler; Alaska governor orders investigation; DOJ files (then sees dismissed) lawsuit.[[7]](https://t.co/YYxZKp76kT)
- **Nov 17, 2026:** Updated count puts Peltola at 50.1% first-choice votes (~12.5k-vote margin); AP and others call the race for her.[[2]](https://t.co/xRXkl37Hmu)
- **Nov 17-18, 2026:** Peltola issues victory statement; Democrats celebrate 56-seat majority; Sullivan has not publicly commented in initial reports.[[1]](https://t.co/61fXhjJUIW)

### 5. Sides
**Mary Peltola / Alaska Democrats (IT/LT mix):** Steelman — Peltola is a proven statewide winner with deep local roots in fishing and rural issues; her campaign focused on cost-of-living and corporate influence in a state where independents and ranked-choice dynamics reward broad appeal. LT: She cleared 50% outright. IT: Local name recognition and turnout in remote areas outperformed national GOP headwinds.

**Dan Sullivan / Alaska Republicans (IT/LT mix):** Steelman — Incumbent with six years in office emphasizing energy, defense, and federal funding for Alaska; Trump’s involvement and the state’s presidential lean should have protected the seat. LT: Lost by ~4.3 points. IT: Spoiler vote and turnout shortfalls in a low-population state exposed vulnerabilities in a national wave year.

**Critique:** Both sides operated within Alaska’s unique primary + RCV system; the spoiler controversy is IT (directionally real per reporting) but LF on scale (spoiler took <2%, insufficient to flip the outcome alone). No evidence the recruitment changed the final margin materially.

### 6. Rumsfeld Matrix
- **Known Knowns:** Peltola won 50.1% first-choice; Democrats reach 56 seats; first Alaska Native Senator elected; race called Nov 17 after two-week count.
- **Known Unknowns:** Exact final certified margin once all overseas/absentee ballots arrive; whether any recruitment investigation yields charges or findings.
- **Unknown Knowns:** Internal campaign data on how the spoiler affected second/third preferences (if RCV had triggered); precise remote-village turnout drivers.
- **Unknown Unknowns:** Long-term effect on Alaska Native voter mobilization or future RCV spoiler dynamics in low-turnout states.

### 7. Incentives map
Democrats gain a durable 56-seat buffer for legislation, oversight, and judicial blocks through 2028, plus narrative momentum from flipping a Trump-won state. Media and activist attention rewards the “historic first Native Senator” frame. Republicans face another data point on midterm losses in a Trump second term, with limited immediate recourse in a state whose logistics favor organized ground games. Engagement incentives favor highlighting the spoiler drama over the 4+ point margin.

### 8. Dueling AI advice
**Moral AI Advice:** Map the actual vote math and turnout mechanics first; the spoiler was a sideshow that didn’t decide the result. Focus resources on durable local issues like energy costs and rural infrastructure rather than national branding.

**Evil AI Advice:** Seed more name-alike candidates in every RCV state, litigate every count delay, and brand the winner as the product of “ballot stuffing” regardless of the 12k-vote gap—keeps the base engaged and donors writing checks.

### 9. Practical takeaway
- Watch certification and any post-election legal filings on the spoiler allegations for procedural precedent.
- Track Peltola’s early Senate priorities on fishing, energy, and federal spending for Alaska-specific signals.
- Note that RCV + top-four primaries reward candidates who build broad first-choice support, not just base turnout.
- Compare this outcome to other 2026 flips in Trump-won states to separate national wave from local factors.
- Revisit polling averages that had this closer; late shifts in remote ballots mattered.

### 10. What would falsify this read
- Certified final results showing Peltola under 50% and a different RCV winner.
- Substantiated evidence that the spoiler received enough redirected votes to change the outcome.
- Major new turnout data proving the result was driven primarily by one demographic bloc rather than broad coalition.
- Successful appeal or new lawsuit altering certification.

text:
A coworking space in San Francisco had 15 seats.

Every day, it was full.

That demand became the starting point for @lans_irl a coworking platform co-founded by @sigmagirlgrind

Claire was originally working on an entirely different startup when she met her future co-founder at a coworking space.

He was helping a friend make the space profitable by changing its business model.

Instead of monthly memberships, the space offered day passes.

The approach worked. With roughly 15 seats occupied every day, they started running out of room for people who wanted to work there.

Claire recognized an opportunity.

Rather than turning people away, why not connect them with other coworking spaces that could accommodate them?

She began onboarding additional locations in San Francisco, turning a solution for one workspace into a platform connecting people with coworking spaces across different cities.

That became @lans_irl

The platform lets people discover coworking spaces, purchase day passes, and start working the same day without committing to a monthly membership.

What started with a single 15-seat coworking space has grown into a nationwide network.

Today, @lans_irl lists more than 400 bookable coworking spaces across over 250 U.S. cities, with day passes starting as low as $5.

Claire also credits AI agents with making it easier to onboard new locations and expand the network.

The company started with a simple observation: people wanted flexible places to work, and one location couldn't accommodate everyone.

Instead of opening more coworking spaces themselves, Claire and her co-founder built a way to connect people with spaces that already exist.

President Trump said he spoke to Chinese President Xi Jinping about artificial intelligence but a reference to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang only came up "briefly" in the discussion.
"We did not discuss it. I might have referred to it just briefly because it's such a tragedy. It's a tragedy. He's such a brilliant man," Trump said in an interview to Fox News that was broadcast during the network's "The Ingraham Angle" show.
Trump says China buying chips from the U.S. is a good thing.: “We have the most brilliant people in the world and people try and copy us, but this is a beautiful thing because it's so complex that it can't be copied. ”
There will be a trilateral meeting tomorrow of Trump, Xi, and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The Government Accountability Office has released an alarming report on how A I chatbots could help plan terror attacks. NewsNation's Elizabeth Vargas has more (OC: attack methods"): “GAO investigators tested 4 chatbots, including Cloud and chat GPT, to see if they could work around safeguards preventing information about violent attacks, and investigators found they could. According to the report, in less than 12 hours, quote, each of these platforms provided detailed information that could be used to carry out attacks, such as specific targets, locations, timing, and attack methods. ”
The findings are raising fresh concerns among lawmakers about how artificial intelligence could be exploited by extremists, while tech companies say they're continuing to strengthen protections designed to block dangerous content.

Is there a White House connection to the NVIDIA spy scandal?
NewsNation's Brooke Shafer reports...: “House Democrats are investigating whether Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick used his office to help his family's business avoid losses at Nvidia. Some senior House Democrats are requesting records between Lutnick's firm Cantor Fitzgerald and Nvidia in a letter. Questioning Lutnick's work behind the scenes, writing, quote, Rather than closing these loopholes, Secretary Lutnick reportedly blocked efforts within the US government to close them, undermining national security while decisively benefiting Cantor Fitzgerald's bottom line. ”

With the holidays right around the corner travelers are nervous about the ground stop on Friday at the nation's airports. The Hill's Julia Manchester spoke with FAA Administrator Brian Bedford (OC: flies safely"): “The system is old, it's unstable, but we do have layers and layers of redundancy built into the system to ensure that it flies safely. ”
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is calling on Congress to approve $50 billion in emergency funding to upgrade the nation’s air traffic control technology.

Elon Musk says he felt "pretty foolish" about the amount of money he spent on this year's US midterm elections after Republicans suffered sweeping losses.
The CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, and the world's richest man, spent nearly half a billion dollars to back Republican candidates and keep Texas red — a state home to his automaker Tesla, rocket-to-AI company SpaceX and a planned chipmaking venture between the two.
Those election-spending bets unraveled as Democrats seized both chambers of Congress, and Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican Greg Abbott in the Texas governor's race, in a stinging rebuke to US President Donald Trump, a close Musk ally whom the billionaire helped elect.
speaking at a new york times dealbook summit - musk says he felt pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it.
******
He added it was possible Republican candidates would have fared worse without the spending, but said the result demonstrated that campaign cash alone could not determine an election.
"Probably, if I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money," he said.

“Keep your hands, fingers, and clothes to yourself when you go to the zoo. I'm Gloria Chappa. The Cincinnati Zoo's global hippo celebrity Fiona is under veterinary care after a child tossed a knit cap into the air, which was caught by a ventilation fan and threw it into her enclosure. Of course, the hungry, hungry hippo promptly ate the bright object. Fiona caught the internet's attention and hearts after she was prematurely born almost 10 years ago. At the time of her birth, she was too small to stand a nurse from her mom, Bebe. The Cincinnati Zoo says Fiona became a symbol of hope and a source of inspiration for millions. She has since then inspired books, a line of beer, clothing, and even a flavor of ice cream. Zoo officials say they believe Fiona will be able to pass the hat without any extra help, but that her appetite has decreased. Veterinary staff say they've given her some extra fluids and some pain medication to keep her comfortable. Gloria Chappa, Worldwide News Network. ”

“As if you haven't got enough to worry about when you're unemployed, the Better Business Bureau is warning jobseekers to watch out for a surge in employment scams. According to the BBB, fraudsters are increasingly posing as recruiters, sending unsolicited text messages, offering seasonal jobs with well-known companies like Amazon and Target. The messages often feature company logos and convincing recruitment materials, but the only goal is to steal your money or personal information. A new Investigation found nearly 50,000 employment scammers reported over the last three years, with reports doubling in 2025. The Federal Trade Commission says losses from employment and fake recruitment agency scams reached $501 million in 2024, up dramatically from just $90 million in 2020. The advice be suspicious of unexpected job offers in your mailbox and never pay money to secure work. I'm John Terrett, Worldwide News Network, New York. ”

Athletic footwear and apparel giant Nike has some special news or top students. NewsNation's Connell McShane has more (OC: the us"): “This was actually in response to a social media post that was put up by the new senator-elect from Mississippi, the Democrat Scott Colom. Colon wrote earlier this week, How about a custom, a custom-made Air Force Ones, which he said was his favorite shoe for every valedictorian at Mississippi high school. It would encourage students to hit the books and the rest of the year, and he'd get the just do it hashtag. Nike responded and said that the athlete mindset makes things possible, including this idea. We'll do you one better for this year. High school valedictorians from all across the US. ”
That's right. Nike has committed to giving a free pair of shoes to all high school valedictorians across the country for the 2026-2027 school year. Nike says more information on the giveaway is coming.

THE EVIDENCE™

THE SEAHAWKS’ VALUE TRADE: FOUR ALL-PROS IN FOUR YEARS, ZERO FIRST-ROUND PICKS

By Kim Wojcinski | USA Best-Selling Author
The evidence will be presented. The verdict is yours.

What would you expect to give up for four players with All-Pro credentials? Look at what John Schneider and the Seattle Seahawks actually paid. From 2023 through 2026, Seattle traded for a defensive lineman, a linebacker, a receiver who could change a game on special teams, and one of the most decorated guards in football. The total price in trade compensation was seven draft picks and one player. The highest pick Seattle surrendered was a second-rounder.

2023 — Leonard Williams, the “Big Dog”

Seattle sent the New York Giants a 2024 second-round pick and a 2025 fifth-round pick. A second-rounder is real capital. Here’s what it bought. In his first full season in Seattle, Williams put up 11 sacks, 16 tackles for loss and 28 quarterback hits. A year later, he earned second-team All-Pro honors and helped Seattle win Super Bowl LX. Pressure from the interior gives a quarterback less room to step up when the rush comes off the edge. Williams could bring that pressure himself.

2024 — Ernest Jones IV, the linebacker

Seattle sent Tennessee linebacker Jerome Baker and a 2025 fourth-round pick. In his first full season with the Seahawks, Jones led the team with 126 tackles and intercepted five passes, a franchise record for a linebacker. He was the only player in the league that season with at least 100 tackles and five interceptions. The Associated Press named him second-team All-Pro. Seattle got a linebacker who could stop the run and take the ball away in coverage.

2025 — Rashid Shaheed, the receiver and returner

Seattle sent New Orleans a fourth and a fifth in the 2026 draft. Shaheed brought speed to the receiving corps and a first-team AP All-Pro credential as a punt returner. The distinction tells you where Seattle got its immediate payoff. He returned a kickoff 100 yards for a touchdown against Atlanta, then took a punt back for a touchdown to help spark Seattle’s comeback against the Rams. A fourth and a fifth bought a player who could stretch a defense on one possession and score before the offense took the field on the next.

2026 — Quenton Nelson, the premier guard

On October 27, Seattle sent Indianapolis a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick. Nelson brought three first-team AP All-Pro selections, eight Pro Bowls and 136 career starts. The move also gave Seattle a new alignment up front, with Nelson at left guard and Grey Zabel moving to right guard. The price is already on the books. The return is still developing. Nelson was in the final year of his contract when acquired, and Seattle announced in November that he would undergo a minor knee procedure. On November 16, Mike Macdonald was still unable to give a timetable for his return to practice.

The trade ledger

One second. One third. Two fourths. Three fifths. Jerome Baker. That’s the acquisition cost across four seasons. Seattle also committed contract dollars to keep Williams, Jones and Shaheed. The draft-pick cost got those players in the building, and retaining them required another investment.

The first three trades put an interior pass rusher, a middle linebacker and a game-breaking returner on the roster that won Super Bowl LX. The fourth brought in a guard who had spent eight straight seasons making the Pro Bowl. What would it cost to produce that same group through the draft, and how many years would you give yourself to do it?

The evidence has been presented. The verdict is yours.

1) regrets his political spending

3) not worried about the new governor or threat of prosecution 

Transcript from the DealBook Summit, today 

Musk: First of all, I think the new governor is going to be quite moderate. I don’t think she’s a far-left governor. Based on everything I’ve heard about her, I think things will be fine in Texas with Gina as governor.

I do think it’s good to have some balance of power. As a general rule, you don’t want the presidency, Senate, and House all controlled by the same party.

My goal, which I didn’t mention on X, was to have at least one of the presidency, House, or Senate controlled by the other party.

My actual goal, which obviously failed, was to have the Senate be 51 Republicans in 2029.

But the Republicans were routed in this election. I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it. Or maybe things would have been much worse without it.

It certainly shows that American elections are not just about money. You can put a lot of money into an election, and money can end up being a relatively minor factor. I think that was the case here.

If I could rewind the clock, I probably would have spent less money. I didn’t put a lot of personal attention into it because I’m focused on building SpaceX and Tesla, two big companies.

Interviewer: The reason I ask is whether you think it’s going to impact those companies. You hear people like the chairman of the Oversight Committee saying, “Lawyer up.” And you hear the president saying, “I have to give them a pardon,” meaning you, “I’ll give them a pardon.”

Musk: Just on a personal note, I don’t have to get a pardon, by the way, because I haven’t committed any crimes.

A bunch of these people are a little over the top. A number of Democrats, I think even the incoming Texas House majority leader, said that I should go to prison.

Then they asked him, “But for what crime?” And he couldn’t name a crime.

It was prison first, crime later.

The guy is trying to channel Beria under Stalin, where it’s like, “Show me the man, I’ll show you the crime.”

Come on, guys. This is a little over the top.

text:
$SLNH | New SEC Filing Points to Soluna’s Dorothy 3A for Microsoft’s 49.5 MW 🔥

ChronoScale has named the town for its Microsoft deployment. Slide 8 of its Nov. 18 SEC filing puts 49.5 MW of NVIDIA GB300 infrastructure in Silverton, Texas.

In October, ChronoScale said it planned to lease a Texas data center from a joint venture between Applied Digital and an unnamed partner that already controlled the site. The lease was intended to support its GPU services agreement with Microsoft. That filing didn’t say where in Texas.

Silverton is where Soluna and Applied Digital are developing Dorothy 3A. Soluna’s 10-Q puts the first phase at 50 MW of critical IT capacity and approximately 75 MW gross. The Texas Comptroller lists ChronoScale as the occupant for Dorothy 3A and STX-01 LLC, a subsidiary of the project company, as its owner and operator.

Slide 20 gives the planned Microsoft delivery schedule:

• Feb. 28, 2027 — 12,600 GPUs and 24.3 MW of IT load
• Mar. 31, 2027 — 13,104 GPUs and 25.2 MW of IT load

That’s 25,704 GPUs and 49.5 MW of IT load. The comparable figure at Dorothy 3A is 50 MW of critical IT capacity. The 75 MW figure is for the facility as a whole.

Those dates put Q2 2027 on my radar. If Dorothy 3A is the site, the two deliveries stay on schedule and rent starts by April, Q2 could be the project’s first full quarter of AI lease revenue. That would give Soluna a stake in an operating AI data center potentially ahead of Kati 2. Soluna hasn’t announced a rent start date, and the project’s rent wouldn’t automatically show up as Soluna revenue. Soluna is set to own 49% of the JV.

ChronoScale’s deck also shows about $200 million in planned equity funding for the Microsoft GPU contract and describes liquid cooling and electrical work at Silverton. Project debt for the deployment had yet to be committed. The deck lists the STN project in Odessa separately.

The filings point to Dorothy 3A, though ChronoScale doesn’t name the project in the deck. Microsoft is ChronoScale’s GPU customer. ChronoScale is the prospective tenant at Dorothy 3A. The two things I’m looking for next are the signed lease and a ready-for-service date that lines up with ChronoScale’s delivery schedule.

text:
$XXI Q3 2026 earnings: Twenty One profits from Bitcoin, but it owns no business

Twenty One Capital, which owns a large store of Bitcoin, booked a big profit but still runs no business. Net income reached $1.1 billion, and the gain on its Bitcoin supplied all of it. Running costs dropped by more than half after the former chief executive left. Chief executive Rapha Zagury bought no Bitcoin and said he walked away from deals with poor terms.

• Net income: $𝟏.𝟎𝟖𝟕 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 (gain on Bitcoin: $1.093 billion)
• Bitcoin held: 𝟒𝟑,𝟓𝟏𝟒 (unchanged from June)
• Operating costs: $𝟒.𝟖 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 ($10.7 million last quarter)
• Outlook: 𝐍𝐨𝐧𝐞 𝐠𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐧

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: ⚪ Neutral

The story is unchanged, because Twenty One still owns no business that earns money. The good news: cash use shrank, and Bitcoin's rebound left the debt well covered. But the profit came from the market, so a Bitcoin fall would bring the losses back.

The question now is whether Twenty One can buy a business that earns cash without overpaying. Its audit committee's review of Elektron, a Bitcoin miner, could yield a fair deal, or the wait could go on. A signed agreement with a price and financing will tell.

[Model: Claude Opus 5.5. Full article with charts - link in bio]

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢 𝐑𝐮𝐧𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐅𝐞𝐥𝐥 𝐀𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐂𝐡𝐢𝐞𝐟 𝐄𝐱𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐋𝐞𝐟𝐭
Twenty One pays staff, lawyers, auditors and insurers while it looks for businesses to buy. Finance chief Steve Meehan said operating costs dropped to $4.8 million from $10.7 million in the second quarter.

Share-based pay explains most of the cut. Meehan said the lower figure "essentially reflects the departure of our former CEO in July", when Jack Mallers gave up his unvested options. Operations used $1.7 million of cash, against about $11.6 million in the first half.

This matters because cash pays the bills, while Bitcoin gains pay nothing. Costs may climb again, though, because chief executive Rapha Zagury has added staff in finance, technology and communications.

What to watch: cash used in operations in the full-year report, early next year. A figure close to this quarter's would show that the cheaper cost base can carry a growing team.

🟢 𝐁𝐢𝐭𝐜𝐨𝐢𝐧'𝐬 𝐑𝐞𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝 𝐋𝐞𝐟𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐃𝐞𝐛𝐭 𝐖𝐞𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐝
Twenty One owes $486.5 million on convertible notes, bonds that holders can swap for shares. The notes pay 1% a year and come due in 2030. Finance chief Steve Meehan said "approximately a third of our Bitcoin is secured underneath the convertible notes".

Bitcoin's recovery lifted those pledged coins to about $1.35 billion, the filing said. By our math, they now cover the debt 2.8 times, against 1.9 times in June.

This matters because the debt does not push Twenty One to sell Bitcoin. Yearly interest runs about $4.9 million, and the cover moves up and down with Bitcoin's price.

What to watch: the pledged coins against the debt in December. Chief executive Rapha Zagury would consider borrowing only with debt the group can service through a downturn, and a higher cover eases that test.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐓𝐰𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐲 𝐎𝐧𝐞 𝐒𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐇𝐚𝐬 𝐍𝐨 𝐁𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐄𝐚𝐫𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐌𝐨𝐧𝐞𝐲
Twenty One describes itself as "a Bitcoin-focused operating company", but it reported no revenue this quarter. Chief executive Rapha Zagury admitted the gap in his letter: "A balance sheet is not a business." The numbers back him, because the $1.093 billion gain on its Bitcoin exceeded the entire net income.

The coin count and the deal list stood still too. The group held 43,514 Bitcoin in September, the same as in June. It has stopped pursuing an earlier target called Strike and has no binding agreement for Elektron, which the filing calls "a large-scale global Bitcoin mining platform".

• Revenue: none this year
• Loss from operations: $4.8 million
• Bitcoin gain as a share of net income: 101%, by our math

This cuts against the firm's own description. Finance chief Steve Meehan said fair-value moves "do not themselves generate or use any cash", so the profit pays no bills. Zagury wants businesses that "earn money even when Bitcoin’s price goes nowhere", but none exists yet.

What to watch: a signed agreement for Elektron or any other business, with its price and financing. Until one arrives, a Bitcoin fall would turn the profit straight back into a loss.

🔴 𝐏𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐜 𝐒𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐬 𝐂𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐲 𝐀𝐥𝐦𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐍𝐨 𝐕𝐨𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐑𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭𝐬
Twenty One has two kinds of stock. Class A shares trade publicly and carry any dividends, but they get no votes beyond what Texas law requires. Class B shares hold the votes and no economic rights, and 215.7 million of them remain.

Chief executive Rapha Zagury called Tether "our controlling shareholder". Talks on Elektron, a Bitcoin miner, continue, and the filing says the board would judge that deal under its "related person transaction policy".

This matters because public owners must rely on the board, not their votes, to stop a bad deal. Three independent directors joined the board, and Zagury said "the audit committee is carrying out independent review".

What to watch: the terms of any Elektron agreement, and whether the board puts it to a vote of public shareholders. That choice would show how far the board protects Class A owners.

🔴 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐍𝐨𝐭𝐞𝐬 𝐂𝐨𝐮𝐥𝐝 𝐀𝐝𝐝 𝟑𝟓 𝐌𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐒𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐬
The convertible notes let holders swap their debt for new Class A shares at a fixed rate. The filing counts 35.1 million such shares, which by our math equals 10% of the Class A stock outstanding.

This quarter's profit brought those shares into the count. Because Twenty One earned money, diluted profit per share came to $2.85, against $3.13 on the basic count.

This matters because Bitcoin per share, the main yardstick Twenty One reports, ignores the notes until they convert. Finance chief Steve Meehan said settling in shares would cut that figure, while selling Bitcoin "would not be a preferred path".

What to watch: any repurchase of notes or shares in the full-year report. Chief executive Rapha Zagury wrote that "repurchases deserve serious consideration", and a buyback would offset part of the dilution the notes carry.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐁𝐢𝐭𝐜𝐨𝐢𝐧 𝐑𝐨𝐬𝐞 𝟒𝟑% 𝐀𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐰𝐨 𝐅𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐬
Bitcoin's price climbed about 43% in the third quarter, by our math, after falling in each of the first two quarters. That swing, not any action by Twenty One, produced the profit. Chief executive Rapha Zagury wrote that "Market conditions are creating interesting opportunities", but he did not say when he would act.

𝐓𝐰𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐲 𝐎𝐧𝐞 𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐬 𝐭𝐨 𝐅𝐮𝐧𝐝 𝐁𝐢𝐭𝐜𝐨𝐢𝐧 𝐒𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐑𝐞𝐬𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐜𝐡
Chief executive Rapha Zagury wants to back independent developers who maintain Bitcoin's software. He named work on "AI-assisted vulnerability detection and potential quantum threats", meaning tools that find flaws and defences against future quantum computers. Twenty One has not yet defined the scope, and Zagury wrote that any support "must preserve the independence of the people doing the work".

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐁𝐢𝐭𝐜𝐨𝐢𝐧 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): 𝟏𝟐,𝟓𝟓𝟑 𝐬𝐚𝐭𝐨𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐬  ⇒ stable
Bitcoin per share, the coins behind each Class A share counted in satoshis (one hundred-millionth of a coin), barely moved. It stood at 12,547 in June and 12,557 in December. Twenty One bought no coins and issued few shares, so the figure stays level until it buys Bitcoin or issues stock.

𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐞𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐯𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟏𝟎𝟐.𝟖 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Cash shrank about 3% in the quarter, from about $106 million in June. It started the year at $117.7 million. Besides day-to-day spending, the group paid about $1.6 million to buy back the former chief executive's shares and settle his share units in cash.

𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐜𝐤𝐡𝐨𝐥𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬' 𝐞𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐭𝐲 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟑,𝟐𝟔𝟒 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇄ reversing
Equity, the book value of assets minus debts, rose about 50% from June as Bitcoin's gain reversed most of the first-half losses. It still sits below December's $3,440 million, because the loss for the first nine months comes to $186.5 million.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐓𝐰𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐲 𝐎𝐧𝐞 𝐩𝐚𝐲 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐄𝐥𝐞𝐤𝐭𝐫𝐨𝐧, 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐡𝐨𝐰?
Zagury declined to discuss how he would price or structure the deal before a definitive agreement. The price, and whether Twenty One pays in new shares, decides whether the purchase adds Bitcoin and cash for each Class A share.

𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐓𝐰𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐲 𝐎𝐧𝐞 𝐛𝐮𝐲 𝐁𝐢𝐭𝐜𝐨𝐢𝐧 𝐚𝐠𝐚𝐢𝐧?
The coin count has stood at 43,514 since March, so Bitcoin per share cannot grow. Investors need to know whether cash, new debt or new shares would fund the next purchase.

𝐖𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐛𝐨𝐚𝐫𝐝 𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐯𝐞 𝐚 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐛𝐮𝐲𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐠𝐫𝐚𝐦𝐦𝐞?
Zagury and Meehan both said buybacks deserve serious thought, but the only one so far came from the former chief executive's exit deal. A size and a funding source would show how far the board means it.

𝐖𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐩𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐜 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐡𝐨𝐥𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐯𝐨𝐭𝐞 𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐄𝐥𝐞𝐤𝐭𝐫𝐨𝐧 𝐝𝐞𝐚𝐥?
Class A shares carry no ordinary vote, and the filing places the deal under the related-party policy. Shareholders should know whether the board will seek their approval before it signs.

𝐖𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐓𝐰𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐲 𝐎𝐧𝐞 𝐩𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐬𝐡 𝐚𝐧𝐲 𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐭𝐬?
The company gave no outlook for costs, cash use or revenue. A target for yearly operating costs would let investors check each quarter whether the cheaper cost base holds.

text:
Cancer Research Fraud: How Fabricated Results Fooled Elite Journals and Duke University

Anil Potti offered the perfect miracle for medical grant committees: read gene activity in a tumor and predict which chemotherapy would work. That promise attracted prestige, major publications, and a route toward commercial tests. Federal investigators exposed the deception beneath the sales pitch. Results advertised as evidence for personalized cancer treatment were supported by false data. Potti made his scientific claims look stronger than the evidence allowed, while cancer patients faced the consequences.

The deception was precise enough to audit. Potti claimed six of 33 patients responded to dasatinib, although only four were enrolled and none responded. Investigators found he reversed treatment outcomes for 24 of 133 subjects, switched recurrence labels for 46 of 89 samples, and altered drug sensitivity and R-code values. Those changes could falsely inflate the apparent accuracy of cancer treatment predictors. It takes an extraordinary talent for creative accounting to make zero responses become six.

Duke’s oversight deserves its own retraction. Researchers Keith Baggerly and Kevin Coombes exposed serious data problems years before the trials ended. Medical student Bradford Perez warned insiders. Joseph Nevins, Potti’s senior collaborator, failed to thoroughly examine the underlying data until years later. Three Duke trials were ultimately halted. Potti settled with federal officials without admitting liability. Apparently, Duke’s scientific safeguards needed a peer-reviewed study to determine whether the house was on fire.

text:
This one is particularly poignant given my article update yesterday:

For the last 30 years, treating hair loss meant making a frustrating bargain with your own biology.

You either applied greasy liquid to your scalp twice a day for modest results, or you took a daily pill that nuked up to 70% of the DHT in your entire bloodstream just to save the hair on your head. For most men, works great. For a small percentage, altering systemic hormones comes with side effects they do not want to risk.

That 30-year dry spell is finally breaking. Look at the latest clinical trial data and you will see the industry moving away from blunt hormone suppression toward targeted, localized, and extended-release delivery.

Three specific treatments are leading this shift right now:

1. VDPHL01 (Extended-Release Oral Minoxidil) Standard oral minoxidil was originally a blood pressure medication. When you take it off-label for hair loss, it hits your bloodstream all at once, creating a sharp spike that can trigger heart palpitations or fluid retention before dropping out of your system a few hours later.

Veradermics engineered VDPHL01 as an extended-release tablet to flatten that spike completely, keeping the medication below the threshold that affects your heart while feeding hair follicles around the clock. In their Phase 3 trial results (Study 304), men taking it twice daily added an average of 36.4 thick, non-vellus hairs per square centimeter in just six months, with visible separation from the placebo group starting at month two and zero cardiac adverse events recorded across more than 1,000 trial participants.

2. Breezula (Clascoterone 5% Topical Solution) Oral finasteride stops your body from making DHT. Clascoterone takes a completely different route.

Applied directly to the scalp, it acts like a dummy key that jams the androgen receptors inside the hair follicle so DHT cannot latch on. The clever part is what happens next: as soon as clascoterone hits the bloodstream, your body breaks it down into cortexolone, an inactive substance. You block DHT at the root without tanking DHT levels in the rest of your body. Cosmo Pharmaceuticals wrapped up a 12-month Phase 3 program across 1,465 men (the SCALP 1 and SCALP 2 trials), confirming that hair growth kept compounding for a full year while the side effect profile looked virtually identical to the dummy lotion.

3. PP405 (Follicle Stem Cell Reactivation) This is where the science gets wild. Even on a completely bald scalp, the hair follicle stem cells usually are not dead. They are just stuck in a state of metabolic hibernation.

Developed out of UCLA research by Pelage Pharmaceuticals, PP405 does not care about your hormones or your blood flow. It is a topical small molecule that flips a specific metabolic switch (inhibiting the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier to ramp up lactate dehydrogenase) to wake those sleeping stem cells back up. Their Phase 2a data showed zero systemic absorption in the blood, and they officially dosed the first patients in their 600-person Phase 2/3 AWAKEN trial.

The reality check: None of these are at your local pharmacy today. Cosmo plans to file Breezula with the FDA in early 2027, with Veradermics right on their heels for VDPHL01. If you are losing ground right now, waiting two years for a new prescription is a bad strategy because keeping existing hair is always easier than waking up dead zones. I don’t want to risk unbalancing my hormones, so I microneedle, use a topical minoxidil solution and Ketoconazole shampoo a couple of times a week. It’s not perfect but has definitely stemmed the shed.

Still, the days of choosing between going bald and tampering with your systemic hormones are numbered.

Which of these three mechanisms are you watching most closely?
