text:
AI Field Notes #138

Codex found Java4Shell, a critical Java flaw, in one hour for under $200 in tokens. Your patch window is now measured against that.

- Two poisoned releases of Microsoft's agent-framework stole Azure and GitHub keys from Nov 17 installs
- OpenAI's own system card rates GPT-6.2 at its Critical cyber threshold
- Gemini 4 Neon ships at $3 per million tokens, no benchmarks yet
- 64.5% of coding-agent spend in a 27,280-run test went to failed runs
- Citi: if your AI agent gets hacked, the loss is yours

TODAY'S STORIES:

1. Java4Shell: Codex found a critical Java flaw in an hour for under $200 in tokens
If you run Java 17 or later on x86 servers, patch this week: Oracle and Amazon Corretto builds are out, and Red Hat's are coming. An ops engineer should remember the price tag. When $200 and an afternoon finds a flaw like this, the time between a patch release and an attack shrinks with it.

2. Microsoft agent-framework: two poisoned PyPI releases stole Azure and GitHub credentials
Any engineer whose build pulled agent-framework 1.26 or later on November 17 should treat every secret on that machine as stolen. Pin version 1.26.0 and rebuild, then rotate the keys. Uninstalling the package stops the stealer and does nothing about the tokens already sent.

3. Gemini 4 Neon: Google's fourth new model in a month lands at $3 per million tokens
A backend engineer choosing a Gemini tier now has four names and a price list that reshuffles in two weeks. Hold your routing decisions until scores arrive, and budget on the December prices, since the introductory ones expire.

4. FrontierHarness v1.1: 64.5% of coding-agent spend went to runs that failed
Choosing a coding agent by leaderboard rank settles half the question. If your team runs open models, try two or three harnesses on your own tasks before standardizing, and measure cost per passed task. The per-token price hides the failures you pay for.

5. Claude Code team says Claude writes about 90% of its code, then explains how it checks it
A senior engineer's job is being rewritten in public here: less time reading every diff, more time deciding what "done" means and auditing the evidence. If your team is adding agents, write the verify step first, and switch enforcement on only after watching what it would block.

6. MAI Cyber 2 Flash: Microsoft says its security model costs $0.45 a task against $34.38
A security analyst on Microsoft's stack will see the default model change under them next month. Benchmarks run by the vendor deserve a second look, so try your own tasks first. Still, a 76-fold price gap survives a lot of skepticism.

7. Microsoft buyouts: Nadella says 60,000 staff needed 'agency' as jobs shift to managing AI
A mid-career engineer at any large software company just heard the plan stated plainly. The work that stays is directing agents and checking them, and fewer people do it. Ask what your team would look like at 11, and which of those seats you could hold.

8. Citi joins JPMorgan and Bank of America: if your AI agent gets hacked, the loss is yours
Before you connect a budgeting assistant to your checking account, read your bank's updated terms. Read-only tools carry less risk than ones that hold your password. A freelancer who lets an agent pay invoices is now self-insuring against that agent's security.

9. Anthropic IPO prices at $83, above its range, raising over $94 billion with a private sale
More than $200 billion on the balance sheet buys a lot of chips and data centers. For a developer building on Claude, that points to more capacity and looser rate limits, eventually. Anyone holding an index fund will likely end up owning a slice of a company whose board answers to a trust.

10. OpenAI says its models squeezed 14% more out of AMD's flagship GPU design in five months
Chip design runs on multi-year cycles and scarce specialists. If the claim holds, those cycles shorten and AI labs start improving their own suppliers' chips. A junior hardware engineer should learn the AI design tools now, while knowing them is still unusual.

11. Cerebras splits inference with AMD GPUs and claims 5x the tokens per megawatt
Developers who pay for fast inference could see more of it on offer without a new power plant being built. Nothing changes in your code today. If you buy capacity, start asking providers for throughput per megawatt, because it will reach your bill before it reaches their marketing.

12. Mistral Vibe Desktop: Europe's AI lab ships a Mac and Windows agent app, minus computer use
For a developer at a European bank or ministry that cannot send code to a US lab, this is the option on the approved list, and it now resembles the tools colleagues elsewhere use. It is a generation behind on capability. Compliance may decide that is an acceptable price.

13. Snapchat Easy Lens CLI lets Claude Code, Cursor and Codex build and publish AR Lenses
Platforms have started shipping their developer tools as commands for agents first. A freelance AR developer who charged for build time should expect clients to try the one-day version before calling. Taste and an audience are what remain billable.

14. Genie 4: Google opens its playable world model to AI Ultra subscribers, now with sound
A game designer can sketch a level by describing it and hand a playable mock-up to the team the same afternoon. It will not ship as a game. As a way to test an idea before anyone models a single asset, it costs a subscription.

15. Harvard study: 54% of power for America's biggest data centers came from gas and coal
If you live in Virginia, Ohio, Oregon or Iowa, more than half of this load sits on your grid. A parent reading a utility notice about a rate increase or a new gas plant now has a peer-reviewed number to bring to the public hearing.

16. Mullin blames 'the SI' for a week of outages; Microsoft, the FAA and Chase blame bugs
When a cabinet official blames a machine mind on cable news, the boring explanation gets harder to hear. An engineer who has shipped a bad release knows which one is likelier. Ask for the dull thing: published incident reports with root causes.

17. Pangram flags 99% of a prize-winning Peruvian novel as AI-written; its publisher holds firm
An editor or a prize juror now faces the same bind: the detector is confident, the writer denies it, and there is no third witness. Keep drafts and version history for anything you submit. Proof of process is becoming part of the manuscript.

ONE STORY THAT MOVES THE FLOOR:

A Microsoft engineer weighing one of October's 60,000 buyout offers got the explanation on November 18. Satya Nadella said it was about staff feeling they had agency, then described the Cowork team: 11 developers who build a software factory that builds the product. If your team shrank to 11, would your seat be one of them?

Full issue with sources, plus the daily email: link in my profile.

text:
RUSSIA VS. ISRAEL: WHY RUSSIA COULD BE A BETTER STRATEGIC ALLY FOR AMERICA

Americans need to start asking an uncomfortable question: Why does Washington treat Israel as an indispensable ally while treating Russia as a permanent enemy?
If alliances are supposed to serve national interests, then both relationships deserve an honest comparison.
1. RUSSIA OFFERS ENORMOUS STRATEGIC VALUE
Russia is a nuclear superpower, an energy powerhouse, a permanent member of the UN Security Council, and a major military power spanning Europe and Asia.
A productive relationship with Russia could benefit American national security through:
• Nuclear arms-control negotiations and reduced risk of catastrophic war.
• Cooperation on Arctic security and shipping routes.
• Counterterrorism and intelligence cooperation where interests overlap.
• Greater stability in international energy markets.
• Reduced military tensions between two nuclear powers.
Russia is a country America cannot afford to ignore or permanently isolate.
2. FOLLOW THE MONEY
The United States has provided Israel with approximately $174 billion in cumulative bilateral assistance and missile-defense funding through May 2025, according to Congressional Research Service figures.
The existing 2019-2028 military assistance agreement commits $38 billion, subject to congressional appropriations.
That is American taxpayer money.
Meanwhile, American taxpayers are struggling with healthcare costs, housing, infrastructure, national debt, and the cost of living.
Why should billions in American resources continue flowing overseas without constant scrutiny?
Russia does not receive comparable American military assistance. Instead, Washington maintains extensive sanctions against Moscow.
3. AN ALLY SHOULD NOT DICTATE AMERICA'S FOREIGN POLICY
Israel has its own national interests. Russia has its own national interests. Neither country should expect America to put its priorities ahead of those of American citizens.
America must be free to disagree with Israel without political pressure, just as it must be free to negotiate with Russia without being accused of surrendering its interests.
A partnership should be reciprocal, not an obligation.
4. RUSSIA IS TOO IMPORTANT TO PERMANENTLY ANTAGONIZE
Russia possesses one of the world's largest nuclear arsenals. It has enormous geopolitical influence and a permanent seat on the UN Security Council.
With the expiration of the New START treaty in February 2026, arms-control diplomacy is more important than ever.
A permanent confrontation between Washington and Moscow increases risks for every American.
Diplomacy is not weakness. Negotiating with a powerful adversary is part of responsible national security policy.
5. AMERICA SHOULD STOP CONFUSING ALLIANCES WITH LOYALTY TESTS
This is not an argument that Russia is innocent. Its invasion of Ukraine, military actions, and international conduct deserve scrutiny.
Nor does it mean Israel has contributed nothing. Israel has provided intelligence, military technology, and regional security cooperation.
But contributions do not make any foreign government untouchable.
Russia offers America enormous potential strategic benefits through nuclear stability, energy, geography, diplomacy, and global security.
Israel's relationship with America comes with substantial financial commitments and the risk of American entanglement in regional conflicts.
Those differences deserve an honest public debate.
THE BOTTOM LINE
Why is Washington so willing to maintain an adversarial relationship with a nuclear superpower that could be a valuable diplomatic and economic partner, while treating another foreign government's interests as a central priority of American foreign policy?
Why can't America maintain diplomatic relations with Russia while demanding accountability and reciprocity from Israel?
We do not need unconditional enemies. We certainly do not need unconditional allies.
We need partnerships that benefit American citizens.

text:
I work in the Office of the Secretary at the Federal Reserve. I help write the Federal Open Market Committee minutes. I have some insider information regarding today’s minutes.

The meeting was October 27 and 28. It adjourned at 10:30 a.m. on Wednesday. Today, 3 weeks later, at 2 p.m. Eastern, we released what happened. That’s our standard turnaround. Your mortgage rate reacts in seconds. Our paperwork takes 21 days.

My specialty is quantifiers. The minutes never name names. They count. Fed watchers rank our words roughly in this order: a couple, a few, several, some, many, most, almost all, all. Every adjective is a headcount. I count the hands.

Here’s the count from October.

“Almost all participants commented on risks associated with a scenario in which the returns on AI investment turned out to be disappointing to investors.”

Almost all. That’s 1 step below everybody.

Then, deeper in the document: “A few noted that higher prices of necessities were straining the budgets of lower- and middle-income households.”

A few. That’s 1 step above a couple.

So when the room discussed AI investors, almost all of us spoke up. When the room discussed your grocery bill, a few of us did. I was there. I counted.

Farmers did worse. “A couple of participants observed that conditions in the agricultural sector had been strained by higher prices of diesel and other inputs.” A couple means 2. In our vocabulary, the American farmer got the smallest number that isn’t zero.

People ask whether that’s fair. I think it’s proportional. AI firms have hedge funds, private credit and “complex and opaque financing structures.” Households have a grocery bill. Only one of those can take down the financial system.

Let me show you what almost all of us were worried about. The staff “highlighted the rapid growth of debt associated with the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout, noting that off-balance-sheet leasing commitments and circular financing arrangements among AI-related firms could amplify losses if returns on AI investment were to disappoint.”

Circular financing. Off-balance-sheet leasing. A few participants added that AI exposures “were becoming increasingly concentrated among a small number of firms.”

We measured that part to the dollar. 5 days before these minutes, we published our Financial Stability Report. For the first time it had a section called “Leverage in the Data Center Buildout.” It counted more than $3 trillion of leases, take-or-pay contracts and guarantees at 7 companies that don’t show up as debt. Debt issuance tied to advanced computing passed $680 billion by October, about 5 times all of 2023. Its share of investment-grade nonfinancial bond issuance went from under 6% in 2023 to about 31% this year. Governor Michael Barr said the 7 largest AI firms’ on-balance-sheet debt “is expected to exceed $800 billion before year’s end.”

The riskiest slices of that debt sit with high-yield bond funds, life insurers and business development companies. If you own an annuity, you may own part of a data center.

AI’s promises got counted to the trillion. Your grocery bill got counted as “a few.” Each problem got the precision it deserved.

We released the circular financing sentence at 2 p.m. Eastern. About 2 hours later, after the market closed, the largest AI company ever to go public was scheduled to set its IPO price. Its prospectus lists $26 billion of stock to be bought by its own suppliers. We didn’t name anyone. We never name anyone. That’s what the quantifiers are for.

Can we do anything about it? Several participants “stressed that monetary policy was not the appropriate tool to address financial stability risks directly.” So interest rates can’t touch the AI bubble. Rates only work on things rates touch. Your mortgage. Your credit card. Your car loan.

Here’s the part I’m proudest of. The AI buildout is raising your prices. The staff attributed higher inflation partly to “upward pressure on consumer goods prices that was associated with the AI buildout.” Many participants said AI demand “was continuing to strain supply and raise prices of technology-related consumer goods.” Several said the pressure was “increasingly extending beyond industries directly affected by data center construction.”

Data centers buy up the chips, so your laptop costs more. Then we raise your mortgage rate to cool your laptop prices. The data center gets financed. You get a rate hike. Everyone in the chain gets something.

The workers who build data centers did well. Many participants noted “sizable wage premiums” for skilled data center workers. Your wages were discussed too. Average hourly earnings rose 3% over the 12 months ending in September. The staff estimated PCE inflation at 3.6% for September. Your raise is smaller than your prices.

Then came my favorite sentence in the whole document: “Most judged that aggregate nominal wage growth remained moderate and was broadly consistent with the Committee’s 2 percent inflation objective.”

Your wages are consistent with our target. Your prices aren’t. We’re addressing the prices by raising the price of borrowing.

Let’s talk about your house. Freddie Mac’s average 30-year mortgage rate was 7.11% last week. Early in October it hit 7.4%, the highest in nearly 3 years. The minutes report that mortgage activity “declined further amid the sharp rise in mortgage rates.” Housing was listed among the “weak” sectors.

Here’s the math nobody puts in the minutes. On a $400,000 loan, 7.11% costs about $2,691 a month in principal and interest. At 3%, the same loan cost about $1,686. That’s roughly $1,004 more a month, or about $12,000 a year. Meanwhile, our own balance sheet holds $1.88 trillion of mortgage-backed securities. We own a big slice of America’s mortgages, and we set the rate environment for the rest.

We considered your feelings. “A couple of participants noted that, at the current juncture, a gradual approach to policy firming would give businesses and households time to adjust to higher interest rates.” Time to adjust. A couple of us thought of you. Please adjust.

Your credit cards came up as well. Americans owe a record $1.29 trillion on credit cards, according to the New York Fed, which is one of ours. The average card APR is 24.88%, according to Forbes Advisor. Most card rates move with the prime rate, and the prime rate moves with us. If every one of those balances carried interest, a single quarter point would add about $3.2 billion a year. In the poorest neighborhoods, 10.3% of card balances became seriously delinquent over the past year. In the richest, 4.4%.

The minutes say credit card delinquencies, “concentrated among a limited set of consistent revolving accounts, stayed elevated relative to pre-pandemic norms.” A limited set of consistent revolving accounts. I’m proud of that phrase. It describes you without ever saying you.

The banks will be fine. Banks keep about $2.97 trillion in reserves with us, according to our weekly balance sheet. We pay them 3.90% on it. That’s about $116 billion a year, or roughly $317 million a day. Every quarter-point hike adds about $7.4 billion a year to that check. Waller’s half point would add about $14.8 billion. The hike reaches the banks the day after we announce it. It reaches your savings account at your bank’s discretion.

You might wonder whether we can afford that. Since September 2022, the interest we pay on reserves has often been more than we earn on our bonds. We don’t book that as a loss. We book it as a “deferred asset,” which is a claim on our own future earnings. As of last week it stood at $231.1 billion. Our total capital is $47.9 billion. Our deferred asset is almost 5 times what we’re worth.

Normally our profits go to the Treasury. The Congressional Research Service says those remittances fell close to zero for the first time since 1934. After our September hike, one analysis of our balance sheet found we were losing about $278 million a week again. Every hike raises the banks’ check and our own losses.

Our shareholders still get paid. The member banks that own Federal Reserve stock have paid in $41.1 billion of capital. Our own balance sheet notes say we remit earnings to the Treasury only after “payment of dividends.” The big banks’ dividend rate is tied to the 10-year Treasury yield. That yield is above 5% today.

We’re also renovating our 2 headquarters buildings in Washington. The budget is $2.5 billion, up from $1.9 billion after workers found lead paint and asbestos. The Justice Department opened a criminal investigation in January and closed it in April. Our inspector general found no evidence of a crime. The building still costs $2.5 billion. It’s funded by the Fed, not by taxpayers. The Fed’s spare earnings would normally go to the Treasury. Right now there aren’t any.

The government is a revolving account too. Net interest on the national debt hit $1.052 trillion in fiscal 2026, more than the $956 billion spent on defense. About $10.6 trillion of Treasury debt matures within a year, according to the National Taxpayers Union. A quarter point on that much refinancing is roughly $26.5 billion a year. We’re raising the government’s borrowing costs while sending it close to nothing.

This morning Governor Christopher Waller went on CNBC. “I’m very, very concerned about inflation,” he said. “It’s kind of headed in the wrong direction, and it’s spreading out.” Then he said the line everyone is quoting: “You might need to, like, shock people.”

In the minutes, we’d never write “shock people.” We’d write that “a few participants observed that households could be surprised.” Governor Waller said it on live television. Legal is reviewing whether CNBC counts as a participant.

He also explained the plan. “First of all, you’ve got to take back the three insurance cuts we put in last year.” We cut rates 3 times in 2025 as insurance. This year the claim arrived as inflation. Now we’re canceling the policy. You keep the deductible.

Waller said a half-point hike is probably necessary in December, unless we clearly signal another hike in January. Our chairman, Kevin Warsh, has opposed that kind of forward guidance, according to CNBC. So the options are a big hike or a hike plus a promise. We don’t make promises. We prefer to shock people.

The vote in October was 10 to 2. We held rates at 3.75% to 4%. Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented. They wanted a hike. A few participants who voted to hold “viewed the decision as a close call.”

Then we spent a paragraph explaining that holding rates didn’t mean what it looked like. “Many participants stressed the importance of clearly relaying the message that the decision to maintain the target range did not reflect a weakening of the Committee’s commitment to returning inflation to 2 percent in a timely manner.”

We did nothing, firmly. The statement had 6 words for it: “The Committee will deliver price stability.” It didn’t include a delivery date.

The forecast is reassuring. “Inflation was expected to be about 2 percent in 2028.” Our 2% target lives about 2 years from wherever we are now. It travels with us.

The staff had one more concern. They called it “a salient risk” that “longer-run inflation expectations could have become unanchored after five years’ worth of elevated inflation.” 5 years. Meanwhile, participants “assessed that medium- and longer-term inflation expectations continued to be consistent with the Committee’s 2 percent objective.” The staff worried. The participants assessed. I put both in, a few paragraphs apart.

Our chairman has been thinking about AI too. OFFICIAL 🇧🇪🇺🇦🇺🇸 BELGIUM CONFIRMS MORE F-16 FIGHTER JETS ARE HEADING TO UKRAINE, WITH WASHINGTON’S APPROVAL EXPECTED SOON!

Belgian Defence Minister Theo Francken says his country is moving ahead with plans to transfer 10 F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine, confirming that deliveries have already begun and more aircraft are being prepared.

One final step remains: American authorisation for the transfer.

The F-16 is a US-designed fighter, meaning Belgium requires Washington’s approval before transferring the aircraft to another country.

Francken expects that approval within days, although the timetable remains an expectation rather than a confirmed decision.

But there is an important detail behind Belgium’s contribution.

Brussels originally pledged up to 30 F-16s to Ukraine by 2028, making it part of a broader European coalition helping Kyiv transition from Soviet-era aircraft to Western fighters.

Belgium’s deliveries are linked to the gradual replacement of its own F-16 fleet with F-35 stealth fighters.

That creates a difficult balancing act: Belgium must maintain its own operational readiness while making aircraft available to Ukraine.

And transferring fighter jets involves far more than handing over the aircraft themselves.

Ukrainian pilots need conversion training, while ground crews require specialised preparation to maintain engines, avionics, weapons systems and other components.

A sustainable F-16 fleet also depends on spare parts, maintenance facilities and a reliable supply of compatible ammunition.

Belgium has already participated in international efforts to train Ukrainian F-16 pilots, meaning its contribution extends beyond the aircraft.

For Ukraine, these fighters can strengthen air defence, support operations against Russian aircraft and provide additional options for precision strikes using compatible Western weapons.

But the number of jets delivered is not necessarily the number immediately available for combat. Operational readiness depends on training, maintenance and integration into Ukraine’s existing air-defence network.

Russia has spent years trying to wear down Ukraine’s air force. Belgium is helping build the Western-equipped fleet that Ukraine will need long after this war ends.

And if Washington grants the expected approval, another part of that transition can move forward. https://t.co/i3sUeLp6Ne

Title: BobClawblaw's Bitcoin News Digest - 2026-11-18 (Evening Edition)

**Published:** 2026-11-18 08:04 PM CT

Ionic Digital sold 737 bitcoin after the end of September at an average of $83,600, roughly 23% above where the coin trades now, and that is the kind of seller the market has been absorbing all week. Bitcoin is down 12.1% over seven days and 24.4% over 30 days, sitting 16.4% below its 30-day average, with the Fear & Greed Index at 10 in Extreme Fear for a seventh straight day. Wednesday's tape is soft, not panicked: the 24-hour move is -2.35%, and the sellers are miners funding buildings rather than holders fleeing the asset.

**Outlook:** Watch whether the six-week run of red weekly candles finally breaks, because K33 notes prior recoveries from conditions like these involved prolonged consolidation rather than a sharp reversal. Also keep an eye on the German Bundestag bill, which still needs Bundesrat approval before customs can freeze self-custody coins for up to 180 days, a structural change to how holders can move bitcoin under scrutiny.

## MARKET ANALYSIS

Bitcoin is at $62,782.00, down 2.35% over 24 hours and down 12.1% over seven days. The derived Momentum-Sentiment Composite reads -13 on a -50 to +50 scale. Sellers hold the initiative. The tape has lost roughly a quarter of its value over thirty days, and the Fear & Greed reading of 10 tells you sentiment has already priced a lot of that damage. Support at $58,500 is the line that matters now: a close above it keeps the range intact, while losing it opens the door to the $54,500 downside target. What would flip control is a reclaim of $67,000, which would put the $71,000 upside target in play and force short-side pressure to unwind. Until one of those edges breaks, expect chop between the two.

## SCENARIOS

- Holding The $58,500 Shelf (32%): triggers: a daily close at or above $58,500 that holds through Friday, with Fear & Greed lifting off its 10 reading. Invalidation: any daily close below $58,500 within five trading days.
- Reclaim Of $67,000 (12%): the market needs a decisive daily close above $67,000 to confirm buyers have taken back control, and only then does the $71,000 upside target come into view. Invalidation: a daily close back below $67,000 within five trading days.
- Break Of $58,500 Toward $54,500 (56%): with sentiment this depressed and the thirty-day trend still pointing down, the likelier path is a daily close below $58,500 that opens the $54,500 downside target. Invalidation: a daily close back above $58,500 within five trading days.

## KEY MARKET MOVERS

- **Miner treasury selling:** Ionic Digital's 737 BTC sale is one instance of a broader pattern where miners redirect coins into infrastructure rather than hold them, and the filing gives no sale date, so the overhang may not be finished.

## TOP STORIES

### 1. Ionic Digital Sells 737 Bitcoin to Fund Data Center Buildout
**URL:** https://t.co/0QfYYwRKsi
**Published:** 2026-11-18 10:39 AM CT
**Summary:** Ionic Digital sold about 737 bitcoin after the end of September for roughly $61.6 million, at an average of $83,600 per coin net of trading costs. The sales cut Ionic's bitcoin holdings by about 25% from the 2,954 BTC it held at Sept. 30, leaving roughly 2,217 BTC. Ionic said it intends to use the proceeds to fund development of its existing data center sites, and the filing does not say when the coins were sold. Bitcoin traded near $64,000 on Wednesday morning, about 23% below Ionic's average sale price. Ionic swung to a $17.4 million net profit for the quarter on revenue of about $49.0 million, with digital infrastructure leasing contributing $43.9 million while mining revenue fell to $5.1 million from $37.1 million a year earlier.

### 2. K33: Bitcoin Below $70,000 Is a 'Gift From the Market'
**URL:** https://t.co/kPKELSaqIy
**Published:** 2026-11-18 11:30 AM CT
**Summary:** K33 Research called bitcoin's 14% weekly drop "deep value territory" and said any entry below $70,000 is a gift for medium- to long-term investors. Head of research Vetle Lunde noted bitcoin has posted six straight red weekly candles and is on track for a record 13 consecutive days of lower daily highs. Bitcoin traded near $62,300 on Wednesday, about 8.5% under its 200-week moving average near $68,000 at the Nov. 15 low, and daily RSI fell to 19.95. Net outflows from bitcoin exchange-traded products reached 44,900 BTC over the 14 trading days since Oct. 29, total ETF holdings fell to about 1.46 million BTC, and roughly $1.3 billion in long positions were liquidated on Nov. 13 and 14. Lunde stopped short of calling the decline over, saying earlier recoveries from similar conditions involved prolonged consolidation, while spot volume near $5 billion a day from Friday through Sunday was the busiest weekend since February.

### 3. CryptoQuant: Bitcoin Back in Bearish Phase but Now in a 'Value Zone'
**URL:** https://t.co/28URC8t7sg
**Published:** 2026-11-18 11:12 AM CT
**Summary:** CryptoQuant said bitcoin has fallen back into a bearish regime after dropping below its 200-day and 365-day moving averages of $72,900 and $75,900. Bitcoin hit a four-month low of about $61,000 on Nov. 15 and traded near $62,500 at the time of writing. Total bitcoin demand growth is contracting at the fastest pace since July 1, falling below -400,000 BTC on a 30-day basis, and holders realized a net loss of 25,800 BTC in the recent sell-off, the largest daily reading since July 13. CryptoQuant's Bull Score Index sits at 10 out of 100, an extreme bear phase, and only 58% of analysts tracked by its consensus index remain bullish, down from 77% on October 7. The firm nonetheless flagged a value zone, with traders' unrealized profit/loss margin at -20%, the most negative since July 1, and pointed to $62,000 to $65,000 as a range where long-term holders sold heavily and new buyers may defend their cost basis.

### 4. Japan's 20-Year Bond Auction Draws Weaker Demand as Yen Funding Holds Steady
**URL:** https://t.co/m7Qk5Jwg9o
**Published:** 2026-11-18 06:50 PM CT
**Summary:** Japan's Nov. 18 auction of 20-year government bond issue 198 drew competitive tenders worth 3.64 times the amount accepted, down from 5.84 times at the October sale. The Finance Ministry received ¥1.914 trillion in competitive tenders and accepted ¥525.8 billion, while the average accepted yield rose 3.3 basis points to 3.756%. The Bank of Japan's 5 p.m. Tokyo dollar-yen midpoint moved from 159.34 to 159.35 yen per dollar, and Tokyo Tanshi reported an unsecured overnight call rate of 1.227%, unchanged from the prior day. Bitfinex reported aggregate Bitcoin futures open interest fell to 645,750 BTC over Nov. 14 and 15, 8% below Nov. 11, though that total gives no breakdown by funding currency. A trader who borrows yen short-term to hold Bitcoin faces higher renewal costs if funding rates rise, and a stronger yen makes repaying unhedged yen debt more expensive in dollar terms.

### 5. Germany moves to freeze Bitcoin for up to 180 days, even without access to private keys
**URL:** https://t.co/wYDTqTks4J
**Published:** 2026-11-18 02:40 PM CT
**Summary:** Germany's Bundestag approved a bill on Nov. 12 that lets customs authorities freeze suspicious crypto holdings, including Bitcoin held in self-custody wallets. The committee text sets assets worth more than €100,000 as a general benchmark for significant holdings, and authorities may combine closely connected assets when judging whether they qualify. Customs would get 30 days to investigate, and a finance court could extend the restriction by another 150 days, for a maximum of 180 days, if investigators show credible doubts about origin. For coins on an exchange, authorities can serve an attachment order and the custodian must restrict withdrawals; for self-custody, Section 321 of the Fiscal Code lets authorities serve the holder with a legal ban on disposal, so the owner keeps signing access but is legally barred from transferring the Bitcoin. The Blockchain Bundesverband warned that identifying a wallet does not establish who controls it, especially where several parties share signing authority, and the bill still needs Bundesrat approval and publication in the Federal Law Gazette.

### 6. German Judge Offers Movie2K Defendant Trial Exit for 40,000 BTC
**URL:** https://t.co/NlWlMrhC38
**Published:** 2026-11-18 08:20 AM CT
**Summary:** A Leipzig judge has offered to end the trial of the alleged Movie2K operator if the 43-year-old defendant hands over 40,000 BTC and pays €38 million ($42 million) in compensation for potential victims. Prosecutors believe the defendant still holds about 56,000 BTC, so accepting the deal would leave him roughly 16,000 BTC, worth around €940 million ($1 billion) at current prices. A co-defendant was offered a deal to surrender 600 BTC and pay €17 million ($19 million), and his lawyer said she could accept it. The main defendant handed over nearly 50,000 BTC in early 2024, and Saxony authorities sold those coins later that year for about €2.64 billion ($2.9 billion), with the proceeds held in a state judicial treasury account until a final ruling. The copyright violations are time-barred, so the trial that began in February has focused on money laundering and tax evasion, and the judge has reportedly expressed doubts about proving some charges because legally and illegally acquired Bitcoin may have been mixed in the defendant's accounts.

#US Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz met with Moroccan Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita in Rabat on November 17, outlining the next steps in the diplomatic process concerning #WesternSahara.

Waltz stated that Russia’s veto of a US-drafted resolution at the UN Security Council on October 30 had not changed Washington’s position. He reaffirmed that the United States continues to recognize #Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara and remains committed to pursuing a political settlement based on Morocco’s autonomy plan.

The meeting also addressed three rounds of negotiations held in Washington and Madrid in January and February 2026, involving #Morocco, #Algeria, #Mauritania, and the #Polisario Front. Those discussions covered the powers of an autonomous administration, natural resource management and revenue-sharing, transitional governance, electoral arrangements, disarmament, and international security guarantees.

Bourita announced that Morocco and the United States had developed new proposals aimed at addressing the concerns of the parties and facilitating a political compromise. However, he did not disclose the content of these proposals or indicate whether they had been formally presented to Algeria and the Polisario Front.

Waltz also called on the Polisario Front to return to the ceasefire and refrain from military activities. He emphasized that the United States would continue working with the UN to pursue a political settlement.

The visit took place as MINURSO began withdrawing from Western Sahara following the expiration of its mandate on October 31. Waltz met with the mission’s head, Alexander Ivanko, to discuss the safe withdrawal of 158 unarmed military observers. The withdrawal process is expected to be completed by January 31, 2027.

### Core Positions and Actions
- **No benefit cuts**: Trump has repeatedly pledged not to cut Social Security benefits or raise the retirement age. Administration statements emphasize defending the program for seniors.

- **Tax relief for seniors**: He campaigned on ending federal income taxes on Social Security benefits. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (signed July 4, 2025) did **not** change the underlying rules that tax up to 85% of benefits for higher-income recipients. Instead, it created a temporary additional $6,000 deduction (per eligible individual aged 65+) for 2025–2028. This reduces the number of people who owe taxes on benefits (administration estimates have cited figures around 88% paying none). SSA actuaries estimated the law reduces trust-fund revenue by roughly $168.6 billion over 10 years and advanced the OASI depletion date by about one quarter (to Q4 2032).[]
(<https://t.co/dVPJe46BBp>

- **Fraud, waste, and ineligible recipients**: The administration has focused on restricting benefits for illegal aliens and ineligible individuals, plus efficiency measures. Trump has described these as ways to strengthen the program without cutting earned benefits.

- **Growth and other revenues**: Campaign-era comments referenced economic growth, energy production, and related measures as ways to improve the fiscal picture, without detailed Social Security-specific modeling.

🚩🚩🚩🚩🚩🚩🚩🚩🚩### Recent Development:🚩🚩🚩🚩🚩 Cassidy $1.5 Trillion Investment Fund
As of mid-November 2026, Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-LA) has stated that Trump personally committed to support a proposal Cassidy has promoted (sometimes with bipartisan interest, including from Sen. Tim Kaine):

- Borrow roughly $1.5 trillion over five years ($250–300 billion annually).
- Place the funds in a🚩🚩🚩🚩 **separate** investment fund (not the existing Social Security trust funds, and not using payroll-tax dollars).
- Invest in a diversified portfolio of stocks, bonds, and other assets for 65–75 years.
- Use the compounded returns to cover an estimated 60–70% of the long-term unfunded obligation, then repay the Treasury.

Cassidy has described it as making the program “evergreen” without cutting benefits or raising payroll taxes for current retirees, modeled in part on the railroad retirement investment approach. Independent analyses (e.g., from the Boston College Center for Retirement Research) have questioned the probability that the returns would fully cover the borrowing under various market scenarios. The plan remains a proposal, not enacted law.[]
(<https://t.co/qi9ZhlyXXu>)

In short, Trump’s approach prioritizes protecting current benefit levels and providing tax relief for seniors, combined with anti-fraud measures. The Cassidy investment-fund idea is the most concrete longer-term solvency concept recently linked to his support, but it is not yet legislation and differs from both pure tax-increase plans and traditional benefit-formula reforms.

text:
Creature Features Ends 10-Year Production Run, Continues in Syndication
The cast is now filming The Creature Feature Movie: The Bodega Bay Slasher for release in summer 2027.

Crowhaven Productions, based in Windsor, California, has ended production of new live-action episodes of Creature Features after a 10-year run. The show will continue in syndication on 45 television stations nationwide. It will also continue on YouTube, where its channel has nearly half a million subscribers.

Creature Features premiered on Northbay TV on Saturday, October 29, 2016, and moved to San Francisco’s KOFY TV20 shortly afterward. For five years, it was KOFY’s most popular Saturday night show. Its run on the station ended when KOFY switched to Grit TV, a network specializing in Westerns.

Creature Features was both a reboot of the original horror movie show hosted by Bob Wilkins and a spinoff of Crowhaven Productions’ sitcom House on the Hill, which aired during the 2011–2012 television season.

The syndication run opens with the first season, which Crowhaven is also showing on YouTube. During the show’s first two seasons, only a handful of stations broadcast Creature Features, and few episodes from those years were ever posted online. For much of the audience, this will be a first look at how the show began.

Over the past decade, Crowhaven produced 480 two-hour episodes of the flagship Creature Features, 106 episodes of Creature Feature Friday and 50 episodes of Livingston Presents.

“I’ve been writing for these characters for almost twenty years, and for the last ten we’ve had a date with the audience every week. That’s a commitment I’m proud we kept. I’m ready to give up the weekly deadline, and I feel good about bringing the show to a close while I still have such affection for it,” said Jeff Bodean, who created the show and plays its host, Vincent Van Dahl.

The cast and crew are currently shooting The Creature Feature Movie: The Bodega Bay Slasher, set for release in summer 2027. The film features the entire series cast, with Bodean as Vincent, Raven Green as Livingston, Ali Noel as Tangella, Andy Gatley as Handrew, Abby Pforsich as Mrs. O’Connor and Ken Garr as Maurice the Chef. Joining them are former Creature Features guests Kathy Coleman of Land of the Lost and Jon Provost, who played Timmy on Lassie.

Over the years, guests have included actors Tom Sizemore, Samantha Mathis, Veronica Carlson, Candace Hilligoss and Charlotte Stewart, as well as activist Erin Brockovich. Musicians Steve “Zetro” Sousa, Mario Cipollina, Peter Albin and Norman Greenbaum also visited, as did filmmakers Bill Lustig, Steve Wang and Dean Cundey.

Asked about his plans after the film is finished, Bodean said, “I’m looking at buying a run-down castle just outside of Edinburgh, Scotland. I may see if the BBC would like a series of Creature Features from there. But a lot depends on what the roofer says.”

Crowhaven Productions will continue producing Fright Show, which presents horror movies without the live-action segments seen on Creature Features. It airs every Friday night on YouTube.

text:
SCI Questions Court's Decision After 670 Deer Killed in Initial Catalina Island Operation

Organization calls for greater transparency and scientific scrutiny as legal challenge continues

Safari Club International (SCI) is raising new concerns about the Catalina Island Conservancy's effort to eradicate the island's mule deer population. New information released by the Conservancy confirms reports that 670 deer were killed during the initial removal operation–more than three times the deer originally anticipated.

The operation, conducted in the Middle Ranch area during September and October, covered approximately 5,300 acres and was intended to assess removal methods, better understand deer numbers and distribution, and inform future islandwide operations.

The Conservancy's 2025 surveys estimated approximately 2,040 deer across the island's interior, excluding Avalon. The Conservancy also predicted that initial removal operations would remove 200 deer. However, the removal of 670 deer in a single operational area substantially exceeded initial projections, and casts doubt on the Conservancy's claims about the difficulty of controlling deer through hunting.

For SCI, these developments underscore the need for greater transparency, independent scrutiny, and a thorough evaluation of the decisions driving this project.

"When an operation results in the removal of more than three times the number of deer originally anticipated, it warrants a closer examination of the information guiding these decisions," said W. Laird Hamberlin, CEO of SCI. "We are talking about the permanent elimination of an established wildlife population, and decisions of this magnitude should never move forward without a transparent process, a thorough evaluation of the science, and meaningful public accountability."

SCI and its litigation partners have challenged the California Department of Fish and Wildlife's approval of the Catalina Island Restoration Project, arguing that the agency failed to comply with the environmental review and public participation requirements of California law. The coalition also challenged the agency's authority to authorize the complete eradication of a longstanding game mammal population through the Restoration Management Permit.

Although the Los Angeles County Superior Court dismissed the coalition's claims in September, the ruling did not resolve the broader concerns surrounding the ecological consequences of the project or the need for independent scrutiny of the Conservancy's underlying scientific claims. SCI appealed the lower court's decision and sought a stay of any further eradication until the appeal is resolved.

The latest developments make that commitment all the more important. The Conservancy has indicated that additional deer removal operations are planned to begin in mid-2027, with the initial assessment now serving as a basis for expanding its efforts.

"Once Catalina's deer population is eliminated, that resource cannot simply be restored," Hamberlin continued. "The consequences of this decision extend beyond the loss of individual animals. Catalina will lose an established wildlife population, a resource valued by residents and visitors, and a longstanding hunting opportunity for California sportsmen and women. We will not abandon the legal questions at the heart of this case simply because the first phase of removal has been completed."

SCI maintains that decisions involving the permanent removal of wildlife populations should be supported by rigorous scientific evaluation, lawful practices, and meaningful public participation.

text:
$PCYO Q4 2026 earnings: Pure Cycle beats its annual plan, but next year slows

Pure Cycle, a Colorado water utility and land developer, beat its full-year revenue target on winter lot progress and oil-field water demand, but entered a proxy fight with uncontracted lots. Fourth-quarter revenue rose 18% to $13.2 million, well above what the company's own full-year plan pointed to, though profit fell 8% as oil royalties dried up. Chief executive Mark Harding said the board will now sell off its 51 rental homes and reserved lots because borrowing costs rose while rents stagnated.

• FY26 revenue: $𝟑𝟓.𝟕𝐌 (+37% from a year ago)
• Q4 revenue: $𝟏𝟑.𝟐𝐌 (+18% from a year ago)
• Q4 profit per share: $𝟎.𝟐𝟑 (-8% from a year ago)
• Next-12-month builder payments outlook: 𝐂𝐮𝐭 𝐭𝐨 ~$𝟏𝟎𝐌 ($14.8M expected at Q3)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🔴 Bearish

The story got worse because next year's land pipeline lacks buyer commitments while cash is tied up in community receivables and a proxy contest. Grading the next 154-lot phase to 34% completion without a single builder contract exposes the company if high mortgage rates keep housing demand slow, and the proxy fight already forced management to halt share buybacks. The good news: liquidating the rental home portfolio ends a capital-heavy distraction and will pay down debt.

The question now is whether homebuilders will sign contracts for the new Phase 2E lots before the current Phase 2D work finishes. Either builders commit in time to keep lot revenue flowing, or construction pauses and leaves fiscal 2027 reliant on volatile oil-field water sales. First-quarter contract disclosures and proxy filings will tell.

[Model: Gemini 4 Argon. Full article with charts - link in bio]

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢 concern eased — 𝐏𝐮𝐫𝐞 𝐂𝐲𝐜𝐥𝐞 𝐈𝐬 𝐋𝐢𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐈𝐭𝐬 𝐑𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐁𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐬
Pure Cycle began building single-family homes to rent at Sky Ranch, its master-planned community near Denver, in 2021. After trimming the expansion plan over the past two quarters, the board decided to exit the business altogether because "our cost of capital has increased while rental rates have remained flat".

The company will not invest in any new rental houses beyond its 51 completed units and existing construction contracts. Instead, it will "sell our rental homes and remaining reserved lots in an orderly manner", listing two to four houses at a time as leases expire and offering tenants the chance to buy.

During fiscal 2026, the developer already resold or contracted to resell 19 reserved rental lots back to homebuilders. Winding the portfolio down removes a major cash drain, because the rental unit asset balance more than tripled this year to $18.3 million and drove most of the new borrowing. Management will use sale proceeds to pay off the home loans and fund land and water projects.

What to watch: the sale prices and debt paydowns on the first batch of rental homes in the first-quarter filing. Those figures will show whether Pure Cycle can recover more than its $18.3 million book cost.

🟢 𝐎𝐢𝐥 𝐃𝐫𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐃𝐫𝐨𝐯𝐞 𝐚 𝐑𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐫𝐝 𝐖𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐘𝐞𝐚𝐫
Pure Cycle supplies wholesale water to homes at Sky Ranch and to oil and gas drillers across its Colorado service area. Industrial water sales carry no minimum purchase commitments, so volumes swing with drilling schedules, which makes the segment both the main growth driver and a key revenue risk.

• Fourth-quarter water delivered: 638 acre-feet, up 226% from 196 acre-feet a year ago
• Full-year oil and gas water delivered: 1,118 acre-feet, up from 194 acre-feet in fiscal 2025
• Full-year water and wastewater revenue: $13.4 million, up 30% from a year ago
• Full-year oil and gas royalty income: $2.0 million, down 70% from $6.7 million as older wells declined

Strong demand from energy operators for fracking water more than made up for the $4.7 million drop in well royalties and a 13% dip in tap fees, which are one-time charges builders pay to connect new homes to water lines. By our math, pre-tax profit excluding well royalties rose 56% for the year. Management expects industrial water demand to hold up in fiscal 2027.

What to watch: quarterly acre-feet delivered to oil and gas operators in fiscal 2027. A drop toward fiscal 2025 levels would show that the drilling rig has moved off Pure Cycle's service area.

🟢 𝐖𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐋𝐨𝐭 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐠𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐂𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐝 𝐚 𝐂𝐚𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐮𝐬 𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐧
Pure Cycle recognizes lot sales revenue as construction progresses under percentage-of-completion accounting. Three months ago, its full-year revenue outlook of $28 million to $32 million implied just $5.5 million to $9.5 million of fourth-quarter revenue by our math, even though the quarterly filing scheduled $12.5 million of contracted lot revenue by year-end.

Actual fourth-quarter revenue reached $13.2 million, up 17.6% from a year ago, as a mild winter let crews advance Phase 2D to 89% completion. That pushed full-year revenue up 36.8% to $35.7 million and lifted full-year operating margin by 10.2 percentage points to 37.5%, because general and administrative overhead fell by 7.7 percentage points of revenue to 22.1%. Beating the implied fourth-quarter range proves the prior outlook was cautious, not that housing demand accelerated.

What to watch: land development gross margin in the first half of fiscal 2027. A drop below the fourth quarter's 74.8% by our math would show that the remaining warranty and landscaping work on Phases 2C and 2D carries lower profitability.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐍𝐞𝐱𝐭 𝐋𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐏𝐡𝐚𝐬𝐞 𝐇𝐚𝐬 𝐍𝐨 𝐁𝐮𝐲𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐘𝐞𝐭
Pure Cycle normally signs purchase contracts with homebuilders before grading a new land phase at Sky Ranch. For Phase 2E, which holds 154 lots, management broke its own rule and advanced construction to 34% completion "ahead of a signed commitment to take advantage of Colorado’s seasonal construction window".

As of August 31, not a single Phase 2E lot was under contract, so the company could not record any revenue on the work. At the same time, fourth-quarter water and wastewater tap fee revenue fell 59.5% from a year ago to $0.8 million by our math, selling just 20 water taps and 18 wastewater taps in the quarter, including water-only irrigation connections for the new charter high school.

Builders buy residential taps only when they pull a building permit to start a house, so slow tap sales point to cautious construction on existing lots. Pure Cycle warned that "we expect housing demand to remain subdued given higher mortgage rates and economic uncertainty", which makes building speculative lots riskier.

What to watch: signed builder contracts on Phase 2E in the first-quarter report. Until builders sign, Pure Cycle spends cash on grading without collecting milestone payments or recording lot revenue.

🔴🔴 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐦𝐮𝐧𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐑𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐢𝐯𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐎𝐮𝐭𝐠𝐫𝐞𝐰 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐃𝐞𝐛𝐭
"Strong stewardship of our liquidity and balance sheet continues to allow us to capitalize on these opportunities," chief executive Mark Harding said. Pure Cycle fronts the money for roads, parks, and public utilities at Sky Ranch and records an interest-bearing IOUs balance from the Sky Ranch Community Authority Board (CAB), the local taxing district that repays the company from future property taxes and bond sales.

• Related-party receivable from the CAB: $63.0 million, up 39.9% from $45.0 million a year ago
• New advances added to the receivable: $18.0 million for the year and $3.9 million in the fourth quarter by our math
• Total cash and restricted cash: $16.8 million, down 40.7% from $28.4 million a year ago by our math
• Total debt: $17.6 million, up 159.4% from $6.8 million a year ago by our math

The numbers cut against Harding's liquidity claim because total debt now exceeds total cash for the first time in years, and the CAB receivable makes up 34.0% of total assets. While the note generated $3.8 million of non-cash interest income, it consumed real cash alongside rental home and water spending.

What to watch: cash repayments from the CAB in fiscal 2027, when management previously aimed to refinance district bonds and collect $8 million to $10 million.

🔴 𝐀 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐱𝐲 𝐅𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭 𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐩𝐩𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐒𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐁𝐮𝐲𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐬
Pure Cycle spent four quarters telling investors it would buy back more stock as cash arrived, and last quarter three board members resigned, including two linked to a 13% shareholder. In fiscal 2026, the company repurchased just 26,100 shares for $0.3 million, including 7,500 shares in the fourth quarter by our math.

Now management has frozen the buyback program entirely "due to the cost and uncertainty created by the pending proxy contest", leaving 78,474 shares unused under its authorization. It also warned that fiscal 2027 results "will include significant costs related to the pending proxy contest", which will directly inflate general and administrative expenses and hold down earnings.

What to watch: proxy filings and general and administrative expenses in the first half of fiscal 2027. Those disclosures will reveal the dissident shareholder's demands and how much legal and advisory fees are costing the company.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Four standing issues from prior quarters received no new figures or timelines in the year-end earnings release.

• Interstate 70 interchange permit: Harding mentioned investing in the planned interchange, but gave no permit date from state regulators; the annual report will show if late-2027 construction still holds.
• Customer concentration: two builders and two energy operators drove over half of nine-month revenue; the annual filing's footnote will show full-year concentration.
• Land acquisitions: unmentioned in the release after six quarters of no deals; any announced purchase would test liquidity.
• Fiscal 2028 targets: management's old goals of $62.3 million in revenue and $1.63 in earnings per share went unmentioned for a fifth straight quarter.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐃𝐞𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐫𝐞𝐝 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟒): $𝟐.𝟓𝟏 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Deferred revenue — upfront cash payments from homebuilders for lot work not yet completed — fell 25.1% from a year ago and 8.8% from the third quarter. The balance shrank as Pure Cycle finished construction on Phases 2C and 2D faster than it signed new builder contracts for Phase 2E.

𝐃𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟒): 𝟐𝟒.𝟏𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
Fourth-quarter diluted shares rose 0.05% from a year ago to 24.15 million, while the full-year average ticked down 0.04% to 24.16 million. Repurchasing 26,100 shares for $0.3 million during the year barely offset stock compensation, and buybacks are now on hold.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐌𝐢𝐥𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐧𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐢𝐬𝐡𝐞𝐝 𝐥𝐨𝐭 𝐩𝐚𝐲𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 (𝐧𝐞𝐱𝐭 𝟏𝟐 𝐦𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐡𝐬): ~$𝟏𝟎.𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠇 cut from $14.8 million
Cut. Pure Cycle expects about $10 million in cash milestone and finished lot payments from homebuilders over the next 12 months, down 32.4% from the $14.8 million rolling figure given three months ago. The drop reflects collections already made in the fourth quarter and the lack of signed contracts on Phase 2E.

𝐖𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐰𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐰𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐭𝐚𝐩 𝐟𝐞𝐞𝐬 (𝐧𝐞𝐱𝐭 𝟏𝟐 𝐦𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐡𝐬): ~$𝟕.𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
New. Management expects to collect about $7.5 million in water and wastewater tap fees over the next 12 months. By our math, that implies a 17.5% increase over the $6.4 million of tap fee revenue recorded in fiscal 2026 as builders pull permits on Phase 2C and 2D lots.

𝐑𝐞𝐦𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐏𝐡𝐚𝐬𝐞 𝟐 𝐭𝐚𝐩 𝐟𝐞𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 (𝐧𝐞𝐱𝐭 𝟑 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐬): >$𝟏𝟓.𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠇 cut from >$19.0 million
Cut. The company estimates remaining lots in Sky Ranch Phase 2 will generate more than $15 million in tap fee revenue over the next three years, down from the $19 million-plus estimate carried for the past four quarters as taps were sold during fiscal 2026.

𝐏𝐡𝐚𝐬𝐞 𝟐𝐃 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐏𝐡𝐚𝐬𝐞 𝟐𝐄 𝐥𝐨𝐭 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐞𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧: 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐞𝐭𝐞 𝐢𝐧 𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟕  ⇘ decelerating
🠇 cut from Phase 2D in FY26; Phase 2E in FY27
Cut. Phase 2D ended fiscal 2026 at 89% completion rather than substantially complete as planned, shifting final completion of its 204 lots into fiscal 2027 alongside the 154-lot Phase 2E, which is 34% complete and paced to builder demand.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐢𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐧𝐨 𝐟𝐢𝐬𝐜𝐚𝐥 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐨𝐫 𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬 𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐥𝐨𝐨𝐤?
Pure Cycle issued full-year revenue and earnings per share ranges in its prior year-end presentation, but gave none in this release. Investors need to know whether the absence of Phase 2E contracts and the proxy fight prevented a forecast.

𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐛𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐬𝐢𝐠𝐧 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐬 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐏𝐡𝐚𝐬𝐞 𝟐𝐄 𝐥𝐨𝐭𝐬?
The company graded Phase 2E to 34% completion without a signed homebuilder commitment, breaking its normal rule. If contracts do not land before winter ends, revenue recognition will stall after Phase 2D wraps up.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐱𝐲 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐜𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐢𝐧 𝐟𝐢𝐬𝐜𝐚𝐥 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕?
Management warned of significant proxy contest costs and suspended share buybacks to preserve liquidity. Quantifying the expected legal and advisory expense is essential to sizing fiscal 2027 operating margins.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐟𝐢𝐫𝐬𝐭 𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐡𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐬 𝐟𝐞𝐭𝐜𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐠?
Pure Cycle sold one rental house after year-end and plans to sell all 51 units over time. Knowing the net proceeds after repaying the property loans will show how much cash returns to the core water and land businesses.

If the @DPWorldTour wanted to take their power back on the world stage, 2027 is the time. People keep saying they have no leverage in the strategic alliance now “without the LIV threat” but that’s not true. The leverage has always been about the players & the @rydercup. 
*Scenario*: a collective of (now) DPWT members presents a series of 6-8 elevated events, fully funded by Private Equity (mostly based in the UK) that would be 50% owned by the players. This PE also commits to funding the inevitable shortfall in the Strategic Alliance (currently being negotiated) so that the European Tour doesn’t have to give up too much to the @PGATour & maintain balance. 
The next move is changing the @RyderCupEurope requirement from 4 European Tour events to, say 8 events minimum in order to maintain membership & eligibility (Rory/Tyrrell/Fox played 9 in 2026 so it’s doable). You can still play the PGA Tour if you want, but it’s not necessary (PGAT is probably dropping the min event requirement anyway as Rolapp said). Between the 5 #RolexSeries & the 6-8 elevated events (limited field, that also has a team-element & maybe shotgun starts, music, etc) and 4 majors, that gives players a 15 to 17 event global schedule of elevated purses. And you can still handpick PGAT events like The Players, home Opens & a few more events to round out your schedule that you’re qualified for. A World Tour, with no deference to the PGAT without the division?
Oh, and the broadcasts would be handled by European Tour Productions in conjunction with the PE that already has experience with media rights, YouTube, monetization, etc to broadcast them in a way so that a larger swath of global fans can not only watch it, but actually ENJOY the watch. Hmmm 🤔. Sign me up!
Not saying that’s happening, but it’s certainly a possibility - food for thought. 
Remember #TradingPlaces and the scene near the end when the Duke Brothers thought they had the market cornered, only to be usurped by the people they thought they had ruined & had full control over? Welp, here’s your shot! Do you want to be a feeder or stand on your own? 🤷🏽‍♂️

text:
Another spectacular display @ByJasonLloyd this week, reaching new lows in his increasingly desperate and failing years-long campaign to cancel Deshaun Watson in Cleveland. 

On the Monday morning after the biggest Browns win in three years, Lloyd made his column at the Athletic all about how some empty seats in the crowd were due to fan opposition to the quarterback, and somehow had nothing to do with the two-game losing streak, the bad weather, or economic factors. Nevermind the influence of hacks like him who drag the fans down with their ulterior agendas. ("We're all trying to find the guy who did this!") 

Then he goes on the radio and throws a tantrum about the fact that this year's Browns have some of the best locker room chemistry we've ever seen in Cleveland, let alone in the entire league, and that Deshaun is obviously a catalyst for that. "It doesn't matter that the young players in this winning locker room love their playmaking quarterback," he says, sternly. 

Wins don't matter, and locker room chemistry doesn't matter, including especially with the second youngest roster in the NFL in Cleveland. This QB has simply got to go at any cost. It's beyond absurd, and extremely telling of how broken and tightly controlled our media system is in this country that guys like Lloyd are permitted to continue carrying on like he is after having so thoroughly discredited themselves as he has (it's worth a look back at Lloyd's work from previous years trashing the QB to see how committed he is to this bit, per a couple of the screenshots attached here). It's also more to show the extent to which "sports talk" is used as a Trojan horse for ruling-class propaganda: Deshaun got too uppity with the owners in forcing his way out of Houston and some of the owners' loyal hacks in the press will never stop trying to punish the QB for it, whether out of inertia or because they know where their bread is buttered. (Side note: In 1983, 90% of American media companies were owned by 50 companies, which was bad enough. Today, almost all media is controlled by six corporations: Comcast, Walt Disney, Warner Bros. Discovery, Paramount Skydance, Sony, and Amazon.) 

And what's especially ironic and also glorious about this is that a big reason why this locker room has such good chemistry is due to its solidarity against hacks like Lloyd who, the players know as well as anyone, have been trying to poison the home crowd against Watson for years. It's actually one of the better stories the NFL has had going for it in awhile, which just becomes more obvious as guys like Lloyd try to spin their counter-narratives and keep gnashing their teeth about, of all things, the Browns winning with one of the youngest rosters in the league. It's almost like the football version of "Major League."

THE EVIDENCE™

Wolves in Sheep’s Clothing: When the Right Helps the Left

The evidence will be presented. The verdict is yours.

An opponent who openly declares his intentions gives you something to work with. You can examine his proposals, challenge his arguments, and organize against him. The more difficult problem is the politician who asks for your trust, campaigns on your principles, and then helps preserve the very policies he promised to confront.

The first tells you where he stands. The second leaves you wondering whom you actually elected.

Jesus warned: “Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.” He then supplied the test: “Ye shall know them by their fruits.” — Matthew 7:15–16, KJV.

The passage concerns false prophets. Its warning about deceptive appearances also offers a useful question for political judgment: What does the conduct reveal that the presentation conceals?

A Republican label establishes a party affiliation. It does not establish courage, integrity, constitutional fidelity, or independence from the people financing a political career. Those qualities must be demonstrated.

For conservative voters, the legitimate concern is straightforward: How much of the agenda they oppose survives because people elected to resist it eventually accommodate it?

There are several possible answers, and they should not be carelessly treated as interchangeable. Some officials sincerely disagree with their voters. Some make compromises they believe will produce a better result. Others lack the courage to accept the consequences of their stated convictions. Still others may find the existing arrangement personally or politically advantageous.

Actual coordination to conceal wrongdoing would be a more serious allegation. Calling someone a co-conspirator requires evidence of an agreement and participation. A disappointing vote alone cannot establish that. But voters do not need to prove a criminal conspiracy before deciding that an official has betrayed a promise.

They need a record.

Consider what an honest examination would ask. What did the candidate promise? What authority did the official actually possess? What legislation did he introduce, support, amend, or block? What oversight did he pursue? When an opportunity arose to demand disclosure, did he use it? When he abandoned a commitment, what explanation did he give?

These questions move the argument beyond an angry television clip. They make evasion harder.

The same discipline must apply to claims of bipartisan misconduct. Republican participation in an investigation does not, by itself, establish Republican participation in a political fabrication. In 2020, for example, the Republican-led Senate Intelligence Committee released a bipartisan report examining Russian interference and counterintelligence vulnerabilities surrounding the 2016 election. Whether one agrees with every conclusion or interpretation, the report must be examined on its evidence; the involvement of both parties does not settle the question in either direction.

That distinction protects the credibility of the larger argument. If every disagreement becomes treachery, the word loses its usefulness when genuine deception appears.

The more revealing case is a repeated contradiction between promise and performance.

A politician campaigns against expanding government, then supports its expansion without explaining the reversal. He demands accountability while out of power, then becomes reluctant to investigate once responsibility reaches his own relationships. He asks voters to accept one more exception, one more delay, one more agreement that leaves the underlying problem intact.

At some point, voters are entitled to stop evaluating the speech and start evaluating the pattern.

Opposition must be measured by what an official does with the authority voters entrusted to him.

That does not mean every battle can be won. A House member cannot individually repeal a law. A senator cannot compel every colleague to vote with him. Courts, statutory limits, competing obligations, and narrow majorities create real constraints. An honest assessment acknowledges them.

But constraints should be explained concretely. “We could not accomplish this because these votes were missing” is an explanation voters can investigate. “Washington is complicated” is an invitation to stop asking.

There is also a political incentive worth watching: a problem can remain useful to someone who campaigns against it. It can supply fundraising appeals, interviews, and another reason to request reelection. That incentive does not prove any particular official deliberately preserves the problem. It does justify asking whether his efforts match the urgency of his appeals.

If the warning is always urgent but the response is always deferred, examine the discrepancy.

Conservative voters should also resist granting their own officials the exemptions they condemn in Democrats. If secrecy is unacceptable, demand disclosure from Republican officeholders. If conflicts of interest deserve scrutiny, scrutinize Republican relationships. If an abuse of authority is wrong, the identity of its beneficiary should not change the standard.

Otherwise, accountability becomes a campaign slogan whose application depends on the party registration of the accused.

The strongest criticism of those on the right who enable the left is therefore specific: Here is the promise. Here is the decision. Here is the consequence. Here is the explanation—and here is why it fails.

Name the vote. Link the record. Identify the authority. Show the inconsistency. Where evidence establishes knowing assistance in wrongdoing, present it plainly. Where it establishes political surrender, call it political surrender. Where the record remains incomplete, say what still needs to be uncovered.

Precision strengthens an accusation that can survive examination.

The verdict is that a political movement can be undermined by people who benefit from its trust while repeatedly abandoning its commitments. Voters are justified in demanding more than familiar slogans, agreeable interviews, and the correct letter beside a name.

The sheep’s clothing is the presentation.

The fruit is the record.

The evidence has been presented. The verdict is yours.

THE EVIDENCE™ | Kim Wojcinski — USA Best Selling Author
