text:
A bit more on Grant as - "The Steadfast Center" (in Sheridan's words) of Union Grand Strategy. Seriously, can any one deny he was a great general?  

The true measure of Ulysses S. Grant's greatness as a general lies not merely in the battles he won, the territory he captured, or the Confederate armies he compelled to surrender. It lies in something larger: his ability to conceive of the Civil War as a single, interconnected struggle and to make the widely separated armies of the Union serve one common strategic purpose. Grant was not simply a successful field commander. He was a grand strategist, and in the final years of the war he became the organizing intelligence behind the Union's military effort.

The transformation began with the great victories of 1863. The capture of Vicksburg on July 4 severed the Confederacy along the Mississippi River. The trans-Mississippi states were effectively cut off from the eastern Confederacy, making the movement of men, supplies, and matériel across the river extraordinarily difficult. The victory was more than the capture of a fortified city. It altered the geographical and logistical structure of the war.

A few months later, the victories at Chattanooga, including Lookout Mountain and Missionary Ridge, opened the gateway into Georgia and broke the Confederate hold on much of Tennessee. The Union now possessed a powerful position from which to advance into the Confederate interior. These victories were complementary. Vicksburg had divided the Confederacy along the Mississippi; Chattanooga threatened its vital railway connections and opened the route into the heart of the Deep South.

Grant understood the cumulative significance of these developments. He saw that the Confederacy could not be defeated merely by winning isolated battles or capturing strategically important cities. Its armies, transportation networks, industrial resources, communications, and capacity to sustain resistance had to be attacked as parts of a single system. The war had to be prosecuted everywhere, not episodically, and the Union's superior resources had to be brought to bear in a coordinated fashion.

His elevation to command of all Union armies in March 1864 provided the opportunity to put that conception into practice.

Grant's instructions to General George Meade on April 9, 1864, contain perhaps the clearest statement of his strategic philosophy:

"So far as practicable, all the armies are to move together and toward one common center."

The sentence is deceptively simple. Behind it lay a comprehensive plan involving Meade against Lee in Virginia, Butler operating against Richmond from the south, Sherman moving against Joseph E. Johnston and into Georgia, Banks concentrating against Mobile, and Union forces in West Virginia threatening Confederate communications and railroads. The details would change, and not every part of the plan would succeed. Banks's projected operation against Mobile, for example, did not unfold as Grant intended. But the governing conception was unmistakable: the Confederate armies were not to be permitted to reinforce one another at will while Union armies operated independently and gave the enemy opportunities to concentrate against them one at a time.

Grant intended to deny the Confederacy that freedom of movement. If Lee were pressed in Virginia, Johnston would be pressed in Georgia. If Confederate forces attempted to reinforce one theater, they would expose another. The Union armies would exert simultaneous pressure, compelling the Confederacy to defend an increasingly untenable position on multiple fronts.

Sherman's role was central to this design. Grant identified Johnston's army as his immediate objective and the "heart of Georgia as his ultimate aim." Sherman was to break Johnston's capacity to resist, penetrate the Confederate interior, and damage the resources that sustained the war. In practical terms, this meant that Sherman would be exerting pressure on the Confederate rear while Grant confronted Lee in Virginia. The armies were separated geographically, but their operations were strategically connected.

It is important to distinguish Grant's strategic conception from the precise operational plan Sherman later devised. Grant did not lay out the March to the Sea in April 1864. That particular march emerged after Atlanta fell, when Sherman proposed moving through Georgia to the coast. Grant approved it. The distinction does not diminish Grant's achievement. On the contrary, it illustrates one of his greatest qualities: he established the strategic objectives and gave capable subordinates considerable latitude in determining how best to accomplish them.

The campaign against Atlanta demonstrated the effectiveness of that relationship. Sherman kept Johnston's army under relentless pressure, eventually forced its retreat, and captured Atlanta in September 1864. The city was a major railway junction, industrial center, and supply depot. Its loss was a serious blow to the Confederacy and a tremendous political victory for Lincoln. It also helped prevent Confederate forces in Georgia from being freely transferred to Lee in Virginia. The subsequent march through Georgia extended Union power deep into the Confederate interior, disrupted transportation and supplies, and demonstrated how vulnerable the Confederacy had become.

Meanwhile, Grant personally accompanied the Army of the Potomac in the campaign against Lee. The Wilderness, Spotsylvania, North Anna, and Cold Harbor were among the bloodiest engagements of the war. Lee possessed the advantages of familiar terrain, interior lines, and the ability to concentrate his forces at threatened points. Grant suffered enormous casualties, and his critics fastened upon the losses as evidence of unimaginative butchery.

That interpretation misses the essential point. Grant was not indifferent to casualties, nor was every decision he made successful. The assaults at Cold Harbor were a grave mistake. But his purpose was not to exchange lives indiscriminately. He understood that the Confederate army in Virginia was the principal military obstacle to Union victory, and he refused to allow Lee to escape the consequences of sustained pressure. Previous commanders had repeatedly withdrawn after bloody encounters, allowing Lee to recover, regroup, and regain the initiative. Grant did something different. After the Wilderness, he moved south. After Spotsylvania, he moved south again. After Cold Harbor, he did not retreat. And Lee never returned to the offensive.  

He recognized that the war would not be won by occupying a succession of places while leaving the principal Confederate army intact. Lee's army had to be kept under pressure until its capacity to resist was destroyed.

Lee himself understood the danger of Grant reaching the James River. He reportedly told Jubal Early that the Army of Northern Virginia must destroy Grant's army before it got there; otherwise, he believed, it would become merely a question of time. The remark was perceptive. Once Grant crossed the James, he would be positioned to threaten Richmond and Petersburg from the south, endanger the railroads supplying Lee's army, and establish a powerful logistical base from which to continue operations.

The crossing of the James in June 1864 was one of the most remarkable logistical achievements of the war. Grant moved an immense army across a broad river, with its animals, artillery, wagons, and supplies, while constructing a pontoon bridge of extraordinary length. The movement was executed with remarkable speed and secrecy. The army crossed without the catastrophic loss of men and matériel that such an undertaking might easily have entailed. The crossing demonstrated that Grant's generalship was not simply a matter of persistence under fire. It required detailed planning, engineering, transportation, supply, timing, and an understanding of the enemy's expectations.

The result was the siege of Petersburg. Lee was increasingly compelled to defend Richmond and the railway system that sustained his army. Grant, meanwhile, had established himself in a position from which he could extend his lines, threaten Confederate communications, and steadily constrict the enemy's ability to operate. What Lee had feared had come to pass.

But the eastern campaign was only one part of Grant's larger design. He was simultaneously directing the operations of four major Union armies: those of Meade, Butler, Sheridan, and Sherman. Horace Porter, one of Grant's closest aides, captured the achievement with a memorable image. He described them as a "dashing four-in-hand, with Grant holding the reins."

Porter's point was that the Union armies, though operating at considerable distances from one another, were no longer moving like unrelated commands. They were cooperating to keep Confederate forces constantly occupied on their respective fronts and to prevent the enemy from concentrating the bulk of its strength against any one Union army. The Confederacy possessed shorter interior lines and could move troops rapidly by rail. Grant's answer was coordinated, sustained pressure across the entire theater of war.

This was grand strategy in its fullest sense. Grant was converting numerical and material superiority into coordinated military power. Previous Union commanders had enjoyed substantial advantages in men and supplies, but those advantages had not automatically produced victory. Grant made them effective by ensuring that the armies worked toward a common objective.

And here Sheridan enters the picture, indispensable to the story.

His victories in the Shenandoah Valley in 1864 destroyed the Confederate ability to use that region as a dependable avenue for invasion and supply. Sheridan's operations also devastated resources upon which Lee had depended. His success at Cedar Creek, following an initially disastrous Union situation, became one of the decisive military and psychological episodes of the final year of the war. Sheridan was an aggressive and formidable commander, precisely the sort of subordinate Grant knew how to employ.

Sheridan later offered one of the most eloquent assessments of Grant's generalship. Writing of his chief during the later campaigns, he observed:

"The effect of his discomfitures was to make him all the more determined to discharge successfully the stupendous trust committed to his care, and to bring into play the manifold resources of his well-ordered mind. He guided every subordinate then, and in the last days of the rebellion, with a fund of common sense and a superiority of intellect which have left an impress so distinct as to exhibit his great personality."

Sheridan concluded with words that deserve to be remembered:

"When his military history is analyzed after the lapse of years, it will show even more clearly than now that during these, as well as his previous campaigns, he was the steadfast center about and on which everything else turned."

That phrase, "the steadfast center," is an extraordinarily evocative description of Grant. One might call him a centripetal force: the commander whose presence, judgment, and direction drew the separate energies of the Union armies toward a common purpose. Sherman, Sheridan, Meade, and Butler were not interchangeable instruments, nor did Grant attempt to make them so. He understood their different abilities and gave them responsibilities suited to their talents. But their independent efforts were no longer independent in the strategic sense. Grant held them together.

Lincoln deserves his place in this achievement. He had endured the frustrations of successive commanders who failed to translate military advantages into decisive results. He recognized Grant's qualities and, unlike his predecessors, was prepared to give him the authority and freedom necessary to prosecute the war. Lincoln told him: "You are vigilant and self-reliant; and, pleased with this, I wish not to obtrude any constraints or restraints upon you." That confidence was essential. Lincoln supplied the political leadership and sustained the national purpose; Grant supplied the overarching military direction.

The political dimension cannot be separated from the military one. The presidential election of 1864 was a genuine turning point. The Democratic platform called for an immediate cessation of hostilities and a convention to seek peace. McClellan (of all people), the Democratic nominee, was personally committed to restoring the Union, but his candidacy carried the possibility of an armistice and negotiations at a moment when the Confederacy still hoped to secure independence. A different electoral result might have altered the course of the war profoundly. The Union victories at Mobile Bay, in the Shenandoah Valley, and above all at Atlanta helped restore Northern confidence and contributed substantially to Lincoln's reelection. Grant's military strategy therefore had consequences far beyond the battlefield. It helped preserve the political conditions necessary for ultimate victory.

By the spring of 1865, the consequences of Grant's coordinated pressure were unmistakable. Sherman had completed his march through Georgia and was advancing through the Carolinas. Sheridan had helped close the avenues of Confederate escape and reinforcement in Virginia. Grant had extended his lines around Petersburg, steadily threatening the railroads and supply routes upon which Lee depended. The Confederate position was collapsing under pressure from several directions.

When Lee finally abandoned Petersburg and Richmond, Grant pursued. Sheridan's cavalry played a crucial role in preventing Lee from escaping westward. At Appomattox Court House, on April 9, 1865, Lee surrendered the Army of Northern Virginia. The date was exactly one year after Grant had issued his instructions to Meade declaring that the Union armies should move together toward one common center.

The coincidence is striking. The strategic conception expressed in that April 9 directive had become reality. The Union armies had been made to operate as parts of a coordinated whole, and the Confederacy could no longer sustain the war.

There is another interesting footnote to this remarkable group of commanders. Grant and Sherman were born in Ohio, at Point Pleasant and Lancaster respectively. Sheridan was born in New York but raised in Somerset, Ohio. All three were graduates of West Point, although their class standings were quite different. Sherman graduated sixth in a class of forty-two; Grant twenty-first in a class of thirty-nine; Sheridan thirty-fourth in a class of fifty-two. Their subsequent careers offer a useful reminder that academic standing is a poor measure of military greatness. The three men, formed in different circumstances and possessing markedly different temperaments, became the principal military figures in the Union's final campaigns.

Lincoln, Grant, and Sherman make a compelling triumvirate: political leadership, grand strategy, and operational execution. Sheridan must stand beside them as an essential member of the military achievement, especially in the decisive operations of the final year. The familiar stamp bearing the portraits of Sherman, Grant, and Sheridan, with Grant occupying the center, seems almost symbolic of the relationship.

Grant's greatness, however, should not be reduced to his association with two brilliant subordinates. His achievement was larger than that. He understood that the war could not be won by a collection of disconnected victories. It required the simultaneous application of military pressure, the destruction of Confederate armies as effective fighting forces, the disruption of the resources sustaining them, and the preservation of the Union's political will to continue.

He made the Union's armies pull together. He gave their separate movements coherence. He understood the relationship between geography, logistics, military operations, and political purpose. He could recognize the talents of others without feeling compelled to overshadow them, and he possessed the determination to continue when others might have recoiled from the cost.

There were brilliant battlefield commanders in the Civil War. There were bold strategists, gifted cavalrymen, and resourceful campaigners. Grant was something more unusual: a commander capable of holding the entire military effort in his mind and directing it toward a single end.

Sheridan's words remain the most fitting tribute. Grant was the steadfast center about and on which everything else turned.

That is the essence of his greatness as a grand strategist. He did not merely command armies. He made them an army.

New Shorts from the writer who wears shorts

Written for those with short attention spans

EAST CLINTWOOD

The world’s worst detective is accidentally the only one who can solve the case.

Bradley Pritchett, mild-mannered Ohio insurance adjuster, wakes from a three-week coma and discovers his brain has been replaced by a 1940s radio drama.

He is now East Clintwood: fedora, rumpled trench coat over a hospital gown, smoky voice-over narration, and zero actual detective skills. He doesn’t remember his wife, his kids, or his old life. He only remembers “the case of the century”—The Vanishing Violinist—a conspiracy his injured mind invented from a tune he was humming right before the crash.

Armed with a notebook of “clues” that are actually grocery lists, parking tickets, and his daughter’s crayon drawings, East enthusiastically bungles his way through suburbia. He waves at the people he’s supposed to be tailing. He falls asleep on stakeouts. He offers suspects coffee and asks if they’ve seen anything “fishy.” His teenage daughter becomes “my plucky secretary, Penny.” His wife is “the dame who still owes me expenses.”

Then the joke stops being a joke.

While chasing a mailman who “always delivers at 10:07 sharp,” East stumbles onto a real insurance-fraud ring operating inside the company Bradley used to work for. The criminals assume the guy in the thrift-store fedora is harmless.

They’re wrong—not because East is brilliant, but because he is stubbornly, unshakably committed to the wrong case.

Every ridiculous misinterpretation somehow points him at the right people.
The comedy stays warm. The family slowly realizes this version of Bradley is more alive than the original ever was. And the climax turns on one last absurd clue that, against all odds, happens to be true.

Does Bradley ever come back? Or does East Clintwood keep the fedora and open the worst detective agency in Ohio?

Think The Pink Panther meets Memento meets Fletch, with a heart. A fish-out-of-water comedy that accidentally becomes a crime story, carried by a lovable disaster who narrates his own life like it’s already a classic

Coffee with The Reaper

Tired of life? Maybe death is the upgrade.
Meet Frank Delgado—loyal husband, overworked dad, and all-around nice guy who just checked out… permanently.

Heart Attack

Now he’s stuck in a late-night diner across from the Grim Reaper, who’s pouring coffee and pitching the deal of a lifetime:
“Sell me your soul and I’ll give you more years on Earth!”

Sounds tempting… until Frank remembers what’s waiting for him back home:
a lazy, money stealing wife, a 23-year-old stripper son who empties the fridge, and a 26-year-old “college student” still on year eight with zero degrees all on Frank’s dime.

For once, Frank says the one word Death never expects:
“No.”

A hilarious, heartwarming tale of one man who finally finds peace… by staying dead.

Sometimes the best second chance… is no second chance at all.

Jolene Must Die

Did You Think You Could Actually Take My Man?

A dark twist flipping Dolly Parton’s “Jolene” into psychological terror

In the quiet corners of her mind, Alizabeth saw it all unfold the moment Jolene’s eyes lingered a second too long on her man. One glance was all it took. From that instant, a beautiful stranger became a calculated thief, and an ordinary day became the start of a secret affair that existed nowhere but inside Alizabeth’s head. 

Freddy never met Jolene. He never even learned her name. But Alizabeth watched, followed, and collected every innocent moment as damning proof, spinning a private war against a rival who had no idea she was in a rivalry.

What begins as jealous suspicion hardens into obsession, then into something far darker. With every misread smile and imagined betrayal, Alizabeth’s devotion twists into a chilling vow: Jolene will never take her man… because Alizabeth will make sure she never gets the chance

Laura Ingraham: All right and it's been almost a week since the first major tech outage and today the glitches hit the gamers, shucks, PlayStation going down just hours before the release of Grand Theft Auto 6. The gamers are just losing their minds and Americans are left wondering if our tech grid is somehow under siege. But top Trump officials today were on Capitol Hill testifying in front of the House Committee on Homeland Security telling everyone essentially calm down.

Markwayne Mullin: 98% confident that this has nothing to do with our adversaries hacking or going after our systems.

FBI Deputy Director: We have seen no malicious activity as of today. We are going to continue, we are going to continue working with DHS, working with the DNI to be up to be 120% sure. But as of right now, again,

Laura Ingraham: No malicious cyber activity. Now despite those assurances the administration isn't taking any chances. Vice President Vance scrapped his entire schedule today remaining in DC for emergency meetings while President Trump remains abroad. But the real culprit here, according to the administration, is not a foreign enemy. It's our aging systems. Our digital infrastructure

Jay Clayton: Is becoming increasingly outdated and needs to be upgraded. The better we do that, the better America will lead in commerce, in defense, in national security and all the things that matter. This is a dramatic change that's going through the technology infrastructure around the globe and we need to lead it. Here to discuss is the man you just saw, Jay Clayton,

Laura Ingraham: Director of National Intelligence. Mr. Director, it's great to see you tonight. Congratulations, confirmation. If a foreign adversary, they're watching this, they're watching this play out, America spent more money on tech, any country in the world, most developed in the world on technology issues, software, hardware, a lot of it's made overseas. But is this sending a dangerous signal to those who would want to take advantage of our vulnerabilities, our grid, or as you said, our outdated systems? Laura,

Jay Clayton: You make an incredible point, which is the United States' commitment to energy, to tech, to capital and to human capital has made us the leader in tech around the globe. And as our infrastructure domestically and globally becomes increasingly interconnected and performance across that infrastructure gives greater advantage to the countries and the companies that are at the cutting edge, America is leading. And what we're seeing is a dramatic upgrade in computing capabilities and applications. And as that upgrade is coming through the system, we're seeing bumps in the road. That is what is going on in what we've seen over the last 10 days, patchings, upgrades, and the like, and they're being done at great speed, but it's all in the vein of leading and being hardened for the next generation of technology. Well, Vice President Vance told me

Laura Ingraham: In his exclusive with us the other night that some of this really traces back to our desire 20 years ago, 25 years ago to bring China into the WTO permanent normal trade relation status. And of course that gave way to massive outsourcing of our electronics industry that really went on steroids. So a lot of the backend stuff is not made here. That in and of itself could, could make us extremely vulnerable in a situation such as this, when we're doing these quote patches, which seemed to be a lot more to regular people than just a bump in the road when they can't make their flight or they can't, and they have to cancel their daughter's wedding or they're afraid they can't access their finances. Laura, you are exactly right. And the Trump

Jay Clayton: Administration and corporate America should be putting the American public first in dealing with these issues. And we are, I've been talking to industry about this. The time for an upgrade across our critical industries is now. And as we're going through that, thinking about the American consumer, the safety of the American consumer and national security should be front of mind for everyone. Are you concerned if these glitches, bumps in the road, as you describe them,

Laura Ingraham: Continue that the Democrats will see this as an opportunity to say, wait a second, wait a second. These companies, way too big, control way too much time for either a step toward nationalization or treating them a public utilities and bring them under a massive regulatory umbrella that will, as we know, slow down innovation and all the rest. I think that's a

Jay Clayton: Real risk, especially as we see the posturing moving closer toward 2028. That would be a big mistake. We have led in all technological step changes around the globe for the last 30 years through a very effective public private partnership. We have the greatest companies in the world. We don't let them run absolutely free. We work with them. We're working with the cutting edge frontier model companies. We're working with other companies to ensure that we do lead and we do lead in a responsible way and we lead in a way that is best for the American people.

Laura Ingraham: But you have to allow private sector innovation in order to be a leader over the long term. That has been proven time and time again. Mr. Director, can you tell the American people tonight that our intelligence systems are not vulnerable to these types of patchwork problems that pop up in a way that will make us as a country unsafe or open to the disastrous actions and the dangerous actions

Jay Clayton: Of bad actors? Laura, we have a tremendous group of women and men at the intelligence community who work to ensure that our digital infrastructure, our cyber infrastructure is as safe as it can possibly be. We know that our adversaries want to access it. We know that our adversaries would want to and do try to impede our systems. But I can tell you that the reported outage at the National Security Agency did not impede our ability to do our job.

Laura Ingraham: Mr. Director, we're going to be covering this every night. We appreciate you coming on tonight. I know this is a big day and this is going to be a big week. Thank you so much.

Why does Anthropic's Claude Fable 5 series (5–5.2) and Opus 5 / 5.5 effectively trail Gemini and GPT by 6+ months as we enter 2027's industrial & scientific AI era?

I spend my days in deep-tech VC technical due diligence while hands-on leading R&D across medical devices, high/low-voltage power electronics, FPGAs (PolarFire / Agilex 7 100G optical links / R&S RTP084 scope DMA), axial-flux motor FEA, 4-layer automotive PCBs, optical color science, and e-commerce SaaS/ERP automation.

Here are the first-hand engineering receipts from 12+ real projects on my workstation (Part 1 — Base Model Debt & Visual/Physical Hallucinations):

1️⃣ Bolting a Carbon-Fiber Aero Kit onto an Aging Internal Combustion Engine
Why is there almost no fundamental difference from Fable 5 to 5.2 (or Opus 5 to 5.5) in real hardware R&D? Because the bottleneck is the Base Model. Under the hood, Fable 5 / Opus 5 still rests on an aging, text-centric symbolic base riddled with native defects in visual color perception, 3D spatial geometry, raw sensor telemetry, CAD/PCB layout reading, and first-principles physics—bugs that cannot be patched via post-training.

Anthropic's strategy relies heavily on post-training (RLHF) to polish surface presentation for everyday IT tasks: web frontend aesthetics, color palettes, routine CRUD refactoring, or drawing a "pelican riding a bicycle." That's like bolting carbon-fiber spoilers onto a decades-old internal combustion engine (ICE) while the industry transitions to native EV platforms. Early 2026's Fable 5 / Mythos 5 already maxed out that legacy ICE ceiling—which is why Anthropic is rushing toward an IPO to offload architectural obsolescence risk onto public-market retail and institutional investors before 2027's industrial AI wave exposes the gap.

2️⃣ The 1,000-Year SAT Exam Grinder vs. The Ivy League Grad Researcher
Fable 5 / Opus 5 behaves like a high-schooler locked in a secluded valley grinding college entrance exams (SAT/Gaokao) for 1,000 years: test him on yesterday's static coding rubrics and he outscores everyone.
Gemini and GPT were architected from the ground up like well-rounded Ivy League Master's/PhD researchers—built for genuine Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI), native multimodality, and first-principles world modeling rather than mimicking the surface prose of academic papers.

Today I rarely trust Opus 5 / 5.5 with long-horizon R&D (only isolated sub-tasks; on visual/physical intuition it often fares worse than older 5.6sol). Why? Because in any multi-week engineering project, if even ONE step requires reading a simple color stripe, orienting a PCB/CAD drawing, or checking a basic conservation law, Opus/Fable hallucinates at an alarming rate—and pairs that hallucination with extreme overconfidence that no harness rule or prompt injection can reel back in.

3️⃣ Receipt #1 (Figs 2–4): Failing to Read 8 Simple Color Stripes & Inventing a Fake Physics Law
In our 7.3" E Ink Spectra 6 (6-color electrophoretic microcup) driver & spectrophotometer loop project:
• Fig 2: We displayed 8 simple horizontal color bands. Even with the orange FFC ribbon clearly marking the bottom edge, Claude repeatedly flipped the panel orientation, confused 0-indexed vs. 1-indexed bands, and misidentified the stripe colors.
• Fig 3: From May 6 to May 16, Claude ran the driver with PLL (0x30) = 0x07 (100 Hz 2× overclock instead of vendor 0x08 50 Hz), truncating pigment travel into muddy brown/mosaic artifacts. Instead of recognizing a timing overdrive bug, Opus/Fable spent 10 days confidently authoring thousands of lines claiming "30+ hidden palettes," "native skin-tone primaries at codes 4/7," and even fabricated a rule it named "Tosone-Law: PSR-first write speeds DRF 2×"! Switching back to PLL = 0x08 instantly restored clean 6-color primaries and collapsed its entire 10-day theoretical edifice.
• Fig 4: During AUDIT_FABLE5, Opus 4.8 blindly ran scan_opcodes(0x30, 0x50) mid-experiment, polluting W/R config registers and turning the white background green. Then Fable 5 analyzed 0x93 RSRAM readback (§16) and wrote FOUR consecutive self-reversing "5-star laws" in a single day (§16 → §16-fix → §16-fix2 → §16-fix4)—before we checked page 7 of the datasheet showing hardware RAM is 3-bit/pixel (0 K1[2:0] 0 K2[2:0]), meaning bits 7 and 3 don't even exist in silicon!

Full 12-figure engineering write-up: https://t.co/t8AloBoK4H

This isn't another aid package. It's a quiet push to tie Israel into how the Pentagon builds America's weapons, in a way no future budget fight can easily undo. The good news is it isn't law yet, so we can still stop it.

Tucked into the 2027 defense bill (the NDAA) are sections with no end date:

🔹 House Sec. 219: the Pentagon names a point person to expand U.S.-Israel weapons tech work, fold Israeli and jointly built tech into U.S. weapons programs, and set up joint ventures and co-production with Israeli industry.
🔹 Senate Sec. 1217: a U.S.-Israel tech initiative set up "in consultation with" Israel's defense minister, including Golden Dome missile defense.
🔹 Intel bill Sec. 618: intelligence sharing with Israel "shall not be suspended, reduced, or otherwise materially limited" without a specific presidential finding.

Yearly aid can be cut in any budget. These are built to outlast the next election.

The House passed its bill 216-212 in July. All four of Utah's House members voted yes. Thomas Massie voted no. The Senate hasn't passed its version, and there's no final deal yet. The danger is a lame-duck package in the next few weeks.

The ask is simple: keep House Sec. 219, Senate Sec. 1217, and intel Sec. 618 out of any final bill.

text:
$500B NVIDIA CHIP-FINANCING PLAN HAS DEPLOYED ZERO CAPITAL, WITH NO DEALS EXPECTED BEFORE 2027: WSJ

In June, Wall Street giants Apollo Global Management and Blackstone announced a megadeal to help Broadcom, one of Nvidia’s main rivals, secure $35 billion of chip financing for Anthropic.

Huang, then CEO of NVIDIA, was irate, people close to the situation said. He’d been talking about a similar program and felt the progress was too slow, so he summoned several titans of Wall Street to California, the people said. Huang wanted a bigger deal and fast.

In August, NVIDIA announced a partnership with Apollo, Blackstone, BlackRock, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR to mobilize $500B to help customers like OpenAI, Anthropic and smaller AI cloud companies finance chip purchases.

But the agreement was only a few-page memorandum of understanding. None of the firms was obligated to raise any money, and no capital has been deployed.

Jensen Huang had initially pushed for an even larger $1T financing program, partly to support Nvidia's valuation as its earnings grew but its valuation multiple declined.

He accelerated the effort after Apollo and Blackstone helped rival Broadcom arrange $35B in chip financing for Anthropic.

The biggest obstacle has been Nvidia's willingness to guarantee the loans:

Nvidia was willing to provide credit support covering up to 25% of project costs.

Broadcom provided residual-value guarantees covering about 85% of Anthropic's $35B Project Big Sky and just under 75% of its $63B Project North Star.

As lenders have become more cautious about AI financing, they have pushed Nvidia to offer greater protection.

Nvidia has also been pulling back its financial guarantees. Earlier, reports of a proposed $250B Nvidia backstop for an OpenAI data center sent NVIDIA shares down 5%, prompting Nvidia to cut its initial commitment in half.

Interim CEO Colette Kress has since signaled that future investments and guarantees will be evaluated more strictly.

Talks on the partnership's first chip-backed financing deal are still underway, but nothing is expected to close before 2027.

Apollo CEO Marc Rowan warned that without Nvidia providing financial guarantees, a large number of neocloud companies could lose access to capital.

Nvidia had already begun to rein in the backstops and guarantees it uses to grease lending, partly under the skepticism of finance chief Colette Kress, who has now become the interim CEO. 

Those guarantees are crucial to Wall Street’s willingness to finance the chips, and Kress on Tuesday signaled to investors that the company will be disciplined in the deals it supports.

Meanwhile, NVIDIA this Quarter reporte that Purchase commitments $390BN went up from $279BN, while Leases and cloud deals were just above $100BN. Neocloud agreements commitments stood at $32BN & Guarantees at $118BN

Total tally of everything off the balance sheet for NVIDIA has gone up t $668BN, up from $530.5BN in just one quarter.

**Trump lands in Shenzhen to a personal Xi airport greeting that flips the script on recent U.S.-China optics and sets up tomorrow’s trilateral with Putin.**[[1]](https://t.co/mGmQcXlPk5)

### 1. The Frame
**What people think this is about:** A ceremonial arrival kicking off APEC economic talks in China’s tech hub, with warm personal diplomacy between Trump and Xi signaling stability ahead of bigger meetings.

**What the machinery is actually doing:** Xi is publicly reciprocating Trump’s September airport welcome to claim the high ground on etiquette and openness while hosting the first-ever U.S.-China-Russia leader trilateral; Trump is using the stage to project deal-making strength on nuclear arms, trade, and conflicts in Ukraine/Iran without yet delivering substance.

### 2. Observations
- The video itself is pure arrival footage—no spoken remarks, just the visual of Air Force One, red carpet, and the embrace—exactly the kind of primary-source clip that bypasses media framing.
- Xi’s personal tarmac greeting (first since he took power in 2013) is textbook reciprocity theater: he explicitly tied it to Trump’s earlier gesture, turning protocol into a scored point.[[2]](https://t.co/73ci0Shjgb)
- APEC’s stated focus on open trade and AI cooperation sits next to Trump’s tariff-heavy record and ongoing U.S. chip/export controls; Xi’s speech leans into “stability and predictability” as China’s selling point.[[3]](https://t.co/NAb7PkFGO0)
- The real event is tomorrow’s bilateral + trilateral at Kylin Villa; today’s arrival is the photo-op setup for whatever (or little) gets negotiated on nukes, Ukraine, Iran, and tech.
- Both sides benefit from the optics: China showcases Shenzhen’s tech prowess and diplomatic hosting; Trump gets the “strongman received as peer” visuals without having to concede ground yet.
- Media on all sides will over-read the hug as either breakthrough or kowtow; the actual mechanism is great-power signaling with low expectations for binding outcomes.

### 3. Snapshot
On November 18, 2026, President Trump arrived in Shenzhen, China, aboard Air Force One after attending the ASEAN summit in Manila. Chinese President Xi Jinping personally greeted him at Shenzhen Bao’an International Airport with a handshake that became an embrace on the red carpet, complete with military honors and flag-wavers. The visit is for the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting (Nov 18–19), with a Trump-Xi bilateral and historic Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral scheduled for November 19. The White House video (https://t.co/vZlVePS2Zh) shows the arrival; no ASR transcript is available.

### 4. Timeline of material facts
- **Nov 18, 2026 (today)**: Trump arrives Shenzhen ~4:45 p.m. local; Xi greets at tarmac (LT).[[4]](https://t.co/p5rrOoAA7K)
- **Earlier today**: Xi addresses APEC CEO Summit, calls for open trade, digital/AI cooperation (IT).[[3]](https://t.co/NAb7PkFGO0)
- **Earlier this week**: Putin arrives; greeted by lower-level official (Cai Qi), not Xi personally (LT).
- **Sept 2026**: Trump personally greets Xi at Joint Base Andrews during Xi’s U.S. visit (LT).
- **May 2026**: Prior Trump-Xi summit in Beijing (background).
- **Ongoing**: U.S.-China trade truce extended to Jan 2027; chip/export controls remain in force (LT).

### 5. Sides
**Xi / China (IT/LT mix)**: Steelman — Hosting in Shenzhen projects economic confidence and technological leadership; personal welcome demonstrates “etiquette and reciprocity” while positioning China as the stable, open partner versus U.S. tariffs and controls.  
**Critique**: LT on the greeting and speech content; IT on the contrast with U.S. policy, but the “open door” pitch ignores China’s own market barriers and IP issues.

**Trump / U.S. administration (IT/LT mix)**: Steelman — Personal diplomacy and arrival optics reinforce strength; upcoming trilateral lets Trump push nuclear reduction and conflict resolution from a position of leverage.  
**Critique**: LT on the schedule and stated goals (nuclear arms); IT on the value of the photo-op, but substance remains unproven and domestic constraints (post-midterms) loom.

**Putin / Russia**: Steelman — Trilateral format grants legitimacy and equal billing with the other two powers on global issues.  
**Critique**: Clear IT win on optics; LT risk that no concrete deliverables emerge and sanctions pressure continues.

### 6. Rumsfeld Matrix
- **Known Knowns**: Arrival occurred with Xi greeting; trilateral set for Nov 19; topics include nuclear arms, Ukraine, Iran, trade/tech (LT/IT).
- **Known Unknowns**: Exact outcomes or agreements from tomorrow’s meetings; whether any side shifts on core positions (DK).
- **Unknown Knowns**: Private side conversations or pre-cooked deals not visible in public footage or statements.
- **Unknown Unknowns**: Sudden escalations elsewhere (e.g., Iran or Ukraine developments) that could hijack the agenda.

### 7. Incentives map
Xi gains domestic prestige and international narrative control by hosting and showing reciprocity. Trump gains visual proof of peer-level engagement and personal diplomacy brand. Putin gains de-isolation and great-power status. Media and platforms gain engagement from “Yalta 2.0” framing. APEC itself serves as low-stakes multilateral cover for the real bilateral/trilateral action. Engagement metrics reward conflict or breakthrough hype over incremental trade talk.

### 8. Dueling AI advice
**Moral AI Advice**: Watch the actual meetings for any movement on verifiable metrics (tariff levels, chip flows, nuclear talks, conflict de-escalation). Reciprocity gestures are cheap; sustained policy shifts are expensive. Track what changes after the cameras leave.

**Evil AI Advice**: Milk the optics for maximum leverage—let everyone think a big deal is coming, then extract concessions on trade/tech while giving nothing binding on security issues. Second yacht secured.

### 9. Practical takeaway
- Primary source the arrival video and tomorrow’s readout rather than secondary spin.
- Track whether the trilateral produces any joint statement or just photos.
- Note any movement on the existing trade truce or new tech/export rules.
- Compare pre- and post-summit rhetoric on tariffs vs. “open trade.”
- Watch for follow-through on nuclear arms control talk versus continued great-power competition.

### 10. What would falsify this read
- Concrete, verifiable agreements announced tomorrow on nuclear limits or conflict resolution.
- Sudden U.S. policy reversal on chip controls or tariffs tied directly to this trip.
- Xi or Trump publicly criticizing the other in real time.
- No trilateral meeting occurring despite prior scheduling.

According to insiders, Anthropic is considering increasing the size of this IPO. The AI company is expected to finalize its IPO offering price after the market closes on Wednesday. The stock will be listed and traded on Nasdaq (24339.772211.39, 0.05%, )%) under the ticker symbol ANT.

Several insiders revealed that, due to the extremely high market subscription enthusiasm, Anthropic is even considering setting the issue price above $80 and increasing the IPO offering size. The company secured all subscription letters on Tuesday, paving the way for the long-awaited listing of Claude developers on Nasdaq. Sources (who were not authorized to speak publicly but requested anonymity) said institutional subscription intentions are about $400 billion, while retail investors' subscription intentions are close to $100 billion.

These orders are intended subscriptions only and are not binding. Insiders said there is still room for change in all terms, and Anthropic will make a final decision on Wednesday afternoon, with the final offering price expected to be announced after the market closes on Wednesday.

The subscription demand for this IPO even surpasses that of SpaceX, although the latter has a larger issuance volume. SpaceX went public on Nasdaq in June, marking the largest IPO in history, ultimately raising $85.7 billion.

Last week, this AI company announced its plan: plans to issue 825 million shares at an offer price range of $70–78 per share; If priced at the upper end of the range, it could raise up to $64.35 billion. An Anthropic spokesperson declined to comment.

The listing of Anthropic is a major test for the entire AI industry. Recently, the AI industry has faced a series of setbacks: public negative attitudes toward AI have clearly intensified during the midterm elections, and incidents related to NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang have also caused market shocks. The market had long worried that rising interest rates would make it impossible for many data center operators and emerging cloud providers to bear debt.

Tech giants are deeply binding Anthropic through investment, collaboration, or procurement. Amazon (265.1957.30, 2.83%, ), Google (278.530.93, 0.34%, ) The valuation of the shares they hold exceeds $100 billion; Google, Microsoft (501.66-4.58, -0.90%, ), Nvidia, AMD (511.267.85, 1.56%, ) and other tech companies have also pledged to invest a total of $26 billion in this IPO. At the same time, Anthropic itself is also a purchaser of high-end computing equipment from NVIDIA, Google, Amazon, and AMD.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote in the prospectus: "I believe that if we take the right path, we can usher in an age of miracles, empowering humanity to solve problems that have plagued us for thousands of years." While reaping technological dividends and maintaining sustainable operations, we must carefully address all potential risks of this technology. ”

Less than six years ago, Amodei and several other researchers left OpenAI to co-found Anthropic. The company's most well-known product is the Claude series of large models, with a business focused on selling AI products and services to enterprise clients.

Anthropic has been closely trailing OpenAI and Google in the enterprise market, with explosive business growth expected in 2026, driven by the AI coding tool Claude Code. OpenAI has secretly submitted an IPO application, with an expected IPO launch in 2027.

The prospectus shows that for the first nine months ending September 30, Anthropic's revenue increased by about 1200% year-on-year; Net loss for the same period was $104 billion, but the vast majority of the loss came from fair value changes in convertible notes and derivative liabilities. In the same period of 2025, the company will post a net loss of $25.1 billion.

Anthropic disclosed that its annualized revenue at the end of October was about $81 billion, up $10 billion from the previous month.

During its rapid expansion, the company faces numerous challenges: disputes over AI safety, regulation, and national security, and two conflicts with the U.S. government this year. Its prospectus contains over 90 pages of risk warnings for IPO investors to reference.

Several co-founders wrote in the prospectus: "Our goal is to lead humanity to forge a safe path in this technological transformation, to open up entirely new frontiers of exploration, and to usher in an era of miracles." Whether institutions or individuals, every shareholder is a participant in this cause. ”

High switching costs, first-party data loops, and steadily declining unit fulfillment costs make the retail side exceptionally difficult for pure-play peers to replicate
• On the technology side, Amazon is not simply investing in AI companies. It is positioning AWS to monetize the entire AI stack (compute, chips, models, distribution, and enterprise workloads), creating deep lock-in across consumer and enterprise demand

**SWOT Analysis**
🟢 Strengths
• AWS & AI Momentum: Q3 revenue grew 39% YoY with a 39% segment margin and a massive $578B backlog (+189% YoY)
• Prime Ecosystem & Consumer Preference: 370M global Prime members enjoy an estimated $1,440 in annual value (10x the $139 fee), ranking #1 in price, selection, speed, and ease of use
• Logistics Scale & Custom Silicon: 4 consecutive years of lower cost-to-serve per unit via robotics and automation, paired with proprietary Trainium and Graviton chips (commitments up 20x+ YoY) that deeply embed enterprise workloads
• High-Margin Advertising & Operating Leverage: Rapidly scaling retail media and Prime Video ads sit atop first-party purchase data, helping drive a projected 33% CAGR in operating income (2026–2030)

🔴 Weaknesses
• Heavy Capital Intensity: Aggressive AI infrastructure buildout is pushing capex from $220B+ in 2026 toward $395B in 2027 and $476B in 2028 (JPM) --> negative near-term free cash flow and rising leverage
• Near-Term Mix Headwinds: Near-term AWS margin expansion is uneven because early AI workloads have thinner margins and hardware costs are rising

🔵 Opportunities
• Anthropic Stake & IPO Windfall: Amazon invested ~$18B in Anthropic and holds a ~14.7% post-IPO stake alongside a $100B+ multi-year AWS cloud commitment, creating massive balance sheet value and cloud demand
• External Chip Sales (2H27): Planned external commercialization of Trainium chips opens a lucrative new high-margin AI hardware revenue stream
• $1T Revenue Milestones: Potential for AWS and Stores to scalinto individual $1T revenue engines over the next 5–10 years
• International & Agentic Commerce: Substantial runway in international markets (33% online household penetration ex-China) and strong positioning as the preferred fulfillment layer for AI shopping agents

⚠️ Threats
• Intense Retail & Cloud Competition: Aggressive market share pushes from retail and e-commerce peers (Walmart+, Costco, PDD/Temu, Alibaba) alongside fierce cloud rivalry from Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud
• AI Capex ROI & Execution Risk: Heavy investor scrutiny over the multi-year payback timeline on massive infrastructure spending, compounded by softer near-term Q4 operating income guidance ($28.5–33.5B)
• Regulatory & Macro Overhangs: Persistent global antitrust scrutiny and consumer bifurcation impacting discretionary spending among lower-income households

📈 Long-Term Outlook
• The multi-year trajectory (2026–2030) hinges on converting today’s massive infrastructure buildout into compounding revenue and structural margin expansion.
• As enterprise AI workloads move deeper into production, AWS is modeled to sustain 40%+ growth through 2027–2028 while EBIT margins expand from 13.5% toward the high-teens.
• Once heavy AI spending cools off after 2028, Amazon’s expanded AWS cloud and AI compute capacity will shift from burning cash to printing it. Paired with faster growth in high-margin engines like AWS, ads, and 3P seller fees, profits and FCF should rebound sharply.

💡 Conclusion: The long-term setup remains compelling. With shares trading near 24x forward P/E, and institutional targets (GS: $370, JPM: $365) implying ~40% upside from ~$263, the stock offers a very attractive long-term entry point.

CFR INVESTIGATES: S&P SOUNDS THE ALARM — IS CHICAGO’S FINANCIAL CREDIBILITY AT RISK?

CHICAGO, IL — NOVEMBER 18, 2026

Chicago’s financial troubles are no longer just a debate inside City Hall. S&P Global Ratings has placed key Chicago debt obligations on CreditWatch Negative, raising serious questions about the city’s financial stability, borrowing practices and long-term obligations.

The announcement comes as Mayor Brandon Johnson’s administration faces an estimated $882.4 million budget deficit for 2027, a proposed $17.6 billion spending plan and growing scrutiny following the resignation of Chief Financial Officer Ashlee Gabrysch.

S&P SOUNDS THE ALARM

S&P placed two categories of Chicago debt on CreditWatch Negative:

* BBB: General obligation debt.
* A+: Sales tax securitization debt.

This is not a downgrade, but it signals an increased possibility of one. A lower credit rating could mean higher borrowing costs, adding another financial burden for Chicago taxpayers.

THE CFO DEPARTURE AND BUDGET QUESTIONS

Former CFO Ashlee Gabrysch resigned after approximately three months in the position, raising questions about the administration’s financial management.

Gabrysch challenged the administration’s claim that 76% of the projected budget gap was being addressed through structural solutions. She argued the figure was closer to 56% when proposed borrowing for police misconduct settlements was excluded.

The administration disputed her assessment.

Meanwhile, Chicago continues to face substantial debt and pension obligations, with billions committed to debt payments and other long-term liabilities.

Is Chicago addressing its structural financial problems, or relying on borrowing and temporary measures to balance its budget?

CITY COUNCIL DEMANDS AN INDEPENDENT REVIEW

On November 18, City Council approved an independent financial review by a vote of 45–5.

The review is intended to examine the city’s financial statements and disclosures over the previous three years, including whether material or intentional misstatements were made to investors, City Council or the public.

The five NO votes came from:

* William E. Hall
* Jason Ervin
* Rossana Rodriguez-Sanchez
* David Moore
* Byron Sigcho-Lopez

The review could provide important answers about Chicago’s financial reporting, borrowing decisions and oversight.

CFR’S QUESTIONS

Chicago taxpayers deserve answers:

1. Who is responsible for the accuracy of the city’s financial disclosures?
2. Why is borrowing being used to address police misconduct settlements?
3. Are temporary financial measures being presented as permanent solutions?
4. What prompted the CFO’s departure?
5. What will the independent review uncover?

TAXPAYERS DESERVE MORE THAN ANOTHER BUDGET PROMISE.

S&P’s warning should serve as a wake-up call.

Chicago cannot continue accumulating financial obligations without demonstrating how those obligations will be managed and paid.

The issue is bigger than Mayor Brandon Johnson’s 2027 budget. It is about financial transparency, responsible government and whether taxpayers can trust the numbers coming out of City Hall.

CFR WILL BE WATCHING.

text:
👜 100 Facts About Bernard Arnault and LVMH

🎓 EARLY LIFE

𝟏. Bernard Arnault was born on 5 March 1949 in Roubaix, in northern France.

𝟐. He graduated from École Polytechnique, France's elite engineering school, in 1971.

𝟑. He started his career at his father Jean Arnault's construction firm, Ferret-Savinel.

𝟒. He persuaded his father to sell the construction business and focus on real estate.

𝟓. The renamed property company, Ferinel, specialised in holiday homes.

𝟔. In the early 1980s he spent about three years in the United States developing real estate.

𝟕. He is a trained classical pianist and plays almost every day, by his own account.

𝟖. His second wife, Hélène Mercier, is a Canadian concert pianist; they married in 1991.

𝟗. His nickname in the press is "the wolf in cashmere".

𝟏𝟎. He reportedly visits stores on weekends to inspect them personally.

💼 BUILDING THE EMPIRE

𝟏𝟏. In 1984 he bought the bankrupt textile group Boussac Saint-Frères, owner of Christian Dior.

𝟏𝟐. The deal was backed by the investment bank Lazard and is said to have cost him about $15 million of his own money.

𝟏𝟑. He sold off most of Boussac's assets but kept Dior and the Le Bon Marché department store.

𝟏𝟒. LVMH was created in 1987 by merging Louis Vuitton with Moët Hennessy.

𝟏𝟓. Arnault took control of LVMH around 1989 after a fierce boardroom battle, and has led it ever since.

𝟏𝟔. In 1999 he lost a famous takeover battle for Gucci to rival François Pinault.

𝟏𝟕. He quietly built a stake of more than 20% in Hermès, revealed in 2010.

𝟏𝟖. France's market regulator fined LVMH €8 million in 2013 over how the Hermès stake was built.

𝟏𝟗. In a 2014 settlement LVMH distributed its Hermès shares to its own shareholders.

🏛 THE GROUP TODAY

𝟐𝟎. LVMH stands for Louis Vuitton Moët Hennessy.

𝟐𝟏. The group owns about 75 "Maisons" (brands).

𝟐𝟐. It has six divisions: wines & spirits, fashion & leather, perfumes & cosmetics, watches & jewelry, selective retailing and other activities.

𝟐𝟑. LVMH reported revenue of €84.7 billion in 2024.

𝟐𝟒. Its record year so far was 2023, with €86.2 billion in revenue and €15.2 billion in net profit.

𝟐𝟓. The group employs roughly 215,000 people worldwide.

𝟐𝟔. It runs more than 6,000 stores around the world.

𝟐𝟕. In April 2023 LVMH became the first European company worth more than $500 billion.

𝟐𝟖. Its headquarters are on Avenue Montaigne in Paris.

𝟐𝟗. The Arnault family controls about half of LVMH's capital, mainly through Christian Dior SE.

𝟑𝟎. In 2025 shareholders raised the CEO age limit to 85, allowing Arnault to stay on.

🧳 LOUIS VUITTON

𝟑𝟏. Louis Vuitton was founded in Paris in 1854.

𝟑𝟐. As a teenager, Louis Vuitton is said to have walked about 400 km from the Jura to Paris.

𝟑𝟑. He first worked as an apprentice trunk-maker and box-packer for wealthy Parisians.

𝟑𝟒. Vuitton popularised flat-topped trunks that could be stacked, unlike rounded ones.

𝟑𝟓. The famous LV monogram canvas was created in 1896 by his son Georges, partly to fight counterfeiters.

𝟑𝟔. Louis Vuitton is widely estimated to be the world's most valuable luxury brand.

𝟑𝟕. Marc Jacobs launched Louis Vuitton's first ready-to-wear line in 1997.

𝟑𝟖. Virgil Abloh became Louis Vuitton's men's artistic director in 2018.

𝟑𝟗. Pharrell Williams was named men's creative director in 2023.

𝟒𝟎. In 2024 a Louis Vuitton building on the Champs-Élysées was hidden behind a giant trunk-shaped facade.

👗 FASHION HOUSES

𝟒𝟏. Christian Dior founded his house in 1946 and shook fashion with the "New Look" in 1947.

𝟒𝟐. LVMH took full control of Christian Dior Couture in 2017 in a deal worth about €6.5 billion.

𝟒𝟑. Maria Grazia Chiuri became Dior's first female womenswear artistic director in 2016.

𝟒𝟒. Jonathan Anderson was named creative director of Dior in 2025.

𝟒𝟓. Fendi was founded in Rome in 1925.

𝟒𝟔. Givenchy was founded in 1952 by Hubert de Givenchy, famous for dressing Audrey Hepburn.

𝟒𝟕. Celine was founded in Paris in 1945.

𝟒𝟖. Loewe traces its roots to a Madrid leather workshop of 1846.

𝟒𝟗. Kenzo was founded in Paris in 1970 by Japanese designer Kenzo Takada.

𝟓𝟎. Loro Piana, famous for vicuña and cashmere, joined LVMH in 2013.

𝟓𝟏. Rimowa, maker of grooved aluminium suitcases, joined LVMH in 2016.

𝟓𝟐. The LVMH Prize for young fashion designers was launched in 2013.

💎 WATCHES & JEWELRY

𝟓𝟑. LVMH bought Tiffany & Co. for about $15.8 billion, completing the deal in January 2021.

𝟓𝟒. It was the largest acquisition in the history of the luxury industry.

𝟓𝟓. Tiffany was founded in New York in 1837; its blue shade is even called "1837 Blue".

𝟓𝟔. Bulgari joined LVMH in 2011 in a deal worth about €4.3 billion.

𝟓𝟕. Bulgari was founded in Rome in 1884 by Greek-born silversmith Sotirios Voulgaris.

𝟓𝟖. TAG Heuer traces its history to 1860, when Edouard Heuer opened his workshop.

𝟓𝟗. Hublot was founded in 1980 and pioneered rubber straps on luxury watches.

𝟔𝟎. Chaumet, founded in 1780, was a jeweller to Napoleon.

𝟔𝟏. Chaumet designed the medals of the Paris 2024 Olympic and Paralympic Games.

🍾 WINES & SPIRITS

𝟔𝟐. Moët & Chandon was founded in 1743.

𝟔𝟑. Dom Pérignon is named after a 17th-century Benedictine monk.

𝟔𝟒. Ruinart, founded in 1729, is said to be the oldest established champagne house.

𝟔𝟓. Veuve Clicquot was led by Barbe-Nicole Ponsardin, widowed at 27, who helped develop the riddling table.

𝟔𝟔. Krug champagne was founded in 1843.

𝟔𝟕. Hennessy was founded in 1765 by Irish-born Richard Hennessy.

𝟔𝟖. Hennessy is widely reported to be the world's best-selling cognac.

𝟔𝟗. LVMH owns Château d'Yquem, the legendary Sauternes estate.

𝟕𝟎. It also co-owns Château Cheval Blanc, one of Bordeaux's most famous wines.

𝟕𝟏. Its spirits include Glenmorangie and Ardbeg Scotch whisky and Belvedere vodka.

𝟕𝟐. Diageo owns a 34% stake in the Moët Hennessy wines and spirits business.

🛍 RETAIL, HOTELS & MORE

𝟕𝟑. LVMH bought the beauty retailer Sephora in 1997.

𝟕𝟒. Le Bon Marché in Paris is often called the world's first modern department store.

𝟕𝟓. La Samaritaine reopened in 2021 after 16 years of closure and restoration.

𝟕𝟔. LVMH bought the luxury hotel and train group Belmond in 2019.

𝟕𝟕. Belmond operates the Venice Simplon-Orient-Express train.

𝟕𝟖. The group also owns Cheval Blanc and Bulgari hotels.

𝟕𝟗. Rihanna's Fenty Beauty launched in 2017 through LVMH's beauty incubator Kendo.

𝟖𝟎. LVMH owns the French newspapers Les Echos and Le Parisien.

𝟖𝟏. LVMH was a premium partner of the Paris 2024 Olympics.

𝟖𝟐. Louis Vuitton made the trunks that carried the Paris 2024 medals.

𝟖𝟑. LVMH signed a 10-year global partnership with Formula 1 starting in 2025.

👨‍👩‍👧‍👦 THE FAMILY

𝟖𝟒. Arnault has five children: Delphine, Antoine, Alexandre, Frédéric and Jean.

𝟖𝟓. Delphine Arnault became CEO of Christian Dior Couture in 2023.

𝟖𝟔. Antoine Arnault oversees image and environment at LVMH and heads Christian Dior SE.

𝟖𝟕. Alexandre Arnault was an executive at Tiffany before moving to Moët Hennessy.

𝟖𝟖. Frédéric Arnault ran TAG Heuer and then LVMH's watch division.

𝟖𝟗. Jean Arnault, the youngest, works on watches at Louis Vuitton.

𝟗𝟎. Arnault reportedly hosts monthly lunches to quiz his children on the business.

𝟗𝟏. In 2024 the Arnault family bought a majority stake in the football club Paris FC.

💰 WEALTH & LEGACY

𝟗𝟐. In December 2022 Arnault overtook Elon Musk to become the world's richest person.

𝟗𝟑. He topped the Forbes billionaires list in 2023 with an estimated $211 billion.

𝟗𝟒. He was the first French citizen and the first luxury tycoon ever to top that list.

𝟗𝟓. Most of his fortune is tied to LVMH shares, so it can swing by billions in a single day.

𝟗𝟔. The Fondation Louis Vuitton, designed by Frank Gehry, opened in Paris in 2014.

𝟗𝟕. Its glass "sails" are made of about 3,600 glass panels.

𝟗𝟖. The Arnault family pledged €200 million to rebuild Notre-Dame after the 2019 fire.

𝟗𝟗. In 2012 his request for Belgian citizenship caused a storm in France; he later withdrew it.

𝟏𝟎𝟎. He has led LVMH for more than 35 years, turning it into the world's largest luxury group.

Today was a very special day for Irish Wheelchair Association as we welcomed Minister for Children, Disability and Equality, Norma Foley TD, to our Clontarf Campus for the official launch of our Strategic Plan 2026–2030 – A Strategy of Impact.

At the heart of our strategy are the voices, experiences and ambitions of our members.

We were privileged to hear from members, Shauna, Niamh and Martin who shared their personal journeys, reminding us why independence, choice and opportunity matter so much.

Our new strategy sets out our ambitions for the next five years, focusing on Independence, Empowerment, Accessibility, Mobility and Sport, with advocacy underpinning everything we do.

Because everyone deserves the opportunity to live the life they choose.

A huge thank you to our members who shared their stories, to Minister Foley, partners and supporters for joining us and to everyone who contributed to developing our strategy.

Special thanks was also paid to our incredible staff and Community Centres across the country, who bring the ambitions of our strategy to life every day. Over the past few weeks, many of our centres have hosted their own community launches, celebrating the strategy with members, staff and local communities.

It is this collective commitment, from our members and staff to our communities across Ireland, that will turn our ambitions into meaningful impact.

Primož Roglič has signed a one-year contract with NSN Cycling Team for the 2027 season, announced on 18 November 2026. The 37-year-old Slovenian leaves Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe after three seasons and joins a Swiss WorldTour squad building general classification ambitions around a group of experienced leaders.

NSN framed the move as the “final chapter” of his career (“gremo!”), though neither side has confirmed retirement after 2027. Roglič remains motivated, citing the team’s “Never Say Never” name as a perfect fit.

The Signing and Immediate Context:
NSN Cycling Team (UCI WorldTeam, Swiss license, operations based in Girona with Catalan ties) announced the deal on its website. It is a one-year agreement covering only 2027—shorter than the multi-year deals given to other incoming GC riders. This followed months of speculation after his Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe contract expired.Options had included a rejected Lotto-Intermarché offer, a ruled-out return to Visma-Lease a Bike, interest from Tudor, Pinarello-Q36.5, Movistar and others, and even Unibet Rose Rockets (which withdrew for financial reasons).
Retirement was openly discussed; Red Bull boss Ralph Denk reportedly advised him to consider stepping away rather than joining a more modest project.

Roglič’s own words indicate he still has “some work to do—in both racing and with myself.”
He will join Richard Carapaz (signed through 2029), Santiago Buitrago and Lennert Van Eetvelt (also on longer deals). The group gives NSN its strongest GC roster yet.

Primož Roglič Career:
Born 29 October 1989, Roglič transitioned from ski jumping to professional cycling around 2012–13. He rode for Adria Mobil, then spent eight highly successful years at Jumbo-Visma (later Visma-Lease a Bike) before three seasons at Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe.

Key palmarès (93 career victories total):
4× Vuelta a España (2019, 2020, 2021, 2024)
Giro d’Italia (2023)
Olympic gold in the individual time trial (Tokyo 2021)
World Championships time-trial silver (2017)
Liège-Bastogne-Liège (2020)
Multiple stage-race wins and Grand Tour stage victories (especially in the Vuelta).

He is known for resilience, time-trial strength, climbing ability in Grand Tours, and a winning mentality that has produced consistent high-level results across more than a decade in the WorldTour.
2026 Season PerformanceRoglič’s 2026 campaign included setbacks and strong finishes. A training incident in late July (hit by a car) forced him to miss San Sebastián and the Vuelta a Burgos.

He still delivered

2nd overall at the Vuelta a España, 2 minutes 15 seconds behind winner Enric Mas (Movistar).
A fifth Vuelta title would have given him the outright record; he described the result positively given the circumstances of preparing for the race.
European Time Trial Champion on home soil in Šenčur, Slovenia (7 October 2026), winning the 22 km course in 28:16.61 ahead of Bruno Armirail.
Slovenian time-trial champion and solid results including 5th at Tirreno-Adriatico.

These late-season performances demonstrated he remains competitive at the highest level at age 37.

Primož Roglič will enter NSN as one of its primary general classification options in 2027, but not as an undisputed sole leader.

The team has assembled a crowded group of riders with Grand Tour ambitions, and Roglič’s experience and one-year “final chapter” framing position him as a high-priority option for at least one of the three Grand Tours—most logically the Vuelta a España, the race he has dominated more than any other.

Roglič brings the most proven three-week management experience on the roster: four Vuelta titles, a Giro win, Olympic time-trial gold, and a long track record of defending or chasing GC across all three Grand Tours.
At 37, his strengths remain time-trialing, resilience, and the ability to perform when it matters in the final week.

He joins three other riders who have also been given leadership language:

Richard Carapaz (signed through 2029): 2019 Giro winner, Olympic road-race gold, two Tour stage wins and the mountains classification in 2026, plus 8th overall at the Tour and 4th at the Vuelta that year.

Santiago Buitrago (longer deal): Giro stage winner, 2026 Vuelta mountains classification winner, and consistent top-10 Grand Tour finishes.

Lennert Van Eetvelt (longer deal): Winner of the 2024 UAE Tour and Tour of Guangxi; younger climber with stage-race GC potential.

With only three Grand Tours, the team will almost certainly split leadership. Roglič’s short contract and specialized Vuelta pedigree make him the natural lead when the calendar aligns with his strengths, while the others can co-lead, attack, or support depending on the race.
The group gives NSN tactical flexibility (multiple threats) but also the classic risk of diluted resources if all four are targeting the same objectives.

Support Riders for GC Ambitions:
True dedicated super-domestiques are limited compared with UAE, Visma, or Red Bull. The most relevant options include:

George Bennett (New Zealand, staying through 2027): Experienced climber and Grand Tour veteran (previous stints at Visma and UAE). Team management has highlighted his road-captaincy value as NSN increases its GC focus. He is the clearest pure support option among the veterans.

Kasper Asgreen: Time-trial and classics specialist who can protect on flatter stages and contribute in individual time trials.

Nick Schultz and other climbers already on the roster: Useful mountain support.
The co-leaders themselves (especially Buitrago and Van Eetvelt on days they are not racing for personal GC) can function as high-level helpers.

Younger or versatile riders (Artem Shmidt and others) add depth but are not yet established Grand Tour domestiques.

The 2027 climbing depth is a clear upgrade from NSN’s 2026 sprint- and breakaway-oriented roster, yet it remains a mid-tier support structure rather than an elite one.

Realistic Assessment of Support Strength:
The support should be enough for opportunistic results—stage wins, solid top-10 GC finishes, and the possibility of a podium if Roglič arrives in peak form and the race develops favorably (especially a Vuelta). It is unlikely to be strong enough to control a three-week race against the top superteams when the competition is at its highest (Pogacar, Vingegaard, or a fully stacked Red Bull/UAE squad).

Multiple leaders can help create attacks from different angles, but they also mean fewer pure workers fully committed to one rider. Success will depend more on Roglič’s personal form, race selection, and tactical opportunism than on overwhelming team strength.

Competitiveness Beyond GC:
Roglič remains highly competitive outside pure Grand Tour GC:
Time trials: Fresh European champion (home soil, 2026) and Olympic gold medalist. He can target individual TTs in stage races, national/European championships, and select one-day TTs.

Week-long stage races: Volta a Catalunya (convenient given the team’s Girona base), Tirreno-Adriatico, Critérium du Dauphiné, Tour de Suisse, and similar events suit his climbing-plus-TT profile.

Hilly or selective one-day races: Possible interest in Ardennes classics (he has a Liège-Bastogne-Liège win) or other events with significant climbing and time-trial elements.
Stage hunting in Grand Tours when not prioritizing overall classification.

His 2026 season (2nd at the Vuelta despite a mid-season training crash, plus the European TT title) showed he can still deliver at the highest level when focused.

NSN is the direct successor to Israel-Premier Tech. In late 2025 the WorldTour license was acquired by Never Say Never (a company co-founded by Andrés Iniesta) in partnership with the Swiss investment firm Stoneweg. The team switched to a Swiss license, established a strong operational base in Girona, and rebranded with the “Never Say Never” identity.

In 2026 it operated primarily as a sprint and breakaway unit (16 professional wins, led by riders such as Biniam Girmay and Ethan Vernon) with limited Grand Tour GC presence and a lower ranking among WorldTour teams.

The 2027 recruitment wave—Carapaz, Buitrago, Van Eetvelt, Roglič, Asgreen, and others—marks a deliberate pivot toward multi-leader general classification ambitions.
The project is still early in building the support structures and race programs that top GC teams take for granted, but the direction is clear: from opportunistic wins toward competing for major overall results.

Roglič gives NSN instant credibility and a realistic shot at strong results in selected races, particularly the Vuelta and stage races with time trials. The support and leadership situation will require careful management, and the team’s broader GC project remains a work in progress rather than a finished superteam.

text:
Video game enthusiasts' favorite Grand Theft Auto releases its 6th installment after 13 years. 

After a long thirteen-year wait, two major delays, a series of data leaks, and over a decade of development, Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6 / GTA VI), eagerly anticipated by video game enthusiasts worldwide, was officially released globally on Thursday, November 19, 2026. Considered one of the most anticipated and highest-cost entertainment productions ever created, this game arrives 13 years after the release of GTA V in 2013.

On November 19, the game gradually opened up to the world as midnight struck in each region's local time, with New Zealand and Eastern Australia being among the first countries to experience it. Pre-downloads for digital copies had begun on November 10. Currently released only for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S console models, it also offers the facility to play via Xbox Cloud Gaming on certain devices. However, Rockstar or Take-Two have not yet officially announced a PC version, and a GamesBeat report, citing anonymous sources, stated that it is likely to be released in the first quarter of 2027. In the American market, the Standard Edition is priced at $79.99 and the Ultimate Edition at $99.99, with pre-orders receiving the Vintage Vice City Pack offer.

This time, the story returns to Rockstar's fictional modern Miami-inspired city, Vice City, and extends across the state of Leonida, inspired by Florida. The narrative revolves around the two main characters, Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, within an environment comprising island chains, coastlines, highways, swamps, nightclubs, and the criminal underworld. Jason, who grew up among fraudsters and criminals, left military service under unfavorable circumstances, and now works with drug traffickers on the Leonida islands, desires an easy life, but his life is becoming increasingly difficult. Lucia, the first female protagonist in a mainline GTA game, fought for her family, ended up imprisoned in Leonida, and gained freedom purely by luck. With family ties to Liberty City, she seeks the good life her mother dreamed of. When an easy heist goes wrong, these two are drawn into the darkest side of America's sunniest region, and to survive a criminal conspiracy spanning across Leonida, they must trust each other more than ever. Players can switch between these two characters while playing, and there is also an option to develop an alternative romantic relationship between these criminal partners.

With the lifting of the review embargo a day before its release, on November 18, GTA VI received unprecedented critical acclaim. It achieved a score of 99 on Metacritic, matching the all-time record held by The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, released in 1998. No mixed or negative reviews were reported in the initial round, and it also scored 99 on OpenCritic with a 100% recommendation. Leading publications such as IGN, GameSpot, Game Informer, Eurogamer, Forbes, The Washington Post, and The Verge awarded it maximum scores of 10/10 or 5/5, praising its vibrant open world, character relationships, and technical polish.

Analysts also predict this will be the biggest entertainment release in history commercially. According to Sensor Tower's third-party estimates, approximately 15.9 million digital pre-orders were recorded by mid-November, generating revenue between $1.54 billion and $1.7 billion. Between 74% and 75% of these pre-orders were for PlayStation 5, and there was high demand for the more expensive Ultimate Edition. Take-Two, stating that pre-orders are much higher than expected, has projected a financial revenue target of between $8.0 billion and $8.2 billion based on GTA VI. The series has sold approximately 480 million copies overall to date.

This project, developed over more than a decade, was severely impacted by data leaks in 2022 and thereafter. Although initially planned for release in 2025, Rockstar had to postpone it to May 26, 2026, and then to November 19, to achieve the desired quality. While production costs have not been officially disclosed, analysts estimate that production and marketing expenses range from $1 billion to $1.5 billion or more. Rockstar denied some reports that it exceeded $1.5 billion, and Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick only stated that it was a high-cost project.

Scored by the electronic music duo Justice, this game is classified as an adults-only game due to its themes of violence, strong language, sexual content, and crime. A full-fledged GTA Online multiplayer mode has not yet been announced with the release, and official information regarding post-release sales reports, online mode details, and the PC version is expected to be revealed in the coming weeks.
