Trump Resents Vance's Failure to Endorse Iran War, While Rubio Gains Favor: The 2028 Succession Contest Heats Up Early
Trump has reportedly complained repeatedly over the past two weeks that Vance has not explicitly supported his decision to go to war. Vance is trying to distance himself from the war's costs without openly opposing Trump, and observers have compared his predicament to Harris's earlier situation.

Differences between U.S. President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance over the Iran war and the Republican Party's midterm election defeat are emerging. Trump initially agreed with Vance's analysis attributing the election defeat to the Iran war, but subsequently grew increasingly dissatisfied with his remarks, believing that Vance had not explicitly emphasized that his decision to go to war with Iran was correct.

Meanwhile, Trump has continued privately praising Secretary of State Marco Rubio, even suggesting that he could become a competitive presidential candidate. As potential competition for the 2028 presidential election gradually intensifies, Trump's differing attitudes toward two key aides have also brought the question of succession within the Republican Party to the surface early.

According to people familiar with the matter who spoke to The New York Times, Trump has repeatedly complained to aides and allies over the past two weeks that, when explaining why Republicans suffered a crushing midterm election defeat, Vance did not explicitly say that the president's decision to launch the Iran war was correct.

Earlier in November 2026, Trump publicly hinted at dissatisfaction with Vance's remarks, saying the vice president should have added “another sentence.” He subsequently explained that Vance should have explicitly answered one question: “If you had to do it over again, would you still do it? The answer is yes.”

In a lengthy social media post after the midterm elections, Vance bluntly stated that the Iran war was the main reason for the Republican defeat. He wrote: “The reason we lost the election was this war.” He also noted that Trump had previously expressed similar views, although Trump also attributed the Republican defeat to multiple factors, particularly emphasizing that he himself was not on the ballot.

Trump initially reacted calmly to this analysis, telling reporters: “I think that's basically true.” But Vance's criticism of the administration's pre-election messaging strategy, along with his failure to explicitly endorse the decision to go to war, appears to have changed the president's attitude.

Vance Tries to Draw Policy Distinctions but Struggles to Distance Himself From Trump

Observers have interpreted Vance's remarks as a subtle attempt at political distancing: acknowledging that the Iran war hurt Republicans' electoral prospects while trying to avoid directly criticizing Trump himself.

However, this approach has not fully eliminated differences within the White House. Before the elections, Vance had expressed reservations about the Iran war within the administration, and when he endorsed Trump in 2023, he pledged not to drag the United States into new wars. After the midterm election defeat, he shifted to publicly discussing the war's political costs.

Trump subsequently announced that Vance would no longer participate in peace negotiations with Iran, directing him to focus instead on investigating allegations of election fraud in areas governed by Democrats. Vance had previously increased his involvement in those negotiations ahead of the elections.

In an interview with Fox News during the week of November 16, 2026, Vance tried to play down differences with the president. Asked whether there was any policy distance between them, he replied: “I don't think there are any differences between me and the president or other senior members of the administration.”

But Alyssa Farah Griffin, an official in Trump's first administration and now a co-host of The View, believes Vance's situation resembles that of then-Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024. That year, when Harris was asked whether she would have changed any of President Joseph R. Biden Jr.'s decisions, she replied that she could not think of anything she would have done differently.

Griffin said Trump's vice president is perpetually caught in a dilemma: he cannot display obvious differences with the president, yet must confront the political consequences of policy mistakes. She believes Vance's statement during the week of November 16, 2026, that there were “no differences” may seem inconsequential but could be quoted repeatedly in future campaign advertisements.

Democratic strategist Rob Flaherty, a former deputy campaign manager for Harris, also noted that it is difficult for a vice president to distance himself from an unpopular president. He believes Vance has already put himself in this predicament, while Harris previously also failed to find an effective way to distance herself from Biden's policies on the Israel-Hamas war.

Rubio Gains Trump's Favor, Shifting the Republican Competitive Landscape for 2028

The pressure facing Vance comes not only from the Iran war but also from Trump's attitude toward potential successors.

Since Trump selected Vance as his running mate for a second term, many Republicans have believed that the former Ohio senator would be the leading contender for the Republican presidential nomination in 2028. But throughout his time in office, Trump has never explicitly committed to supporting Vance.

Vance himself has also said he has not yet decided whether to run. In his Fox News interview, he said: “I haven't made a decision yet. We'll think about it sometime in 2027.”

Vance's allies say he is indeed still weighing his political future. Family considerations could influence his choice: his fourth child was born in July 2026. In addition, Vance pays close attention to political analysis and election data, and if he concludes that he lacks a path to victory, he may choose not to run for now. Further developments in the Iran war will also be crucial. Some allies believe that if Trump decides to resume large-scale military action against Iran, the likelihood of Vance running will decline significantly.

By contrast, Rubio has recently continued to receive praise from Trump both publicly and privately. Speaking about Rubio while attending the ASEAN summit in Manila on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, Trump said: “How popular is Marco now? Isn't he doing a great job? He's doing a fantastic job.”

Rubio also took on more public-facing duties during Trump's trip abroad, including responding to public concerns about several recent technical system failures in the United States and emphasizing that there was currently no evidence that the incidents were caused by cyberattacks.

More importantly, Rubio's staunch support for the Iran war has won Trump's approval. In an interview with The New York Times, he said Trump “deserves enormous credit” for ordering strikes on Iran, and said leadership means being willing to take actions that are politically unpopular but necessary for the country and its long-term future.

Rubio previously expressed support for Vance and denied that he was preparing to leave the administration to run for president. However, his allies say he could change his decision if Trump encouraged him to run. Trump is currently in no hurry to settle on a successor and instead enjoys keeping his advisers in competition with one another.

The Republicans' severe midterm election setback has also created room for other potential contenders. Democrats achieved a victory on a scale that neither party had attained in a midterm election since Watergate. Texas Senator Ted Cruz and Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, among others, are also considering whether to enter the 2028 presidential race.

Vance's allies believe that choosing the next Republican presidential nominee through a competitive primary, rather than settling on a candidate within the party in advance, could be more conducive to consolidating support. They view Harris's rapid acquisition of the Democratic presidential nomination in 2024, followed by her eventual general election defeat, as an example of the risks of insufficient competition within a party.

But former Republican New Jersey Governor Chris Christie believes that anyone serving in Trump's second administration will face greater political baggage. He is also considering another presidential run and offered this assessment: “Anyone who serves in Trump's second administration cannot win the general election in the fall of 2028. They will be seen as another four years of Trump in office, and that image is very difficult to sell to American voters.”

For Vance, the real challenge is not only how to manage his relationship with Trump, but also how to determine what kind of Republican Party he will represent in the future. From publicly criticizing Trump in 2016 as “unfit for the nation's highest office,” to seeking Trump's endorsement and winning the Ohio Senate election in 2022, and then becoming vice president, Vance's political trajectory itself reflects the evolution of his political alliance with Trump.

text:
Nvidia's $500 Billion AI Financing Plan Has Yet to Deploy Any Funds. Why Is Wall Street Starting to Pull Back?
The agreements Nvidia signed with several Wall Street institutions are mainly memoranda of understanding and do not require participants to raise funds. The financing plan, once presented as a major pillar of the AI investment cycle, is far less binding than the market imagined.

Nvidia (NVDA.O) has sought to join forces with Wall Street to open financing channels for the AI supply chain, but according to The Wall Street Journal, the plan, worth as much as $500 billion, has yet to actually deploy any funds. With the company's chief executive, Jensen Huang, stepping down over an extramarital affair scandal and financial guarantees being tightened, financial institutions have become more skeptical about whether the plan can be implemented.

The financing arrangement was originally intended to help AI startups such as OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as smaller cloud computing providers, obtain the funds needed to buy Nvidia chips, ensuring continued growth in chip demand. Nvidia now faces not only difficulties in implementing the financing plan itself, but also the need to demonstrate to investors that it will not take on excessive credit risk to sustain AI demand.

Nvidia's finance chief, Colette Kress, has now taken over as interim chief executive. On the earnings call on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, she said the company was rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments and guarantees. She emphasized that Nvidia's role in supporting the AI ecosystem deserved recognition, but that related transactions would be approached more cautiously in the future.

Huang Pushed to Accelerate the Financing Plan, but the $500 Billion Agreement Is Largely a Statement of Intent

In pushing this plan, Huang initially hoped to use Wall Street capital to address AI customers' financing difficulties. According to people familiar with the matter, early in 2026, despite Nvidia's extraordinary profits, its valuation multiple declined, prompting Huang to seek new initiatives that could bolster market confidence. He had envisioned establishing a financing partnership with Wall Street worth as much as $1 trillion.

Nvidia had previously negotiated for months with institutions including Goldman Sachs (GS.N), Blackstone (BX.N) and Apollo Global Management (APO.N), hoping to support loans through credit guarantees so that customers with weaker credit profiles could also obtain funding to buy chips. But these transactions are structurally complex, and negotiations progressed slowly.

In June 2026, Nvidia's main competitor, Broadcom (AVGO.O), reached a chip-financing arrangement worth around $35 billion with Apollo and Blackstone to provide financing support for Anthropic. Huang was displeased, believing Nvidia was moving too slowly on similar projects. He subsequently convened executives from several Wall Street financial institutions in California for discussions, hoping to launch a larger plan that could be implemented more quickly.

In August 2026, Nvidia announced partnerships with institutions including Apollo, Blackstone, BlackRock (BLK.N), Brookfield (BN.N), Goldman Sachs and KKR (KKR.N), with the goal of mobilizing $500 billion. Huang appeared on CNBC alongside financial industry executives including Goldman Sachs Chief Executive David Solomon and Blackstone President Jonathan Gray to promote the plan. Solomon called it a "pivotal moment in a historic AI investment cycle."

But the agreement was far less binding than its announced scale suggested. People familiar with the matter said the memorandum of understanding signed by the parties was only a few pages long, mainly setting out financing targets, types of potential customers and Nvidia's willingness to consider providing credit guarantees on a project-by-project basis. Participating institutions did not commit to raising any funds, and the $500 billion was not a binding fundraising commitment.

The arrangement's primary function was therefore to signal to the market that AI companies could gain access to more financing channels in the future, while encouraging Wall Street institutions to explore how to provide large-scale funding for chip purchases. To date, the related plans have still not seen any actual funds deployed.

Disagreements Over Guarantee Levels Intensify as AI Financing Becomes Harder to Obtain

One important reason the financing plan has remained unimplemented is disagreement between Nvidia and financial institutions over risk sharing.

Earlier in 2026, The Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia had considered providing $250 billion in guarantees for OpenAI's data center in Ohio. The day after the news was released, Nvidia's shares fell 5%, wiping out $250 billion in market capitalization. The market feared Nvidia might take on too much financing risk. The company subsequently halved its initial financial commitment to OpenAI and sought to bring in other investors to share the funding burden.

In August 2026, Huang said Nvidia was willing to provide credit support of no more than 25% of a project's cost. That proportion was significantly below the level of guarantees Broadcom provided in related financing transactions.

Under the "Big Sky" project announced in June 2026, Broadcom provided a residual value guarantee of approximately 85% for the $35 billion in financing secured by Anthropic. In the subsequent $63 billion "North Star" financing project, Broadcom's guarantee ratio was also slightly below three-quarters.

A residual value guarantee provides a certain level of protection for the residual value of the relevant assets or project if the borrower cannot repay the loan, thereby reducing potential losses for lenders.

But since August 2026, credit markets have become more cautious toward lower-rated AI borrowers. People familiar with the matter said investors wanted Nvidia to provide residual value guarantees above 25% before they would be willing to lend to the relevant projects. If Nvidia insists on reducing guarantees, this will become a major obstacle to advancing the financing plan.

Meanwhile, the financing environment for AI infrastructure construction is also tightening. Lenders have begun scrutinizing related projects more rigorously, low-cost funding is in short supply, and cloud computing providers with weaker credit profiles are particularly vulnerable.

The parties are still discussing the first customer financing transaction secured by Nvidia chips, but people familiar with the matter expect it could be completed in 2027 at the earliest.

Nvidia Still Has Incentives to Support Financing, but Is Becoming More Cautious About Guarantee Obligations

Even if the $500 billion target ultimately cannot be achieved, Nvidia and Wall Street still have incentives to bring some financing projects to fruition.

For Nvidia, customers' ability to obtain funding directly affects their capacity to purchase chips. AI startups and emerging cloud computing providers need to keep investing enormous sums in building data centers. If financing channels are obstructed, chip demand could also be affected.

For financial institutions, financing AI infrastructure likewise represents potential business opportunities. But with borrowers' credit risks rising and investors demanding higher guarantee ratios, banks and asset managers are unwilling to shoulder too much risk on their own.

Apollo Chief Executive Marc Rowan said on CNBC on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, that Nvidia had a strong commercial incentive to get the relevant projects underway. If Nvidia stopped providing the guarantees needed for bank financing, many emerging cloud computing providers would lose access to capital.

Nvidia's recent quarterly results and guidance remain strong, but how customers will raise funds to keep buying chips has become an important factor in investors' assessments of the company's growth prospects and stock valuation.

Following Huang's departure, whether Nvidia can continue to serve as a credit backstop for financing the AI industry will depend on how much risk the new management is willing to assume. Kress has clearly signaled a more cautious approach, suggesting that future financing arrangements may place greater emphasis on project quality and risk controls rather than simply pursuing funding scale.

text:
Nvidia’s $642 Billion Bind: Locking in the Boom as the Outlook Softens

While markets fixated on Nvidia’s $115.8 billion quarterly revenue, the deeper signal sat in the company’s disclosures. 

In the six months leading into late October, the chipmaker’s purchase commitments to suppliers more than tripled from $119 billion at the end of April to $279 billion by the end of July, then to $390 billion as of October 25. 

Management attributes the bulk of that surge to multi-year memory purchases. The balance sheet reflects the same urgency: raw materials inventory climbed from $3.8 billion in January to $15.8 billion by October.

Those supplier deals form only part of a far larger set of forward obligations. Data center leases and cloud service agreements rose from $74 billion to $102 billion in a single quarter.

Separate arrangements with neocloud providers firms that buy Nvidia systems and rent out the resulting compute total another $32 billion. 

Financial guarantees expanded even more sharply, from $3.5 billion in July to $118 billion in October. 

Of that figure, $105 billion backs the Ohio campus that OpenAI is leasing. Added together, Nvidia now stands behind roughly $642 billion in commitments and guarantees.

That total is twelve times the $53.5 billion in cash and marketable debt securities the company holds, a cash pile that has actually declined from $56.7 billion a year earlier. 

It also exceeds twice the revenue Nvidia generated over the past nine months. Most of these arrangements stretch across multiple years, and many cannot be unwound without significant cost or reputational damage.

The timing is awkward. On November 13, SemiAnalysis reduced its forecast for global AI chip spending in 2029 by 41 percent, from $1.352 trillion to $796 billion. 

For Nvidia specifically, the firm cut its 2029 shipment outlook by 56 percent. The primary reasons cited were slower growth in new recurring revenue at the leading AI labs during the third quarter and growing reluctance among investors to finance large-scale buildouts. 

On Nvidia’s own earnings call, the company noted that token prices have fallen nearly 60 percent since May. 

The customers writing the checks are earning less per unit of output even as the company that supplies the chips is signing ever-larger multi-year obligations.

Nvidia’s management presents a coherent case for the strategy. The company guided to $130 billion in revenue for the coming quarter. Memory remains scarce, so early commitments can prevent competitors from securing supply. 

A purchase commitment is not the same as debt, and some guarantees may never be drawn. The CFO has also indicated that the next quarter should mark the low point for gross margins. 

Yet the $105 billion Ohio guarantee is instructive: when a supplier must underwrite its customer’s long-term leases, it is effectively acknowledging that the customer cannot carry the risk alone.

If the more cautious demand trajectory SemiAnalysis now projects materializes, Nvidia would still be required to take delivery of the memory, fund the leases, and honor the guarantees it has extended. 

The company has bet that locking up supply and underwriting customer infrastructure will preserve its position through the next phase of AI expansion. 

The scale of those bets means the outcome is no longer solely dependent on how much demand materializes it also depends on how much of the risk Nvidia has already agreed to absorb.

from grok:  **Evanston Township High School (Evanston) has produced the most NFL players among Illinois high schools (25), which is the strongest available proxy for the most Division I college football scholarships historically.**

### Key data points:
- **Evanston** leads with **25 NFL players**.
- Next are **Mount Carmel (Chicago)**, **Oak Park and River Forest**, and **Lane Tech** (tied at 18 each).
- **East St. Louis** and **Thornton Township** follow with 17 each.

There is no comprehensive public all-time ranking that tallies every Division I scholarship (including non-NFL players). NFL production is the best available long-term measure, as nearly all NFL players come through Division I programs.

### Context on other top programs:
- **Mount Carmel** is widely regarded as Illinois’ most successful high school football program historically (most state titles) and a consistent D1 talent pipeline. It ranks just behind Evanston in NFL alumni and routinely has multiple Power Four / Division I commits in recent classes.
- Other frequent high-volume producers in recent years include **Simeon**, **East St. Louis**, **Brother Rice**, **Loyola Academy**, **Lincoln-Way East**, and **Morgan Park**. These schools regularly send multiple players to Division I programs in a given cycle.

In short: **Evanston** holds the all-time lead by the NFL metric, while **Mount Carmel** is the strongest overall historical football power and talent factory.

🇮🇷|TEHRAN’S SECURITY CHIEF MOURNS A MARJA WHO STOOD ON THE FRONT LINES: REZAEI’S CONDOLENCE EXPOSES THE WESTERN LIE THAT RELIGION AND RESISTANCE ARE SEPARATE

Major General Mohsen Rezaei, Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council of Iran, has offered his condolences on the passing of Grand Ayatollah Hossein Vahid Khorasani. The message is not a routine obituary. It is a political and spiritual statement that directly challenges the Western narrative which tries to confine Shia religious authority to quietist ritual and separate it from the struggle against oppression.

Rezaei emphasized that the reassuring presence of this esteemed Marja on the front lines of the struggle between truth and falsehood, along with his profound and enlightening remarks addressed to the fighters for the cause of Islam, served as a testament to his deep understanding of the vital importance of the presence of such combatants in the arena of defending the very essence of Islam.

This is the key sentence. It defines the Marja not as a secluded scholar issuing abstract rulings, but as a guide who understood that the defense of Islam requires bodies on the front lines and that the scholars must stand with them. The Western media will ignore this dimension because it contradicts the convenient fiction that Shia clerics are either apolitical quietists or Iranian state functionaries. Ayatollah Vahid Khorasani was neither. He was a Marja whose authority was rooted in scholarship and piety, and whose vision extended to the battlefield where truth confronts falsehood.

The condolence message itself is addressed to a wide circle of authority and devotion. Rezaei extends condolences to the Remnant of God, Imam al-Hujjah ibn al-Hasan, may God hasten his noble reappearance, to the Leader of the Islamic Revolution, to the other Grand Ayatollahs, to the Islamic seminaries, to his students and followers, and in particular to his noble family, his esteemed sons, his relatives, and especially to Ayatollah Amoli Larijani.

The structure of the message matters. It begins with the Hidden Imam and moves through the Leader of the Islamic Revolution to the seminaries and the family. This is not a list of formalities. It is a map of legitimate authority in the Shia world. The Marja is not appointed by a state. He is recognized by the faithful, by the seminaries, and by his peers. Rezaei, as the Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, is placing the security apparatus of the Islamic Republic in the service of that authority, not above it. He is mourning a Marja whose independence from state structures was precisely what gave his words weight on the front lines.

The Western narrative tries to present Iran as a country where religion is a tool of the state. The condolence message refutes this by showing that the state’s security chief is the one bowing to the Marja, not the other way around. Ayatollah Vahid Khorasani’s authority came from his scholarship, his piety, and his connection to the faithful. His presence on the front lines was not a state assignment. It was a decision made by a man who understood that the defense of Islam is not a metaphor.

The message also specifically mentions Ayatollah Amoli Larijani, a detail that the mainstream will overlook. This is a signal of continuity within the religious and political leadership of Iran. The Marja’s family and close associates are part of the fabric of the Islamic Republic, not separate from it. The condolence is addressed to them personally because the loss is personal, but it is also institutional. A node of knowledge and guidance has been closed, and the entire structure of Shia authority feels the break.

Rezaei’s message is therefore not just a tribute. It is a declaration that the front lines of truth and falsehood are real, that the Marja understood this, and that the security apparatus of Iran is committed to the same struggle. The Western media will not report this because it cannot fit the Marja into its framework. It cannot explain why a 105-year-old scholar would concern himself with fighters on the front lines. It cannot explain why the Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council would mourn him as a comrade in arms rather than a ceremonial figure.

The answer is that Ayatollah Vahid Khorasani was not a ceremonial figure. He was a Marja who understood that Islam is defended not only in seminaries but on the ground, and that the scholars who remain silent while the faithful are attacked have abandoned their duty. His presence on the front lines was a living refutation of the quietist narrative that the West prefers. Rezaei’s condolence is a reaffirmation that the Islamic Republic and the Marja’iyya share the same understanding of what is at stake.

The loss is heavy. The message is clear. The struggle continues. And the Western narrative that tries to separate religion from resistance is exposed, once again, as a lie.

text:
Strings Attached: U.S. Arms Export Controls, Alternative Suppliers, and the Question of Indirect Responsibility

When the United States sells arms abroad, it does not simply ship weapons and walk away. U.S. law and the contracts underpinning those sales impose binding conditions: recipients must not retransfer the equipment to third parties without Washington’s written consent, and they must not use it for purposes other than those for which it was furnished without prior authorization. The Pentagon and State Department operate end-use monitoring programs—Golden Sentry for government-to-government sales and Blue Lantern for direct commercial sales—to check compliance, and violations can trigger reporting to Congress and suspension of future sales. The financial stakes are enormous: the U.S. defense industry benefits from tens of billions of dollars in foreign military sales annually, supporting hundreds of thousands of American jobs. But the United States is not the only arms exporter, and its restrictions are not unique in kind—only in scale and legal formality. Two further questions follow: Do other suppliers impose comparable restrictions? And if Washington profits from weapons that are later used in atrocities, does it bear indirect responsibility for war crimes? This report examines both.

Other Major Arms Suppliers and Their Restriction Regimes

France requires recipients to sign a final-use certificate and a non-retransfer undertaking. French law mandates that the importer and end-user commit not to transfer the equipment to any third party, in any form, without the prior agreement of the French government. The French exporting company must have the signatures authenticated by a French embassy or diplomatic mission and must retain copies of the non-retransfer clauses for ten years. French export licences also carry conditions on final use and re-export outside the European Union. France therefore operates a consent-based system for retransfer and end-use that is structurally similar to the U.S. model, though its post-shipment monitoring is generally less publicly documented than the American Golden Sentry and Blue Lantern programs.

The United Kingdom’s export licensing regime is explicitly risk-based and human-rights-sensitive. Under the Arms Trade Treaty and UK regulations, export licences should be denied where there is a clear risk that the arms might be used to commit serious violations of international humanitarian law or human rights law. The UK has suspended licences where items covered might be used in ways inconsistent with international humanitarian law. However, independent reviews have argued that the UK’s end-use monitoring remains a weak link and that parliamentary scrutiny should be strengthened. The UK therefore imposes meaningful pre-export restrictions but has been criticized for weaker post-shipment verification than the U.S. system claims to provide.

Germany has developed a formal post-shipment control system. Since 2015, Berlin has required end-use certificates in which the recipient state grants Germany the right to conduct on-the-spot checks. The purpose is to verify that weapons supplied are still present in the recipient country and in the possession of the declared end-user; random checks are used for large quantities. If non-compliance is found or inspections are refused, consequences follow under Germany’s political principles on arms exports. Germany has conducted a limited number of on-site inspections, and the system covers war weapons and specific firearms destined for state recipients. The German regime is narrower in scope than the U.S. system but explicitly includes physical verification abroad.

Russia’s arms export contracts require foreign customers to use the equipment only for the purposes declared in the end-user certificate and not to re-export or transfer it to third countries without Russia’s consent. A 2006 government resolution established a formal post-shipment verification mechanism: the exporter must follow up to confirm that the items were received and used as intended, and violators can be placed on a watch list of unreliable foreign recipients subject to restrictions or bans. Russia does not, however, publish detailed monitoring data, and it is not a party to the Arms Trade Treaty. The system is real on paper but far less transparent than the American or German frameworks.

China requires recipient governments to commit not to transfer Chinese-origin arms to any third party without prior consent of the Chinese government, and it operates a licensing system with end-user and end-use certification. China’s stated principles are that arms exports should enhance the recipient’s self-defense capacity, should not harm regional or international peace and security, and should not interfere in the recipient’s domestic affairs. However, analysts have noted that China’s regulations do not comprehensively address end-use monitoring, that enforcement capacity is underdeveloped, and that investigations often rely reactively on intelligence from the U.S. or Europe. The Chinese regime therefore contains formal non-retransfer conditions but lacks the institutionalized post-shipment verification architecture found in the U.S. or Germany.

Israel’s Defense Export Control Law of 2007 establishes a licensing system administered by the Defense Export Controls Agency within the Ministry of Defense. All defense exports require licences, and the system includes end-user and end-use verification, post-shipment verification in some cases, record-keeping for at least ten years, periodic reporting, and compliance audits. Exporters must provide certifications verifying the end-use and end-user to prevent diversion. Israel’s system is formal and legally codified, though its application to exports to entities whose conduct is contested is itself a matter of international controversy.

South Korea requires buyers to provide end-user certification legally prohibiting re-export or transfer to third parties without the prior written consent of the South Korean government. Exporters must verify the identities of purchasers, ultimate consignees, and end-users, as well as the intended end-use, before applying for an export permit. South Korea has been urged to strengthen post-export monitoring and to use a denial list for high-risk entities. Its regime is therefore consent-based on retransfer but still developing in post-shipment oversight.

In comparative terms, most major suppliers impose retransfer and end-use conditions, and several—especially Germany, the United States, and Israel—have formal post-shipment verification mechanisms. The United States is distinctive in the scale, legal codification, and congressional oversight of its system, but it is not alone in attaching strings. France, the UK, Germany, Russia, China, Israel, and South Korea all impose, in varying degrees, retransfer restrictions and end-use conditions, and several operate post-shipment verification mechanisms. What distinguishes the U.S. system is its scale, legal formalization, and congressional oversight—not the mere fact that conditions exist.

Why Countries Buy from the United States Despite the Strings

If U.S. arms come with conditions and monitoring, why do so many governments still buy them? The reasons are strategic, institutional, and financial. Defense procurement is rarely a purely commercial decision. Armament purchases are often used to reinforce a strategic or security partnership. Buying American equipment signals alignment with Washington and can be a way to secure or deepen U.S. security commitments. Analysts note that for many buyers of systems like the F-35, the purchase is understood as buying not only an aircraft but also a U.S. security guarantee. In this sense, the restrictions are part of the package: the buyer accepts conditionality because the relationship with Washington is the point.

Militaries also want to operate alongside allies. If a country’s partners already use U.S. systems, buying the same equipment creates interoperability—shared communications, logistics, tactics, and supply chains. This creates a network effect: the more militaries procure a system, the stronger the incentive for others to follow. The U.S. actively leverages this dynamic, and its reluctance to share source code and intellectual property can make integration of non-U.S. systems harder, reinforcing the pull toward American platforms.

The U.S. government’s Foreign Military Sales system offers a one-stop shop: training, maintenance, logistical support, and government-backed financing can be bundled with the equipment. Foreign Military Sales can reduce procurement timelines and administrative burdens, and it allows buyers to derogate from EU procurement rules where applicable. Foreign Military Financing provides loans or grants that make U.S. equipment more affordable for allies. For a government facing urgent security needs, the Foreign Military Sales package can be more attractive than piecing together a deal with a European or Asian supplier.

After Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, short-term availability became a decisive factor. The United States had larger production capacity, maintained stocks, and could deliver or promise equipment at greater speed than many European suppliers after decades of downsizing. Past acquisitions also shape future ones: militaries want to replenish existing systems, buy upgraded versions of equipment they already know, and avoid the cost of retraining and rebuilding logistics for a new supplier. In some segments—such as certain drones, tactical ballistic missiles, and long-range artillery rockets—there may be no comparable non-U.S. option available on the market due to decades of underinvestment by other suppliers. Where alternatives exist, U.S. systems may offer similar performance at a competitive cost when only the purchase price is considered, because American producers benefit from economies of scale. The restrictions, in other words, are not necessarily a deal-breaker. They are one attribute of a package that also includes strategic alignment, interoperability, financing, availability, and often unrivaled capability.

Does the United States Bear Indirect Responsibility for War Crimes?

This is the hardest question, and it does not admit of a single yes-or-no answer. International law recognizes a concept of complicity in the wrongful acts of another state, but its application to arms sales is contested and fact-dependent. Under customary international law, as reflected in Article 16 of the International Law Commission’s Articles on State Responsibility, a state that knowingly aids or assists another state in the commission of an internationally wrongful act is responsible for that assistance if the act would be wrongful if committed by the assisting state and the assisting state does so with knowledge of the circumstances. The Arms Trade Treaty reinforces this logic: Article 6 prohibits transfers where the exporting state has knowledge that the arms would be used in the commission of genocide, crimes against humanity, or war crimes, and Article 7 requires an export risk assessment. The Arms Trade Treaty’s obligation to conduct human rights risk assessments is built on the complicity principle: states must not transfer arms where they will contribute to serious violations. The key legal questions are therefore what the supplying state knew and what it should have known. A state that sells arms with no reason to anticipate their use in atrocities is differently situated from a state that continues to supply weapons after credible evidence of systematic violations has emerged.

Two cases dominate contemporary debate. In Saudi Arabia and Yemen, the United States has provided Saudi-led coalition aircraft with refueling, targeting intelligence, and munitions used in a bombing campaign that has caused extensive civilian casualties. Critics, including U.S. legislators, have described American logistical and intelligence support as making the United States complicit in the devastation of Yemen. Investigations have documented the use of U.S.-origin guided bombs and white phosphorus in strikes affecting civilians. The United States did not directly drop the bombs, but it supplied the aircraft, the munitions, the intelligence, and the spare parts that made the campaign possible. In Israel and Gaza, since October 2023, the United States has provided Israel with military assistance and arms sales at levels described as unprecedented. Amnesty International has stated that Israeli forces have repeatedly used U.S.-origin weapons in violations of international law, and that by continuing to provide arms, the U.S. government risks complicity in genocide and other serious violations of international law. Human Rights Watch has argued that U.S. arms transfers to Israel constitute unlawful acts under international law and that U.S. military personnel risk responsibility for aiding and assisting Israeli forces. These are allegations by leading human rights organizations, not judicial findings; Israel rejects them, and the U.S. government disputes the characterization. But they illustrate the legal logic: where a supplier continues transfers after being put on notice of systematic violations, the complicity argument becomes more difficult to dismiss.

There are serious counterarguments, and a balanced assessment must state them. First, the U.S. system is consent-based and monitoring-based, not operationally directive. Washington does not select targets or authorize individual strikes. The legal responsibility for how a weapon is used rests primarily with the recipient state, which has its own obligations under international humanitarian law. Second, the United States argues that its end-use monitoring and diplomatic engagement are forms of due diligence. The existence of Golden Sentry, Blue Lantern, congressional notifications, and suspension authorities can be presented as evidence that the United States is not a passive enabler but an active regulator. Third, attribution matters. International law generally attributes conduct to the state that carries it out. Complicity requires a showing that the assisting state knowingly contributed to the specific wrongful act, not merely that its weapons were present in a conflict zone.

The counterarguments are weakened, however, by the gaps in the U.S. monitoring system itself. The Government Accountability Office has found that U.S. end-use monitoring was not designed to identify foreign partners’ violations of transfer agreements regarding use for authorized purposes. As of February 2025, the Defense Department was tracking more than 150 incidents of potential end-use violations, and the State Department’s investigations and reporting have been incomplete. A Pentagon inspector general report found that the United States had failed to properly track significant amounts of military aid to Israel, maintaining records for only 44 percent of defense articles subject to enhanced monitoring at one point. If the monitoring system does not reliably detect misuse, the claim that monitoring constitutes meaningful due diligence becomes harder to sustain. The legal consequence is not automatic. But under the complicity framework, knowledge is the pivotal variable. A state that continues to supply arms after credible, repeated, and public warnings that those arms are being used in violations cannot easily claim ignorance. The more documented the pattern, the stronger the argument that continued transfers constitute knowing assistance to wrongful acts.

Conclusion

The United States is not unique in attaching strings to arms exports. France, the United Kingdom, Germany, Russia, China, Israel, and South Korea all impose, in varying degrees, retransfer restrictions and end-use conditions, and several operate post-shipment verification mechanisms. What distinguishes the U.S. system is its scale, legal formalization, and congressional oversight—not the mere fact that conditions exist. Countries buy American weapons because the package includes strategic alignment, interoperability, financing, availability, and capability that alternatives often cannot match. The restrictions are accepted as part of a broader relationship. On the question of indirect responsibility, the honest answer is that the legal case is strongest where knowledge is clearest and monitoring is weakest. International law does not make arms suppliers automatically liable for every misuse of their weapons. But the complicity principle, codified in the Arms Trade Treaty and reflected in state responsibility doctrine, creates a real obligation of due diligence. When a supplier continues transfers after credible warnings of systematic atrocities, and when its own monitoring system is not designed to catch the relevant violations, the gap between formal conditions and effective control becomes a gap in accountability. The strings are real. The question is whether they are pulled tightly enough to matter.

Sources

This report draws on statements by Amnesty International USA and Human Rights Watch on U.S. arms transfers to Israel; reports by the U.S. Government Accountability Office on end-use monitoring and arms transfer violations; findings by the U.S. Department of Defense Inspector General as reported; French final-use and non-retransfer certificate requirements; UK export licensing and international humanitarian law risk assessment rules; the German post-shipment control framework; Russian end-use and post-shipment verification provisions; Chinese end-user certification rules and assessments of enforcement limitations; the Israeli Defense Export Control Law framework; South Korean end-user certification and retransfer consent requirements; analyses of the factors driving foreign purchases of U.S. defense equipment; Article 16 of the International Law Commission’s Articles on State Responsibility; the Arms Trade Treaty’s complicity provisions; and congressional and advocacy statements on U.S. complicity in Yemen.

"The strong do what they can, and the weak suffer what they must." - Thucydides, "History of the Peloponnesian War"

Dictator Kim Jong-un, who didn't mince words and unleashed a torrent of harsh words and insults against Trump in 2017. 

At the beginning of his first presidential term, Trump called Kim Jong-un a "rocket man" and "madman," and later, "short and fat," to which Kim responded with insults. 

Kim received a huge barrage of insults after threatening to completely destroy the DPRK. Kim Jong-un, as an Asian with an excellent education, was very inventive and unrestrained in his verbal sparring with Trump. 

He used sophisticated, vivid, and accurate insults against him: "imbecile and madman," "psychotic, senile old man," "poisonous mushroom," "worm," "gangster," "executioner," "rabid dog." Moreover, the insults were not delivered all at once, but in various speeches by Kim and in writing on Twitter.

The DPRK press launched a campaign against the US president, making him the target of humiliating personal remarks. Although, in the DPRK, insulting the leader of the country and members of his family is punishable by death.

And the DPRK, although a poor, hungry, and insignificant country in every respect, a dictatorship of an autocratic ruler, despised by the civilized world, knows that it can always threaten a nuclear strike against anyone who encroaches on its country. 

Therefore, he himself decides whether to meet with Trump at the APEC summit now or not. This is where Trump's patience is extremely surprising, as he has repeatedly tried to send letters to Kim Jong-un to resume dialogue, but DPRK diplomats refused to accept them. 

Moreover, Trump was not offended, but said that the DPRK behaved "non-threateningly" and "respectfully" towards him in 2017, and offered Kim to make peace with the US.

Now, when the relationship between Trump and Kim has become unexpectedly warm, personal, and friendly, although they have gone from a state of harsh confrontation to direct negotiations and mutual sympathy, Trump wants to meet with Kim at the APEC summit. 

He wants to discuss with him the issue of denuclearization of the DPRK and to solidify it as a victory over the "arrogant fat man." 

In return, Trump promises to reduce the US military contingent in South Korea and reduce military aid to it. But Kim is adamant. 

He says that he will never give up nuclear weapons, that he doesn't care about Trump's threats, that "the world already knows what the United States does after it forces a country to give up nuclear weapons" - and cites Ukraine as an example.

In general, Pyongyang is not dependent on the United States, and the country is not interested in Trump if he does not recognize peaceful coexistence with a nuclear DPRK. 

Kim is unlikely to agree to any agreements with Trump without receiving some serious benefit from it. And a serious benefit will undermine Trump's position even more than it will give him something he could present as a victory.

And China is not interested in the US having a separate track of negotiations with the DPRK. For China, a DPRK that is dependent on it is more convenient. And all issues Trump must resolve with Xi, as his word must be decisive.

"To show a senile old man, who does not understand the meaning of words and repeats only his own words, through actions - that is the best option."
- Kim Jong-un

Whether Kim will meet with Trump at the APEC summit and where - is a closely guarded secret to avoid backlash from the West.

🚩Agniveer extension: use the two years provided to fix the scheme

(Thought provoking Article which says that the Union Cabinet changed the terms of the exit of Agniveers. The 75% not retained in regular service may now opt for a "second tour of duty" of two more years, with enhanced pay and Seva Nidhi. At the end of six years, those who wish to stay will be considered for regular enrolment, subject to objective selection criteria.But a deferral is not a solution: The extension changes the date of the prob lem, not its nature. Enrolment after six years is a consideration, not a guaran tee.India must move from term-end uncertainty to career predictability to make the plan sustainable.The nation asked these young Indians for four years, and now asks for six. They gave us their youth, and some of them gave everything.The Agniveers have delivered. Now it is the nation's turn )

On 4 November, barely three weeks before the first Agniveers were due to hand back their uniforms, the Union Cabinet changed the terms of their exit. The 75% not retained in regular service may now opt for a "second tour of duty" of two more years, with enhanced pay and Seva Nidhi. At the end of six years, those who wish to stay will be considered for regular enrolment, subject to objective selection criteria.

Media debates have split into tWO camps, calling the move a masterstroke or a U-turn. Both miss the point.

The armed forces have just paid the Agniveer the highest compliment an institution can by concluding that they cannot afford to let him go,

The most expensive academy in the sworld: No institution in India trains young people people the the way v the armed forces do. The classroom is a glacier at 20,000 feet, a bunker on the Line of Control, or the deck of a warship. The examinations are real, and mistakes return home in body bags. In October 2023, Agniveer Gawate Akshay Laxman died on the Sia chen Glacier, the first Agniveer to lay down his life in the line of duty. In May 2025, Agniveer Murali Naik was killed by cross-border shelling during Operation Sindoor. The nation has paid dearly for this academy: in pay, equipment and lives. In return, the Agniveers carry what no corporate leadership programme  replicate: discipline under exhaustion, responsibility for a comrade, irreversi ble decisions made on incomplete information. After four years, the Chief of Defence Staff called the feedback. "very positive," and the services wisely decided that this capital was too valua ble to lose,

But a deferral is not a solution: The extension changes the date of the prob lem, not its nature. Enrolment after six years is a consideration, not a guaran tee. Some will not qualify. Others will choose to leave, India will face the same exit in 2028, and the stakes will be higher.

An Agniveer who left at 22 could still start over, enrol in college or sit for competitive examinations alongside his peers. At 24 to 27, he will have lost the years in which his peers finished degrees and started careers. Many will have families to support. Every extra year in uniform raises the cost of a bad landing.

For generations, in the villages of Haryana, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, a son in the army settled his fam-ily for life, through 20 years of service and a pension. The army was the rural middle class's most reliable socioeco nomic ladder. Agnipath rewrote that covenant, and the feeder villages. noticed. By 2024, a Rohtak coaching centre that once prepared 200-250 aspirants for army rallies had 15-20. The extension buys time. Only an assured landing will restore the covenant.

An army gets the best talent only when service is seen as a launchpad, not a dead end. The US understood this in 1944. The GI Bill sent 7.8 million veter-ans to college or vocational training. whose ranks produced Nobel laureates, Pulitzer Prize winners and Supreme Court justices. The programme cost about S1-4 billion and paid for itself in higher taxes within 20 years. It was not spending. It was investment. A 17-year-old in Jhunjhunu will not read the cabinet note. He will watch the

Agniveer from his village who is dis charged in 2028. If that young man is working, studying and respected, the boy will queue at the recruitment rally. If he is idle and his potential squan-dered, the boy will queue at the pass port office. Good rehabilitation creates suction. Poor rehabilitation creates. repulsion.

Two years to build the bridge: Quotas alone will not do it. The home ministry has reserved 50% of paramilitary con stable vacancies for ex-Agniveers. But in 2021, against a 10% reservation in cen tral government Group C posts, ex-ser vicemen held just 1.3%. That gap was tolerated for decades because those sol diers drew a pension. For an Agniveer without one, the same gap would be the scheme's death knell.

The larger opportunity is in the private sector. Corporate India spends heavily to teach young hires resilience, teamwork and ownership. The Agniv eer arrives with all three, and the employer pays nothing for that training. Seizing it needs a structured bridge, and two years is enough time to build one, if the work begins now.

First, the second tour must earn a credential. Every Agniveer should leave in 2028 with a recognized degree or diploma earned during service. Second, every exit must come with a job offer, a college seat or a funded plan in hand, Third, the reserve must actually exist: registered, reachable and periodically retrained. Fourth, large employers must commit to annual hiring numbers, published and audited like corporate social responsibility spending. Finally, the family of an Agniveer who dies in ser vice must never feel the nation values. that life less. On this, the extension is silent. Murali Naik's mother has had to go to court for a family pension.

The nation asked these young Indians for four years, and now asks for six. They gave us their youth, and some of them gave everything.

The Agniveers have delivered. Now it is the nation's turn.

text:
Why Thomas Jefferson Is Our Greatest President

For decades, major surveys of historians and political scientists, including the Siena College Research Institute polls, the C-SPAN Historians Survey, and the Presidential Greatness Project, have graded every president on categories like crisis leadership, economic management, and moral authority. Across these polls, Thomas Jefferson almost always lands in fourth or fifth place, sitting behind Abraham Lincoln, George Washington, Franklin D. Roosevelt, and often Theodore Roosevelt.

That consensus misses the single most important measure of presidential greatness: the impact on the American people. When judged by raw, foundational reach and a lasting influence that spans every generation and still shapes everyday life today, Jefferson does not belong in fourth or fifth place. He stands alone at number one, and no other president even comes close.

Consider the monumental achievements of those other leaders. George Washington led the Continental Army to victory and anchored the survival of the new republic. Abraham Lincoln preserved the Union through the furnace of the Civil War, and Franklin D. Roosevelt steered the nation through the Great Depression and World War II. Largely shaped by the crises of their times, those triumphs were extraordinary. Each of those leaders responded brilliantly to save the nation during an urgent, specific emergency.

Saving a house from a fire is heroic, yet drawing the blueprint, pouring the foundation, and raising the walls are what make a great nation even possible and worth saving in the first place. That requires a level of intelligence, foresight, and political savvy that few presidents possess. Jefferson's influence is not confined to a single war or economic emergency. It is architectural and built to drive the future.

Because his presidency served as the executive culmination of the democratic blueprint he spent his life building, his achievements before, during, and after his time in office form one continuous foundation that defines our country best and makes him the most American president. Simply put, Thomas Jefferson is synonymous with America. As the historian James Parton famously observed, "If Jefferson was wrong, America is wrong. If America is right, Jefferson was right."

At the core of that foundation was a revolutionary idea that shattered the old world order: self-governance. In the late 18th century, nearly every nation on earth bowed to kings, emperors, or hereditary aristocrats who believed ordinary people were fit only to be ruled. Even among America's founders, powerful elites feared popular democracy and fought to keep authority locked in the hands of a wealthy few.

Jefferson crushed that worldview. He insisted that citizens were not helpless infants needing paternal guardians, declaring that the people themselves are the only safe depository of a nation's ultimate power and that public education is the key to sharpening their judgment. The closer power stays to the people, the better. In the Declaration of Independence, he proclaimed the radical truth that governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed. He staked the survival of the United States on his fierce confidence that educated citizens could govern themselves without monarchs or masters, launching a democratic experiment that permanently altered human history and toppled thrones across the globe.

Skeptics often dismiss Jefferson as an armchair theorist rather than a decisive executive, yet his presidential record destroys that myth. Rather than micromanaging like a monarch, he commanded through disciplined, collaborative leadership, empowering top minds like Secretary of State James Madison and Treasury Secretary Albert Gallatin to shape policy before bringing final decisions to him. He held his administration to one uncompromising rule: the sole object of good government is to protect human life and secure the happiness of its citizens.

That clarity produced staggering results, supported by strict personal integrity. In 1803, he seized the Louisiana Purchase for $15 million, doubling the size of the United States overnight through peaceful diplomacy rather than military conquest, and dispatched Meriwether Lewis and William Clark to chart the continent through treaty-making and scientific discovery. Even while financing that continental expansion, he slashed the national debt by more than 30 percent, wiped out every federal internal tax, and left the presidency with zero scandals, sacrificing his family finances rather than ever enriching himself in public service. He would not even hire his own cousin for a government position out of a self-imposed rule against nepotism.

While critics often charge that Jefferson abandoned his strict-constructionist principles by purchasing the Louisiana Territory without a constitutional amendment, they overlook that his decision reflected careful constitutional counsel rather than hypocrisy. Jefferson initially drafted an amendment to authorize the deal and circulated it to his cabinet, consulting directly with his Secretary of State, James Madison, the primary architect of the Constitution. Madison advised that the treaty-making power already implied the authority to acquire new territory. When the Father of the Constitution assures you the power is there, few can argue otherwise. Meanwhile, urgent intelligence warned that Napoleon was experiencing seller's remorse and might revoke the offer if ratification dragged on. Faced with a fleeting opportunity to secure the Mississippi River and eliminate a European empire on America's doorstep, Jefferson heeded Madison's counsel and submitted the treaty directly to the Senate for swift ratification.

His resolve extended just as forcefully to foreign affairs. While European empires bled each other dry in the Napoleonic Wars, Jefferson kept the United States out of continental war and economically surging. Yet peace never meant weakness, and he refused to tolerate maritime extortion when even naval superpowers like Great Britain and France paid regular tribute and ransoms to the Barbary states to protect their merchant ships. When Tripoli demanded higher tribute payments in 1801, Jefferson answered with steel instead of gold, sending the young Navy and Marines across the Atlantic to blockade and defeat Tripoli's forces. His decisive action forced a peace treaty that ended annual tribute payments to the Barbary state and proved to the world that a free republic would fight to defend its commerce.

Nonetheless, some historians fault Jefferson for shrinking the army and navy, arguing that his budget cuts left the country vulnerable before the War of 1812. In reality, trimming a bloated peacetime military was central to his vision of a debt-free republic safe from domestic tyranny and foreign entanglements. Rather than squandering tax dollars on idle warships, he founded the United States Military Academy at West Point in 1802 to cultivate a professional officer corps and freed up the financial resources needed to deploy decisive force abroad, making his successful campaign against the Barbary pirates possible without bankrupting the treasury. His disciplined approach relieved the nation of crippling debt while building the institutional foundation for future defense.

Even his most controversial decision, the Embargo Act of 1807, was a calculated effort to protect a young, vulnerable nation from a catastrophic war. With Britain and France locked in conflict, both superpowers routinely seized American merchant ships and forced thousands of American sailors into British naval service. Going to war against either empire with a tiny navy and minimal standing army risked national ruin, while submitting to foreign decrees meant surrendering American independence. Instead, Jefferson chose peaceful economic pressure, keeping American ships and sailors safely in port while cutting off vital American crops and goods to force European powers to respect neutral rights. Although the measure caused real economic hardship at home, it avoided bloodshed, spurred early American manufacturing, and bought the United States nearly five critical years to strengthen its defenses before the War of 1812.

His commitment to peaceful diplomacy also shaped his approach to Native American nations amid rapid westward expansion. Recognizing that surging settler populations would inevitably push into western lands, Jefferson sought to prevent bloody frontier wars by relying on formal treaties, trade, and voluntary land sales rather than military conquest. He instructed federal agents to respect tribal occupancy rights while encouraging Indigenous communities to adopt settled agriculture and livestock farming, arguing that transitioning from vast hunting grounds to smaller farms would allow tribes to prosper alongside American settlers and voluntarily sell surplus territory. While critics point to later administrations that resorted to forced military expulsions and tragic marches like the Trail of Tears, Jefferson pursued negotiated agreements and peaceful coexistence to manage a volatile frontier without bloodshed. 

Beyond expanding and defending the nation, Jefferson also forged the legal and moral framework of American freedom. Modern critics often reduce his legacy to the contradiction between his ideals and his life as a Virginia slaveholder, ignoring the fact that Jefferson did not invent slavery, nor was he a dictator who could abolish it by decree. The institution had existed across the world for thousands of years and had been entrenched in Virginia for more than a century before he was even born. Against that ancient consensus and apathy, Jefferson represented a bold turning point for humankind, repeatedly drafting legislation and using his public power to attack the system he inherited even when fellow lawmakers refused to supply the votes.

As a young Virginia legislator in 1769, he backed an early effort to legalize freeing enslaved workers, only to see the slaveholding assembly angrily reject it. In 1778, he helped draft and secure the passage of a Virginia law banning the importation of enslaved Africans into the state. In 1784, he wrote an antislavery ban for all western territories that failed in Congress by a single vote, yet laid the groundwork for the 1787 Northwest Ordinance that kept slavery out of the Midwest, and his exact words banning slavery and involuntary servitude were later written directly into the 13th Amendment to abolish slavery nationwide.

Even his contemporaries and political rivals recognized that his anti-slavery convictions were no empty rhetoric. During the 1796 and 1800 presidential campaigns, Southern federalist newspapers and pamphleteers deliberately reprinted Jefferson's condemnations of slavery from Notes on the State of Virginia alongside his gradual emancipation proposals to alarm slaveholders that electing him would endanger their slave property.

Decades later, staunch anti-slavery champion John Quincy Adams likewise attested that ending slavery was "a darling project of Thomas Jefferson from his first entrance into public life to the last years of his existence." Jefferson carried that lifelong commitment into the presidency with executive determination, strategically using his December 1806 message to urge Congress to outlaw the transatlantic slave trade at the earliest constitutional moment. He signed the federal ban into law in March 1807, and it took effect on January 1, 1808, the very first day the Constitution allowed.

Above all, by declaring in the Declaration of Independence that all men are created equal, Jefferson placed a ticking moral time bomb under slavery. He handed Abraham Lincoln and civil rights leaders from Frederick Douglass to Martin Luther King Jr. the exact moral weapon and patriotic cover they needed to destroy the institution and demand equal citizenship.

At the same time, Jefferson actively fortified everyday liberties and built a fiercely democratic political culture. From his post as minister to France, he relentlessly pressured James Madison through letters until Madison agreed to add a Bill of Rights to the Constitution. Upon taking office as president, he saved the First Amendment by immediately pardoning citizens jailed under the Sedition Act for criticizing the government, reinforcing the wall of liberty he had first built through the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom. True to his famous declaration that he would prefer newspapers without a government over a government without newspapers, Jefferson endured relentless, often vicious attacks from opposition editors throughout his presidency without ever prosecuting a single critic, cementing freedom of the press as an untouchable pillar of American democracy.

Following the bitter election of 1800, he engineered the world's first peaceful transfer of executive power between rival political parties, unifying a fractured nation by declaring that we are all republicans and we are all federalists. Eight years later, he cemented the two-term presidential precedent by refusing to run for a third term, explicitly warning that without a strict limit on tenure, the presidency could degenerate into a lifetime monarchy.

That anti-monarchical spirit earned him one of his most enduring nicknames, "Man of the People." Supporters embraced the label during his lifetime to celebrate his devotion to ordinary farmers, everyday citizens, and decentralized self-government. Ironically, his political opponents tried to weaponize the exact same phrase as an insult, with federalist writers warning voters that being a "man of the people" made him a dangerous demagogue. Yet Jefferson turned their attack into a badge of honor, proving that trusting ordinary citizens was the true strength of the republic rather than a threat to it.

He even stripped the presidency of aristocratic pomp so the office would belong entirely to the people. He abolished royal-style ceremonies, walked on foot to and from his own inauguration, and enforced a strict rule of egalitarian seating at White House dinners where guests sat wherever they pleased rather than being ranked by title or social status. That democratic simplicity set the benchmark for future populist leaders, a point Andrew Jackson underscored in 1825 after watching John Quincy Adams escorted to his inauguration with what Jackson dismissed as a "pomp and ceremony of guns & drums." Contrasting that spectacle with Jefferson's unpretentious 1801 induction, Jackson prayed that the nation's leadership would remain "based upon the sovereignty of the people and adorned with no forms or ceremonies save those which their happiness and freedom shall command."

That relentless drive to empower ordinary citizens reshaped the daily mechanics of American life. His 1784 plan for coinage persuaded Congress to establish our decimal currency system of dollars and cents, making the United States the first nation in the world to adopt decimal money. In Virginia, he dismantled feudal inheritance laws like entail and primogeniture so land and wealth could not remain hoarded by a permanent aristocracy.
As the nation's first Secretary of State, he served as the original patent examiner under the Patent Act of 1790, enforcing a 14-year limit on patents so breakthroughs would flow to the public rather than create permanent monopolies. That policy reflected his lifelong devotion to science, which spearheaded a national culture of American ingenuity and objective inquiry. Serving simultaneously as President of the United States and president of the American Philosophical Society, Jefferson championed evidence over superstition, engineered an improved moldboard plow to boost farming, and embraced the smallpox vaccine in 1801, personally vaccinating roughly 200 people and sending the vaccine west with Lewis and Clark.

His devotion to public knowledge and national strength raised permanent institutions and ideas that still anchor the country today. Believing that an educated citizenry was the ultimate safeguard against tyranny, Jefferson drafted a pioneering 1779 bill for tax-funded public primary schools to teach every free child reading, writing, and arithmetic regardless of wealth, laying the philosophical foundation for universal public education in America. When British troops burned the Capitol and destroyed the congressional library in 1814, he sold his personal collection of 6,487 books to Congress, creating the core of the modern Library of Congress. Alongside West Point, which he established to train American engineers and officers, he later designed and founded the University of Virginia to champion public higher education.

Because his breakthroughs transformed every pillar of American life, Jefferson commands an unmatched ideological reach. Across the political spectrum, every major American tradition claims him as its own. Progressives champion his crusade for universal public education, human equality, and his insistence that laws must advance with the progress of the human mind. Conservatives champion his fierce defense of limited federal government, religious liberty, free speech, and fiscal discipline. Moderates rally around his call for national unity and peaceful self-government.

That universal force is why Jefferson stands as the ultimate president's president, respected and studied by every commander in chief who followed him. He directly mentored James Madison and James Monroe, and his political philosophy served as the guiding star for Andrew Jackson and Martin Van Buren. In fact, Jefferson's direct reach touched every single one of the nation's first 12 presidents, from George Washington all the way through Zachary Taylor. He personally knew every president through John Tyler, whose father was Jefferson's college roommate, inspired James K. Polk as a devout Jeffersonian following in the footsteps of his father and grandfather, and even signed Zachary Taylor's first army commission while in the White House. Such was the unstoppable momentum of this ideological influence at America's founding, laying the territorial, democratic, and institutional bedrock that enabled the United States to rise into the world's greatest superpower today.

Even leaders from rival traditions bowed to his stature. George Washington, a famously stoic figure who rarely offered lavish praise, wrote to the Marquis de Lafayette that he had early imbibed the highest opinion of Jefferson. Washington later told Jefferson that no other person could better execute the duties of Secretary of State, urged him not to retire because he could not see where he would find another character to replace him, and insisted even after their political paths diverged that he had never discovered anything in Jefferson's conduct to raise suspicions of insincerity.

Similarly, Theodore Roosevelt, despite his fierce loyalty to Alexander Hamilton, acknowledged to historian Frederick Jackson Turner the inadvisability of taking a negative tone toward Jefferson and praised Jefferson's genius in securing the Louisiana Purchase, which established the United States as the greatest nation of the Western Hemisphere. Speaking before Chicago's Hamilton Club, Roosevelt even admitted that Hamilton lacked the one great quality Jefferson possessed: trust and belief in the people. After all, how could an American president be great without submitting to the will of the people?

More remarkably, generations of opposing contenders battled not to reject Jefferson, but to claim his mantle as their own. In the bitter presidential contests of 1824 and 1828, both John Quincy Adams and Andrew Jackson ran under Jefferson's banner, with Jackson championing Jeffersonian populism and limited government while Adams carried forward his vision for science, internal progress, and national education. A generation later, Abraham Lincoln and Stephen A. Douglas clashed over Jefferson's legacy on the campaign trail, as Douglas appealed to Jefferson's faith in local self-government while Lincoln anchored the Republican Party in Jefferson's Declaration of Independence, declaring that "the principles of Jefferson are the definitions and axioms of free society." In the modern era, opposing standard-bearers Ronald Reagan and Bill Clinton both claimed Jefferson as their guiding inspiration. Reagan invoked Jefferson's warnings against big government and high taxes, while Clinton, who carried Jefferson's name and began his 1992 inaugural journey at Monticello, championed Jefferson's vision of public education and democratic opportunity.

Across every era and party, from Lincoln, Franklin D. Roosevelt, and John F. Kennedy to Nixon, Ford, Carter, Reagan, both Bush presidents, Clinton, Obama, and Biden, commanders in chief have continually drawn strength from his vision. That unbroken chain of reverence continues in the current administration, as President Donald Trump opened his 2026 State of the Union address by celebrating the 250th anniversary of the independence Jefferson authored and closed by proudly invoking Jefferson's name.

Despite wielding more lasting influence over the presidency and the nation than any other leader, Jefferson refused to cling to the trappings of power. When designing his own tombstone, he deliberately left off the title of President because he viewed political office as temporary compared to ideas that liberate the human mind. Instead, Jefferson chose to be remembered for three immortal achievements, serving as author of the Declaration of Independence, author of the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom, and father of the University of Virginia.

Most presidents maintained our freedom, while a few exceptional presidents bravely defended the house of liberty when it caught fire. Yet Jefferson stands alone as the one who drew the plans, laid the stone, strengthened the foundation, expanded the yard, doused fires of his own, and instilled the timeless, empowering principles that modern Americans still live by and cherish today. Just as he once declared, "We are all republicans, we are all federalists," we can now proudly say, "We are all Jeffersonians." Therefore, Thomas Jefferson is the most American president, and that makes him our greatest not only in history, but for our present and future.

text:
You can have the sharpest idea, the best product, or a solution that genuinely changes someone's business or life—and yet, in 2026, you are basically held hostage by platform algorithms, follower counts, and dead inboxes.

Look at the actual numbers on digital outreach right now:

- Across 2M+ cold emails analyzed, the average human reply rate dropped to 0.45%—and the actual "interested" positive reply rate is 0.64% (literally 1 in 157 people).

- Harvard Business Review research proved a face-to-face request is 34 TIMES more successful than an email. Not 34% better. 34x.

- Meanwhile, Stanford research showed people replacing real-world social contact with AI chatbots actually end up more lonely and disconnected, and Gallup's global data found 93% of people report having a close friend in-person vs. just 37% online-only.

Think about how insane that is.

We spend hours crafting "the perfect DM", tweaking cold emails, chasing X impressions, begging LinkedIn algorithms for reach, and prompting AI all day.. just to get ignored by 99.3% of people.

And why? Because everyone's digital attention is completely fried. Mega-texting platforms, Slack pings, and AI-generated noise ruined the signal. You don't need another "growth hack" or another 1,000 automated DMs.

Fuck the impressions. Fuck the endless cold-messaging treadmill.

If you want your ideas, offers, and solutions heard by the right people, here is what actually works:

1- Stop prompting AI, start prompting real humans. AI is a tool, not a dinner table. Real leverage happens when two sharp people sit across from each other, read body language, and build actual trust in 15 minutes instead of 15 weeks of Slack threads.

2- Kill the "audience" dependency. You shouldn't need 50,000 followers or viral luck just to meet someone who needs what you're building—or someone who has the exact answer you're looking for.

3- Switch from message-based to intent-based IRL. Imagine skipping the cold DMs, skipping the small talk, and skipping the algorithm completely—just matching directly on real intent and meeting face-to-face in the real world.

I don't know about you, but I'm both a workaholic on my laptop all day, and also fully in on anything IRL👌
